docs.text:
An open-source watershed model with plain-text inputs and outputs.

Get started What is SWAT+

    Install SWAT+, run the reference dataset, and learn the shape of a project folder.

  • Model theory

docs.title: About this site
docs.text:
This documentation describes SWAT+ revision 62.0.1. Each SWAT+ release has a separate version of the site, chosen with the version selector at the top of the page; latest is the newest.

The pages are written for model users. Every statement about model behaviour has been checked against the Fortran source of the release, and the commit is recorded in each page's front matter. Where the source does something unexpected, the page says what the model does. Source files and variable names are listed in a collapsed Sources block at the end of each page.

The model source is at github.com/swat-model/swatplus. Every page can be downloaded as a PDF, alone or with its section (Download as PDF).

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
SWAT+ can change model parameters from inside the model, using two kinds of calibration data.

Hard data are measured time series at a point, such as daily streamflow at a gauge, sediment or nutrient loads, or groundwater levels. Fitting the model to hard data is done by an external tool (SWAT+ Toolbox, SWAT-CUP, a script) that writes a parameter change list to calibration.cal, runs SWAT+, compares the output with the observations and repeats. SWAT+ applies the change list at start-up, before the simulation begins.

Soft data are estimates of individual processes that are not measured at the site, or only as long-term averages: the share of precipitation that leaves as surface runoff or evapotranspiration, the baseflow share of streamflow, or an average county crop yield (Seibert and McDonnell, 2002; Arnold et al., 2015). SWAT+ fits these itself. After the normal run it adjusts a few water balance and plant parameters one at a time, rerunning the simulation after each change, until the average annual values for each land-use group match the targets.

The usual order is soft calibration first, so that each part of the water balance is about right, then hard calibration against the gauge record, which should then need mostly adjustments to peaks and recessions.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A row of calibration.cal can be followed by condition lines. SWAT+ then changes the parameter only on the objects that meet every condition of the row. Conditions are checked once, at start-up, against the state of each object after the inputs are read.

Conditions and object lists are the two ways to calibrate parts of a watershed separately, for example one set of curve number changes for cropland and another for forest, or different groundwater parameters upstream and downstream of a gauge.

docs.title: Condition lines
docs.text:
The number of condition lines is given in the conds column of the change row, and the lines follow the row directly. Each line has one of two forms.

Range condition

range  <variable>  <min>  <max>

The object's value must be greater than <min> and less than <max>.

Text condition

<variable>  <operator>  <number>  <text>

The object's value must equal <text>. All four values must be present. The operator and number are read but none of the existing conditions uses them, so any placeholder works (for example = and 0).

When a row has several condition lines, an object must meet all of them.

docs.title: Condition variables
docs.text:
Variable Form Objects Condition met when cal_group text HRU the cal_group of the HRU's land use in landuse.lum equals the text landuse text HRU the HRU's land use name (the lu_mgt entry of hru-data.hru) equals the text hsg text HRU the hydrologic soil group of the HRU's soil (hyd_grp in soils.sol) equals the text, for example C texture text HRU the texture of the HRU's soil in soils.sol equals the text plant text HRU the first plant of the HRU's plant community is the named plant pl_class text see below res_typ text reservoir decision table the decision table's name equals the text res_pvol range reservoir the principal spillway volume, in 10⁴ m³ (ha-m, as in hydrology.res), is between <min> and <max>

The HRU conditions apply to parameters whose object type is hru, sol or plt. They compare against the HRU with the same number as the object being changed, so with other object types (aquifers, channels) they test an unrelated HRU.

Text comparisons are exact and case sensitive, and an unknown variable name is ignored, so a misspelt condition lets every object through.

Notes on specific variables:

  • plant: only the first plant in the community is checked. For a community of corn and soybean in that order, plant = corn matches and plant = soyb does not. For the plant parameters lai_pot, harv_idx and phu_mat the plant condition has a second role: it names the plant whose value is changed (see Plant parameters).
  • pl_class: compares the class of the plant at the same position in plants.plt as the object number. It does not look at the HRU's plants, so it is not useful for selecting HRUs.
  • res_pvol: both limits are taken from the last range line of the row.

docs.title: Calibration groups
docs.text:
The most direct way to calibrate regions or land-use groups separately is the cal_group column of landuse.lum:

  1. Give each land use a group name in cal_group, for example crop_north, crop_south, forest. Land uses that share a name form one group.
  2. Write one change row per group, each with a cal_group condition.
cn2      pctchg   -8.0   1   0  0  0  0  0  0   0
cal_group  =  0  crop_north
cn2      pctchg    4.0   1   0  0  0  0  0  0   0
cal_group  =  0  forest

The same cal_group names are used by soft calibration to match its water balance targets to HRUs.

docs.title: Object lists
docs.text:
The other way is to list the objects in the row itself (obj_tot and the numbers after it), for example the HRUs, aquifers or channels upstream of a gauge. A negative number closes a range, so 3 1 -120 245 selects objects 1 to 120 and 245. Object lists work for every object type.

Object lists and conditions can be combined: the conditions are then checked only on the listed objects.

docs.title: Scheduled land use updates
docs.text:
SWAT+ also reads a file named scen_dtl.upd from the project folder, if it exists. It lists decision tables from the scenario decision table file (scen_lu.dtl by default, named on the decision_table line of file.cio) that are checked for every HRU at the start of every simulated day. Their actions can change land use, management or other HRU settings during the run, for example to simulate land use change at a set date.

  • Line 1: title.
  • Line 2: number of tables.
  • Line 3: header.
  • One line per table: maximum number of times the table may act, table type, and table name.

The maximum and the type are read but not used in 62.0.1: every listed table is checked every day for every HRU.

This file is separate from calibration.cal. Its changes happen during the run, while calibration.cal changes happen before the run starts. See Decision tables for how tables are written.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Hard calibration fits the model to measured time series such as streamflow, sediment or nutrient loads at a gauge. SWAT+ does not search for parameter values itself. An external tool (SWAT+ Toolbox, SWAT-CUP, a script) picks a set of parameter changes, writes them to calibration.cal, runs SWAT+, compares the output with the observations, and repeats. Each run of SWAT+ applies the changes in calibration.cal once, at start-up, and then simulates the full period with the changed parameters.

The input files are never edited. A change exists only for the run that reads it, so the same TxtInOut folder can be reused for every trial.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Two files, both named on the chg line of file.cio, drive hard calibration:

  • cal_parms.cal lists every parameter that may be changed, the object type it belongs to, and the lowest and highest value it may take. SWAT+ Editor writes this file and it rarely needs editing.
  • calibration.cal is the change list for one run. Each row names a parameter from cal_parms.cal, the type and size of the change, and optionally the objects to change and the conditions they must meet.

If either slot is null or the file is missing, no changes are applied. The column layouts and the full list of parameter names are on Parameter change files.

docs.title: Run sequence
docs.text:
1. SWAT+ reads all input files and sets up every object (HRUs, soils, plants, channels, aquifers, reservoirs).
  2. It reads cal_parms.cal and calibration.cal.
  3. For each row of calibration.cal, in file order, it goes through the listed objects (all objects of that type when none are listed), checks the row's conditions for each object, and changes the parameter on every object that meets them.
  4. The simulation runs once with the changed parameters.

Because the changes are applied after the inputs are read and before the first day is simulated, they act for the whole simulation period. The year and day columns of calibration.cal only limit changes to the precipitation and temperature records (see Climate changes).

Rows are applied in order, and a later row for the same parameter acts on the value left by the earlier row. Two pctchg rows of 10 for cn2 give a 21 % increase.

docs.title: Change types
docs.text:
Type New value Example (current value 70, change 5) absval the change value replaces the current value 5 abschg current value + change 75 pctchg current value × (1 + change / 100) 73.5 relchg current value × (1 + change) 420

After every change the result is limited to the range abs_min to abs_max given for that parameter in cal_parms.cal. Use one of the four types; any other text in the change type column gives an undefined value.

docs.title: Object types
docs.text:
The obj_typ column of cal_parms.cal tells SWAT+ which objects a parameter belongs to. When a row of calibration.cal lists no objects, every object of that type is changed.

Type Objects changed when none are listed Example parameters hru every HRU cn2, esco, epco, perco, lat_ttime, canmx sol every HRU, in the soil layers from lyr1 to lyr2 awc, k, bd, usle_k plt see Plant parameters lai_pot, harv_idx, phu_mat hlt every HRU of the simplified hru-lte type cn2_lte, awc_lte aqu every aquifer alpha, revap_co, flo_min sdc every channel chn, chk, bank_exp swq every channel nutrient parameter set rs1, bc1, mumax res every reservoir k_res, evrsv, nsed rdt every reservoir decision table drawdown_days, withdraw_rate bsn the basin (applied once) surlag, cdn, nperco gwf every gwflow cell aquifer_K, aquifer_Sy gwf_riv every channel connected to gwflow stream_K, stream_thk gwf_sgl applied once stream_bed, reservoir_K cli see Climate changes precip, temp

docs.title: Soil layers
docs.text: For sol parameters, lyr1 and lyr2 in calibration.cal set the first and last soil layer to change. A lyr1 of 0 starts at the top layer, and a lyr2 of 0 or more than the number of layers ends at the bottom layer.

docs.title: Reservoir decision tables
docs.text:
For rdt parameters (drawdown_days, withdraw_rate) the five integer columns after conds select which storage zones of the decision table to change. A non-zero value in the column switches that zone on:

Column Zone lyr1 exclusive flood control storage lyr2 seasonal flood control storage, non-flood season year1 seasonal flood control storage, flood season year2 multiple use storage, non-flood season day1 multiple use storage, second zone

docs.title: Plant parameters
docs.text:
Plant parameters with object type plt are changed in the plant community of each listed HRU, for the plants named in the row's conditions. Only phu_mat, lai_pot and harv_idx are handled this way. Each row needs a condition that names the plant (see Conditions and regionalization); a row without one changes nothing.

Give the HRUs to change in the object list of the row. When the list is empty, SWAT+ goes through as many HRUs as there are plants in plants.plt, starting from HRU 1.

To change epco use object type hru. That changes the HRU value and sets the same value for every plant in the HRU's community. With object type plt, an epco row changes lai_pot instead.

The plant carbon parameters bio_e, hvsti, rdmx, t_opt and t_base are listed with object type plt in the SWAT+ Editor cal_parms.cal. In 62.0.1 rows for these parameters change nothing.

docs.title: Climate changes
docs.text:
Precipitation and temperature records can be changed over a date window with the parameters precip and temp, giving object type cli in cal_parms.cal. The change is applied to every daily value from day day1 to day day2 of each year from year1 to year2 (calendar years, inside the simulation period).

List the records to change in the object list of the row. With no list, nothing is changed. List one record per row. When a row lists several records, the change is applied to every listed record once for each record in the list, so a pctchg of 10 on three records gives a 33 % increase on each. In 62.0.1 temp rows do not change the listed temperature record.

docs.title: Unknown names
docs.text: A row whose name is not in cal_parms.cal, or whose name SWAT+ does not recognise as a parameter, is skipped without a message. Check spelling against the parameter list if a change seems to have no effect.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
cal_parms.cal is the list of parameters that calibration may change: the name of each parameter, the type of object it belongs to, and the lowest and highest value it may take. calibration.cal is the change list for one run: each row picks a parameter from cal_parms.cal, says how to change it, and optionally limits the change to some objects or to objects that meet conditions. How SWAT+ applies the list is described on Hard calibration.

Both files are named on the chg line of file.cio, in the first two positions (defaults cal_parms.cal and calibration.cal). A null name or a missing file switches the change list off.

All values are free format and separated by blanks. Names must not contain blanks.

docs.title: cal_parms.cal
docs.text:
• Line 1: title (skipped).
  • Line 2: number of parameter rows.
  • Line 3: column header (skipped).
  • Then one row per parameter.
# Column Description 1 name Parameter name, as listed under Parameter names. 2 obj_typ Type of object the parameter belongs to: hru, sol, plt, hlt, aqu, sdc, rte, swq, res, rdt, bsn, pst, gwf, gwf_riv, gwf_sgl or cli. It decides which objects are changed when a row of calibration.cal lists none. 3 abs_min Lowest value the parameter may take. Every change is limited to this value. 4 abs_max Highest value the parameter may take. Every change is limited to this value. 5 units Units, for information only.

SWAT+ Editor writes this file with suitable limits for each parameter, and it rarely needs editing. A narrower range for a calibration run belongs in the calibration tool; the range here is the physical limit.

Example from refdata/Osu_1hru in the SWAT+ repository:

cal_parms.cal: written by SWAT+ editor v2.2.0 on 2023-03-22 04:25 for SWAT+ rev.60.5.4
186
name                       obj_typ       abs_min       abs_max             units
cn2                            hru      35.00000      95.00000              null
cn3_swf                        hru       0.00000       1.00000              null
usle_p                         hru       0.00000       1.00000              null
ovn                            hru       0.01000      30.00000              null
elev                           hru       0.00000    5000.00000                 m
slope                          hru       0.00010       0.90000               m/m
slope_len                      hru      10.00000     150.00000                 m
lat_ttime                      hru       0.50000     180.00000              days

The count on line 2 must match the number of rows. Rows past the count are not read.

docs.title: calibration.cal
docs.text:
• Line 1: title (skipped).
  • Line 2: number of change rows.
  • Line 3: column header (skipped).
  • Then one row per change, each followed directly by its condition lines, if it has any.

docs.title: Change rows
docs.text:
# Column Description 1 name Parameter name. Must also be in cal_parms.cal. 2 chg_typ absval (replace), abschg (add), pctchg (percent change) or relchg (relative change). See Change types. 3 val Size of the change. 4 conds Number of condition lines that follow this row. 0 for none. 5 lyr1 First soil layer to change, for sol parameters (0 = top layer). For reservoir decision tables, a zone switch. 6 lyr2 Last soil layer to change, for sol parameters (0 = bottom layer). For reservoir decision tables, a zone switch. 7 year1 First year of the window, for precip and temp. For reservoir decision tables, a zone switch. 8 year2 Last year of the window, for precip and temp. For reservoir decision tables, a zone switch. 9 day1 First day of the year in the window, for precip and temp. For reservoir decision tables, a zone switch. 10 day2 Last day of the year in the window, for precip and temp. 11 obj_tot Number of entries in the object list that follows on the same line. 0 means every object of the parameter's type. 12... object list obj_tot object numbers.

The object numbers are the sequence numbers of the objects (the first HRU is 1, and so on). A negative number closes a range started by the number before it, so obj_tot = 3 with the list 1 -20 35 means objects 1 to 20 and object 35.

docs.title: Condition lines
docs.text:
Each change row is followed by conds condition lines. A condition line has one of two forms:

  • range <var> <min> <max>: the object's value of <var> must lie between <min> and <max>. Only res_pvol is recognised.
  • <var> <alt> <targ> <targc>: a test against the text value <targc>. <alt> and <targ> must be present but are not used by the conditions that exist.

The variables and how they are tested are on Conditions and regionalization.

A row that changes cn2 by +5 only on HRUs 1 to 20 and HRU 35, and only where the hydrologic soil group is C:

hsg         =           0      C

docs.title: Parameter names
docs.text: The names SWAT+ 62.0.1 recognises are listed below with the object type to give in cal_parms.cal and the input the parameter comes from. A name that is in neither list is skipped without a message. Some recognised names have no effect at 62.0.1, or change a different value; the notes with each name say which.

docs.title: Soil layer parameters (sol)
docs.text:
Changed in soil layers lyr1 to lyr2 of each HRU.

Name Input Notes z layer depth dp, soils.sol bd, awc, k bd, awc, soil_k, soils.sol Dependent water contents are recomputed after awc changes. clay, silt, sand, rock clay, silt, sand, rock, soils.sol alb, usle_k, ec, cal, ph alb, usle_k, ec, caco3, ph, soils.sol anion_excl, crk anion_excl, perc_crk, soils.sol Whole profile values. cbn carbon, soils.sol No effect: the soil carbon pools are set up after the change list is applied. lab_p, hum_c_n, hum_c_p lab_p, hum_c_n, hum_c_p, nutrients.sol No effect, for the same reason.

docs.title: Plant parameters (plt)
docs.text:
Changed for the plants named in the row's plant conditions, in the plant community of each listed HRU. See Plant parameters for how to write these rows.

Name Input lai_pot lai_pot, plants.plt harv_idx harv_idx, plants.plt phu_mat heat units to maturity of the plant in the HRU's community, computed at start-up from the plant and the climate

bio_e, hvsti, rdmx, t_opt, t_base and usle_c are recognised names, but rows for them change nothing.

docs.title: Basin parameters (bsn)
docs.text:
Changed once for the whole basin.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A sensitivity analysis shows which parameters change a chosen model result the most, so that calibration can concentrate on them. SWAT+ does not include a sensitivity analysis. It is run by an external tool that writes calibration.cal, runs SWAT+, reads a result from the output files, and repeats for many parameter sets. Each run applies the changes in calibration.cal at start-up and leaves the input files untouched, so one project folder serves every run.

SWAT+ Toolbox does this from a graphical interface. The steps below are what any tool or script has to do.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Choose the parameters to test and a range for each. The names are those on Parameter names. The abs_min and abs_max values in cal_parms.cal are physical limits; a narrower range around reasonable values usually gives more useful results.
  2. Generate the samples: use a sampling design that matches the analysis method: Sobol (Saltelli sampling), FAST, Morris (elementary effects), Latin hypercube with one-at-a-time changes (LH-OAT), and so on. Each sample is one set of parameter values. Libraries such as SALib (Python) or sensitivity (R) provide both the sampling and the analysis.
  3. For each sample, write calibration.cal with one row per parameter, run SWAT+ in the project folder, and compute the result of interest: total or peak flow at an outlet, a performance measure against observations (NSE, KGE, percent bias), a sediment or nutrient load.
  4. Compute the indices: pass the sample matrix and the vector of results to the analysis method: first-order and total-order indices for Sobol and FAST, mean and spread of elementary effects for Morris.

The runs are independent, so they can be spread over several processor cores, each in a separate copy of the project folder. Sample sizes of several hundred to a few thousand runs are common.

docs.title: Writing calibration.cal
docs.text:
A sample with three parameters, written as relative and absolute changes:

sensitivity sample 17
3
NAME     CHG_TYP     VAL   CONDS  LYR1  LYR2  YEAR1  YEAR2  DAY1  DAY2  OBJ_TOT
cn2      pctchg    -6.2    0      0     0     0      0      0     0     0
esco     absval     0.71   0      0     0     0      0      0     0     0
alpha    absval     0.048  0      0     0     0      0      0     0     0

Points to watch:

  • pctchg scales each object's current value, so HRUs keep their differences. absval sets every object to the same value.
  • Every parameter name must also be in cal_parms.cal, and its limits there still apply. A sample value outside abs_min to abs_max is cut to the limit, which flattens the response near the edges.
  • A misspelt name is skipped without a message. Check a first run by comparing two extreme samples before starting the full set.
  • Some parameter names have no effect in 62.0.1, or work only with restrictions; see the notes on Parameter change files and Hard calibration before including them.

docs.title: Reading results
docs.text: Daily channel output is in channel_sd_day.txt (or .csv), with flow out of each channel in the flo_out column (m³/s). Switch on only the output the analysis needs in print.prt; writing every file for thousands of runs costs a lot of time and disk space. The output files are described in the Output Reference.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Soft calibration adjusts a small set of HRU and plant parameters until the simulated average annual water balance and crop yields match targets given for each land-use group. The targets are soft data: regional estimates such as the fraction of precipitation that leaves as surface runoff or evapotranspiration, the share of streamflow that is baseflow, or an average county yield. They are not time series.

Soft calibration runs inside the normal swatplus executable. After the base simulation ends, SWAT+ changes one parameter at a time and reruns the whole simulation period after each change. Each rerun is labelled on screen (first esco adj, cn3_swf adj, epco adj, and so on). A water balance calibration adds up to 17 full simulations in mode a and 20 in mode b, and plant calibration up to 13 more. The calibrated values are written to new files (see Output files); the model inputs are left unchanged.

In 62.0.1 two components work: the HRU water balance (hyd switch) and crop yield (plnt switch). The other switches are read, but they do not adjust anything. The status column of the switch table gives the detail for each.

docs.title: Run sequence
docs.text:
1. At start-up SWAT+ reads the seven soft calibration files. A missing file, or a null name in file.cio, gives an empty table and that part is skipped. Without codes.sft soft calibration is off.
  2. Any changes in calibration.cal are applied (see Hard calibration), so soft calibration starts from the changed values.
  3. The base simulation runs as usual. At the end of each simulated year every HRU's annual water balance is added to its land-use group, and each harvest adds its yield to the plant targets.
  4. If any switch in codes.sft is on, soft calibration runs next. It first sets the print.prt codes back to their defaults, which are mostly off, and turns on the average annual basin water balance. The warm-up period (nyskip) is kept. Most output files therefore contain the base run, and basin_wb_aa.txt gains a record for each calibration run.
  5. Each adjustment step changes one parameter for every HRU in each land-use group that is outside its tolerance, restores the starting state of the model, and reruns the full period. The steps are listed under Adjustment steps.
  6. The calibrated parameters are written out.

docs.title: Input files
docs.text:
The chg line of file.cio names nine files. The first two are the hard calibration files described in Parameter change files. The last seven belong to soft calibration:

Position on chg line Default name Earlier name Content 3 codes.sft codes.cal component switches 4 wb_parms.sft ls_parms.cal limits for the water balance parameters 5 water_balance.sft ls_regions.cal water balance targets by land-use group 6 ch_sed_budget.sft ch_orders.cal channel erosion targets 7 ch_sed_parms.sft ch_parms.cal limits for the channel parameters 8 plant_parms.sft pl_parms.cal plant parameter start values and limits 9 plant_gro.sft pl_regions.cal crop yield targets

A file is only read when its name is on the chg line. A project written by SWAT+ Editor 4.0.1 can contain the .sft files while their names on the chg line are null. In that case edits to the files have no effect.

All files are free format. Values are separated by blanks, and names must not contain blanks or slashes. The first line of every file is a title and is skipped.

docs.title: codes.sft
docs.text:
• Line 1: title.
  • Line 2: header.
  • Line 3: eight one-letter switches in the order below.
# Column Values Status in 62.0.1 1 hyd n, a, b, y Works. a and b select the mode; y behaves as b. 2 landscape n, y Not usable. It is meant for simplified (hru-lte) HRUs, but its target table is never set up. 3 plnt n, y Works, crop yield targets only. 4 sed n, y Not usable, see Upland sediment. 5 nut n, y Nothing is calibrated. Setting y starts the soft calibration runs and changes nothing. 6 ch_sed n, y Channel results are summed, but no parameter is adjusted. 7 ch_nut n, y Nothing is calibrated. 8 res n, y Nothing is calibrated.

Soft calibration runs when hyd is anything other than n or any other switch is y.

Mode a calibrates each water balance component against a separate ratio of precipitation. Mode b uses only the water yield ratio and the baseflow share (wyr and bfr in water_balance.sft) and derives the other targets from them. The steps for each mode are under Adjustment steps.

Example (SWAT+ Editor 4.0.1 layout with hyd set to b):

codes.sft: written by SWAT+ editor v4.0.1 on 2026-09-13 21:18 for SWAT+ rev. 62
hyd           landscape     plnt          sed           nut           ch_sed        ch_nut        res
b             n             n             n             n             n             n             n

docs.title: water_balance.sft
docs.text:
• Line 1: title.
  • Line 2: number of regions.
  • Line 3: header.
  • For each region: a line with the region name and the number of land-use rows. If that number is above zero, a header line follows, then one target row per land-use group.

Use a single region. The HRU list of a region is filled only when the region is named basin or the file has one region, and in both cases the region contains every HRU. A second region gets no HRUs and is not calibrated. HRU areas are taken from ls_unit.ele (the bsn_frac of element i is used for HRU i).

Target rows:

# Column Units Description 1 name none Land-use group. Matched to the cal_group column of landuse.lum. The name basin matches every HRU. 2 surq_rto fraction of precipitation Surface runoff / precipitation. Mode a target for cn3_swf. In mode b the value is replaced when the file is read by wyr × (1 − bfr). 3 latq_rto fraction of precipitation Lateral flow / precipitation. Mode a target for latq_co. In mode b it is replaced by 0.1 × wyr × bfr. 4 perc_rto fraction of precipitation Percolation below the soil profile / precipitation. Mode a target for perco. In mode b it is added to wyr to form the esco target. 5 et_rto fraction of precipitation Actual ET / precipitation. Mode a target for esco and pet_co. Not used in mode b. 6 tileq_rto fraction Read; not used as a target. 7 pet mm Read; not used. 8 sed t/ha Upland sediment yield target for the sed switch. 9 wyr fraction of precipitation Water yield / precipitation. Mode b target for pet_co and esco. 10 bfr fraction of water yield Share of water yield that is baseflow. Mode b only. Converted when the file is read to baseflow / precipitation (wyr × bfr), the target for perco. 11 solp kg/ha Read; not used.

The simulated values are built from the HRU annual water balance (the columns of hru_wb_yr), weighted by HRU area:

  • precipitation: precip
  • surface runoff: surq_gen
  • lateral flow: latq
  • percolation: perc
  • ET: et
  • water yield: surq_gen + latq + perc + qtile
  • baseflow: latq + perc + qtile

An HRU is left out of these sums once it has received more than 10 mm of irrigation in total. Its parameters are still changed with the rest of its group. The ratios in a row are not checked to add up to 1.

Example written by SWAT+ Editor 4.0.1 for revision 62. The row contains mode a ratios. wyr and bfr are zero, so in mode b every target would be zero and nothing would be calibrated.

water_balance.sft: written by SWAT+ editor v4.0.1 on 2026-09-13 21:18 for SWAT+ rev. 62
1
name                   num
basin                    1
    name                  surq_rto      latq_rto      perc_rto        et_rto     tileq_rto           pet           sed           wyr           bfr          solp
    basin                  0.20000       0.10000       0.10000       0.50000       0.00000       0.90000       0.00000       0.00000       0.00000       0.00000

docs.title: wb_parms.sft
docs.text:
• Line 1: title.
  • Line 2: number of rows.
  • Line 3: header.
  • Then one row per parameter: name chg_typ neg pos lo up.

SWAT+ uses the rows by position and does not look at name or chg_typ. Keep the ten rows in the order below; renaming or reordering them changes which limits each step uses.

Row name Parameter changed Used by How it is changed 1 cn2 curve number of simplified HRUs landscape switch; pos is also used by the sed switch added 2 esco esco in hydrology.hyd modes a and b added 3 latq_co latq_co in hydrology.hyd modes a and b added 4 petco pet_co in hydrology.hyd modes a and b multiplied 5 slope HRU slope sed switch subtracted 6 tconc time of concentration sed switch divided 7 etco ET coefficient of simplified HRUs landscape switch added 8 perco perco in hydrology.hyd modes a and b added 9 revapc revap coefficient of simplified HRUs landscape switch added 10 cn3_swf cn3_swf in hydrology.hyd, with the curve numbers recomputed modes a and b added

For the HRU water balance rows (2, 3, 4, 8, 10):

  • neg and pos limit the adjustment made for one land-use group. For petco they limit the multiplier (Editor default 0.54 to 1.85). A group that reaches a limit is flagged, and some later runs skip it.
  • lo and up bound the HRU parameter value after every change.

Mode b narrows the petco range for its first PET step. It halves neg and pos and moves lo and up halfway toward 1, then restores the full range for the second PET step. See Limits in 62.0.1 for what this does with the Editor defaults.

cn3_swf and perco are not changed on tile-drained HRUs. At start-up those HRUs are set to cn3_swf = 0.95 and perco = 0.1.

esco                        abschg      -1.00000       1.00000       0.00000       1.00000
latq_co                     abschg      -1.00000       1.00000       0.00000       1.00000

docs.title: plant_gro.sft
docs.text:
• Line 1: title.
  • Line 2: number of regions.
  • Line 3: header.
  • For each region:
    • a line with name, the number of plants (lum_num), nspu, and then nspu HRU numbers;
    • if lum_num is above zero, a header line and one target row per plant.

With nspu = 0 the region covers every HRU. Otherwise nspu numbers follow, and a negative number closes a range: with nspu = 3, the list 1 -20 35 means HRUs 1 to 20 and HRU 35. Each HRU belongs to one plant region. plant_parms.sft is read second, so its region assignment is the one that applies.

Target rows:

# Column Units Description 1 name none Plant name. Matched to the plant named in the harvest operation (harv or hvkl in a management schedule, harvest or harvest_kill in a decision table). 2 yield t/ha Target yield. Compared with the total harvested yield divided by the total harvested area over the whole run. 3 npp t/ha Read; not used. 4 lai_mx none Read; not used. 5 wstress none Read; not used. 6 astress none Read; not used. 7 tstress none Read; not used.

docs.title: plant_parms.sft
docs.text:
• Line 1: title.
  • Line 2: number of regions. Region i here is paired with region i of plant_gro.sft.
  • Line 3: header.
  • For each region:
    • a line with name, lum_num, parms and nspu;
    • if lum_num is above zero, a header line and lum_num × parms parameter rows.

Set nspu to 0 here, which puts every HRU in the region. With nspu above zero the region line is read a second time without the parms field, so the HRU list is misread.

Set parms to 4. The rows form four blocks of lum_num rows each, in this order: pest_stress, epco, lai_pot, harv_idx. Within every block the plants must be in the same order as in the matching plant_gro.sft region. SWAT+ finds a row by its position in the block and always runs all four steps.

Parameter rows:

# Column Description 1 var pest_stress, epco, lai_pot or harv_idx 2 name plant name 3 init_val start value, applied when the file is read to every plant of that name in the region's HRUs. This happens whether or not plnt is on. 4 chg_typ read; not used 5 neg lower limit of the adjustment. For epco it is the lowest epco value the calibration may set. 6 pos upper limit of the adjustment. For epco it is the highest epco value the calibration may set. 7 lo lower bound on the plant's value 8 up upper bound on the plant's value

docs.title: ch_sed_budget.sft and ch_sed_parms.sft
docs.text:
These two files are read, but no channel parameter is adjusted.

ch_sed_budget.sft layout:

  • Line 1: title.
  • Line 2: number of regions.
  • Line 3: header.
  • For each region: name, the number of target rows (ord_num), nspu and nspu channel numbers (0 means all channels). A header line always follows, then ord_num rows of name chw chd hc fpd.

The row fields are channel widening (mm/yr), downcutting or accretion (mm/yr), headcut advance (m/yr) and floodplain accretion (mm/yr).

ch_sed_parms.sft has the same layout as wb_parms.sft. Only name and chg_typ of its first row are used, and only when writing the channel summary.

The channel results are only summed when ch_sed is the only switch on, and only target rows named basin collect them.

docs.title: Adjustment steps
docs.text:
In every step:

  • The tolerance is the relative difference |target − simulated| / target, taken over the average annual values of the land-use group.
  • A step only reruns the simulation if at least one group is outside tolerance.
  • The first run of a step moves the parameter by a fixed rate. Later runs use a secant estimate from the last two runs.

docs.title: Water balance, mode a
docs.text:
Step Parameter Target compared Tolerance Runs First-run change wb_parms.sft row 1 esco et_rto × precipitation vs simulated ET 1 % 1 + 2 + (target − simulated, mm) / 500 2 2 pet_co same as step 1 1 % 2 multiplied by a ratio near 1 4 3 cn3_swf surq_rto × precipitation vs surq_gen 2 % 1 + 2 − (target − simulated, mm) / 100 10 4 latq_co latq_rto × precipitation vs latq 10 % first run, 5 % after 1 + 1 + 0.0025 × (target − simulated, mm) 3 5 perco perc_rto × precipitation vs perc 5 % 1 + 3 + 0.001 × (target − simulated, mm) 8 6 cn3_swf as step 3 2 % 1 + 2 as step 3 10

For example, with surq_rto = 0.2, 800 mm of precipitation and 120 mm of simulated surface runoff, the target is 160 mm, the difference is 40 mm, and the first cn3_swf run lowers cn3_swf by 0.4.

docs.title: Water balance, mode b
docs.text: Step Parameter Target compared Tolerance Runs 1 pet_co, half range wyr × precipitation vs simulated water yield 1 % 2 2 esco (wyr + perc_rto) × precipitation vs simulated water yield 1 % 1 + 2 3 pet_co, full range as step 1 1 % 2 4 cn3_swf wyr × (1 − bfr) × precipitation vs surq_gen 2 % 1 + 2 5 latq_co 0.1 × wyr × bfr × precipitation vs latq 10 % first run, 5 % after 1 + 2 6 perco wyr × bfr × precipitation vs latq + perc + qtile 5 % 1 + 3 7 cn3_swf as step 4 2 % 1 + 2

docs.title: Crop yield
docs.text:
Each plant's average harvested yield is compared with its plant_gro.sft target:

  1. Aeration stress. If the yield is more than 20 % below target, HRUs growing that plant that have no tile drain and an accumulated aeration stress above 50 get perco = 0.95. One run.
  2. epco, with a 3 % tolerance. The first run sets epco to 1, or to a low value when the yield is more than 10 % above target. Four more runs narrow the interval between 0 and 1. The value is kept within neg and pos of the epco block.
  3. pest_stress, changed by the relative yield error. One run.
  4. lai_pot, 1 LAI unit for every 20 % of yield difference, then secant. 1 + 2 runs.
  5. harv_idx, half the relative yield difference, then secant. 1 + 2 runs.

docs.title: Upland sediment
docs.text:
The sed switch is meant to fit the sed targets by shortening the time of concentration and lowering the HRU slope, with the USLE slope-length factor recomputed. In 62.0.1 it does not work:

  • Its loops run over the number of channel regions instead of the number of water balance regions.
  • Simulated sediment is only summed when hyd is also on.
  • The secant runs always compute a change of zero.

Treat the sed switch as unavailable.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
File Written when Content hydrology-cal.hyd hyd or plnt on One row per HRU with the calibrated hydrology.hyd values, written at the end. plant_parms.cal plnt on Same layout as plant_parms.sft, with init_val updated to the calibrated values and nspu set to 0. hru-out.cal any switch on Header only, except with the landscape switch, which appends the simplified HRU parameters. hru-new.cal hyd on Opened but left empty.

To use the results in later runs, point file.cio at the new files:

  • Use plant_parms.cal as plant_parms.sft. Its init_val values are applied when the file is read, also with plnt = n.
  • Use hydrology-cal.hyd as hydrology.hyd, after the edits in the warning below. Rows are written per HRU under the name of its hydrology.hyd record, so every HRU needs a separate record. The extra 16th column (perco_lim, labelled NOT_USED) is ignored when the file is read.

Converting hydrology-cal.hyd back to an input

Two edits are needed before hydrology-cal.hyd can replace hydrology.hyd:

  • LAT_TTIME contains the value after the start-up conversion, 1 − exp(−1 / days). Read back as an input it is taken as days and converted a second time, which makes lateral flow drain much faster. Put the original lat_ttime values back before using the file.
  • When hyd and plnt are both on, the file contains the title, header and HRU rows twice. Keep only the second set, which is written after plant calibration.

docs.title: Limits in 62.0.1
docs.text:
• Only one water balance region works (see water_balance.sft).
  • wb_parms.sft and plant_parms.sft rows are found by position, so the row order is part of the format.
  • In mode b the first PET step halves neg and pos for petco. With the Editor defaults (0.54, 1.85) the upper limit becomes 0.925. When simulated water yield is too high the step should raise PET; it caps the multiplier at 0.925 and lowers PET instead.
  • plant_parms.sft must use nspu = 0 and parms = 4.
  • The landscape, sed, nut, ch_sed, ch_nut and res switches do not calibrate anything (see codes.sft).
  • Annual sums include the warm-up years, but the averages divide by the printed years only. Target ratios are unaffected because precipitation is treated the same way. The fixed first-run rates, which are in mm, act on values scaled by the same factor.

docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text:
This section is for people working on the SWAT+ Fortran source: building from a clone, running the test suite, and submitting changes back to swat-model/swatplus.

If you only need to run a prebuilt SWAT+ executable, see Install instead.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
• Build with CMake. The build used on every platform: configuration, compilers (gfortran, ifx, ifort), compiler options, debug and release builds.
  • Visual Studio on Windows. Visual Studio 2022 with the Intel oneAPI Fortran compiler: cloning, configuring, and debugging against an input dataset.
  • VS Code Codespaces. Running a SWAT+ build and debug session inside a GitHub Codespaces virtual instance. Useful when you do not want to install a Fortran toolchain locally.
  • Testing. The scenario regression test that compares model output with reference outputs, and how to run it at 62.0.1.
  • Tagging and releases. How the version number comes from the Git tag and reaches the executable, and how a release is made.
  • Coding conventions. Fortran 90/95 style rules for SWAT+ source contributions: portability, readability, reliability, arrays, I/O, and obsolescent features to avoid.
  • Contributing. Reporting problems, pull requests, and contributing to this documentation.
  • Code of conduct. The Contributor Covenant, applied to the SWAT+ project community.

docs.title: Build with CMake
docs.text:
SWAT+ is built out of source: all intermediate and final files go into a build folder, so the source tree stays clean and several builds (different compilers, debug and release) can exist side by side.

The build is defined in CMakeLists.txt at the root of the repository. It compiles every .f90 file in src/ into one executable.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• CMake 3.22 or newer
  • a Fortran compiler: gfortran, Intel ifx, or Intel ifort (ifort is no longer included in Intel oneAPI from the 2025 release on)
  • Git, which the build uses to find the version number. Configuration stops if Git is not installed; in a copy of the source that is not a Git clone (a downloaded archive), the version becomes unknown.
  • make or Ninja

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
From the swatplus folder:

cmake -B build -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

This writes the build system into build/ without compiling anything. Give a build type: Release for an optimized executable, Debug for one with run-time checks and debugger symbols. Without a build type neither the optimization nor the debug flags are added.

To choose the compiler:

cmake -B build -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -D CMAKE_Fortran_COMPILER=gfortran
cmake -B build -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -D CMAKE_Fortran_COMPILER=ifx

On Windows, configure from the Intel oneAPI command prompt to use the Intel compilers, or use Ninja with gfortran:

cmake -B build -D CMAKE_GENERATOR_TOOLSET=fortran=ifx
cmake -B build -G "Ninja" -D CMAKE_Fortran_COMPILER=gfortran -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

CMakePresets.json also defines debug and release presets for gfortran (Linux, Windows, macOS), ifx and ifort; list them with cmake --list-presets.

docs.title: Compile
docs.text:
cmake --build build -j 8

The executable is written to build/ as

swatplus-<version>-<compiler>-<system>_<arch>[-Rel|-Dbg][.exe]

for example swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-lin_x86_64-Rel. The compiler part is gnu, ifx or ifo (Intel Fortran Classic), and the version comes from the Git tag (see Tagging and releases).

To start again from scratch, delete the build folder (rm -rf build, or rd /s /q build in Windows cmd). To remove only the compiled files and keep the configuration:

cmake --build build --target clean

docs.title: Compiler options
docs.text:
Compiler Always Release Debug gfortran (Linux, macOS) free form, no line length limit, implicit none, local variables set to zero, strict rounding -O -Wall -fcheck=all -ffpe-trap=invalid,zero,overflow,underflow -fsignaling-nans gfortran (Windows) as above, plus -fcheck=all and the floating-point traps -O -Wall ifx free form, -fpe0, traceback -O -warn all -O0 -check bounds ifort free form, -fpe0, traceback -O -warn all

From 62.0.1 the gfortran run-time checks and floating-point traps are used only in Debug builds on Linux and macOS. Earlier releases also applied them to Release builds, and those executables could stop with an illegal instruction error on macOS when a system math routine raised a harmless floating-point flag.

docs.title: Linking
docs.text:
• Linux, gfortran: linked statically, except on Arch, Arch-based and Fedora systems, which do not ship the static libgfortran; there the executable needs the gfortran run-time libraries at run time (ldd <executable> lists them).
  • macOS, gfortran: the gfortran, quadmath and gcc run-time libraries are linked statically, so the executable runs on Macs without Homebrew's gcc installed. A fully static macOS executable is not possible.
  • Intel compilers and Windows gfortran: linked statically.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
cmake --install build copies the executable to the root of the source folder, whatever --prefix is given. To put it somewhere else, copy the file from build/ yourself.

Sources
  • CMakeLists.txt: version from git describe --tags (lines 20 to 34), compiler flags (fdialect, fdebug, frelease) and static linking (lines 36 to 100), executable name (SWATPLUS_EXE), install(TARGETS ${SWATPLUS_EXE} DESTINATION RUNTIME DESTINATION ${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}).
  • CMakePresets.json and doc/Building.md.

docs.title: Code of conduct
docs.text:
The SWAT+ project follows the Contributor Covenant. Everyone taking part in the project, in issues, pull requests, reviews and discussions, is expected to follow it.

The full text, including how to report a violation, is in CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md in the source repository.

Sources
  • CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md and doc/code_of_conduct.md at 62.0.1.

docs.title: Fortran coding conventions
docs.text:
Conventions for writing SWAT+ Fortran source. The goal is portable, readable and reliable code that compiles cleanly on every supported compiler and operating system.

Each item is tagged with one of three levels:

  • Required: mandatory. Pull requests that violate these will not be merged.
  • Recommended: strongly preferred. Deviations need justification.
  • Encouraged: optional. Apply for consistency where reasonable.

The list below is ordered by decreasing impact on code quality. Most subjective style items (indent width, capitalization) are in the lower tiers.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Source must conform to the ISO Fortran 95 standard.
  • No compiler-specific or platform-specific extensions.
  • No use of compiler-dependent error specifier values (IOSTAT, STAT).
  • The source must compile with gfortran from GCC, even if the production build uses the Intel compiler.
  • EXIT(N) is the F90/95 standard exit. Prefer it to STOP. STOP does not always return an error code. If you need an error code passed back to a script, use EXIT, and keep its call sites in one central place.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text:
• For floating-point precision and integer size, use the F90/95 KIND feature. Do not depend on a vendor-supplied default precision flag.
  • Do not use tab characters. Tabs are not part of the Fortran character set and break portability.

docs.title: Encouraged
docs.text: • For code that interacts with external frameworks, declare every variable with a KIND type to make integration easier.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Free-form source.
  • Consistent indentation, at least two spaces per level.
  • Organize source into modules.
  • Do not use Fortran keywords (DATA, etc.) as variable names.
  • Use meaningful names for variables and parameters. Recognized abbreviations are fine when full names would be unwieldy.
  • Every externally-called function or subroutine has a header describing what it does, its arguments, and the author. Small internal routines can use a few descriptive comments instead.
  • No magic numbers. Physical constants (pi, gas constants) go in PARAMETER statements, not hard-coded into expressions.
  • Do not hard-code numeric literals in argument lists. The compiler's default precision for literals is not guaranteed.
  • No GOTO. If you must use one, document why.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text:
• Name your loops and other constructs (subroutines, functions, modules, interfaces) where the name aids readability, especially in nested loops.
  • Comment input, output, and local variables. Grouping comments across similar variables is fine when their names speak for themselves.
  • Comment to mark major functional sections.
  • Do not use Fortran statement names or intrinsic function names as symbols.
  • Prefer named parameters over numeric literals: REAL, PARAMETER :: PI = 3.14159, ONE = 1.0.

docs.title: Encouraged
docs.text:
• In new code, follow a consistent style. When editing existing code, match the style around you.
  • Indent comments the same way as code.
  • Group related procedures and data into modules.
  • Keep lines to 132 characters or fewer.
  • Use <, >, <=, >=, ==, /= instead of .lt., .gt., .le., .ge., .eq., .ne..
  • Name modules the same as the file that contains them. Avoid putting multiple modules in one file.
  • Use blanks around operators, around =, and in declarations to separate syntax elements.
  • Always use the :: notation in declarations, even when there are no attributes.
  • Line up attributes, variable names, and trailing comments vertically in declarations.
  • Remove unused variables.
  • Remove debug code once the bug is fixed.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• IMPLICIT NONE in every program, module, and procedure.
  • Use PRIVATE in modules by default, then explicitly mark what should be PUBLIC. Exception: modules that exist only to expose public data (constants, for example) can stay fully public.
  • Initialize every variable. Do not rely on the machine's default.
  • Do not initialize a variable of one type with a value of another type.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text:
• Do not use == or /= on floating-point values. Compare against an explicit tolerance instead (an epsilon check).
  • In mixed-type expressions and assignments, write the type conversion explicitly. Do not let the compiler do it implicitly.
  • No INCLUDE files. Use USE with modules.
  • Derived types belong in a separate module, together with the procedures that operate on them.
  • Each procedure should do one thing.
  • Module-level (global) public variables should contain only static or rarely-changing data.

docs.title: Encouraged
docs.text:
• Always use parentheses to make expression evaluation order explicit.
  • Prefer derived types (% field access) over loose collections of arrays.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Subscript expressions must be integer.
  • Do not assume any particular array passing mechanism when passing arrays as arguments.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text:
• Use array operations and intrinsics where they apply.
  • Pass arrays as assumed shape.

docs.title: Encouraged
docs.text: • Declare DIMENSION on every non-scalar.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Prefer ALLOCATABLE arrays over pointers where possible. Reduces leak and fragmentation risk.
  • Pointers are allowed when a subroutine needs to return a declared array to its caller.
  • Initialize every pointer to NULL() in its declaration: INTEGER, POINTER :: x => NULL().
  • Prefer automatic arrays for transient allocations. ALLOCATABLE and POINTER arrays need explicit DEALLOCATE.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text:
• Always deallocate. Especially inside subroutines and loops.
  • Check the STAT argument on ALLOCATE and DEALLOCATE.
  • Do not repeatedly ALLOCATE, DEALLOCATE, then ALLOCATE a larger block. Heap fragmentation follows.

docs.title: Encouraged
docs.text:
• Dynamic allocation is preferred over fixed-size declarations with worst-case dimensions.
  • Use automatic arrays in subroutines for simplicity.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: • No GOTO for loop exit or continuation. Use EXIT or CYCLE.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text: • No numbered DO loops (DO 10 ... 10 CONTINUE).

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Avoid SAVE. Keep state in module variables instead.
  • No ENTRY statements in functions.
  • Functions must not return pointers.
  • Do not name a user function the same as an intrinsic (SUM, etc.).
  • A procedure that returns a single value should be a function. The value can be a derived type.
  • Communicate through arguments or through the variables of the procedure's module.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text:
• Every dummy argument that is not a pointer has an INTENT.
  • Avoid type-specific intrinsics (AMAX, DMAX). Use the generic (MAX).
  • Do not declare static-dimensioned array arguments.
  • Validate argument values where it matters.

docs.title: Encouraged
docs.text:
• On an error, print a message that includes the routine name. You may terminate inside the routine, or pass an error flag back through the argument list.
  • Use overloading when the same operation works on multiple types.
  • Use modules or CONTAINS for explicit interfaces.
  • Avoid external routines. They need separate interface blocks that drift out of sync.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• External-file I/O statements include err=, end=, and iostat= as appropriate.
  • All global variables, if any, are initialized at startup.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text:
• Avoid NAMELIST I/O.
  • Use WRITE instead of PRINT for non-terminal I/O.
  • Use character parameters or in-line format specifiers in READ and WRITE. Do not use labeled FORMAT statements.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• No common blocks. Use modules.
  • No assigned or computed GO TO. Use CASE.
  • No arithmetic IF. Use a block IF.
  • Use REAL, not DOUBLE PRECISION.
  • Avoid DATA, ASSIGN, labeled DO, BACKSPACE, blank COMMON, BLOCK DATA.
  • Do not branch to an END IF from outside its IF block.
  • No non-integer DO loop counters.
  • No Hollerith constants.
  • No PAUSE.
  • No multiple RETURN, no alternate RETURN.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text: • No EQUIVALENCE. Use pointers or derived types.

docs.title: Encouraged
docs.text: • Do not implicitly reshape arrays when passing them. This was common in F77 and is forbidden by F90 but still possible through external routines without interface blocks.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Document every function interface: argument name, type, units, description, constraints, defaults.
  • No INCLUDE. Use USE.
  • Keep lines (including comments) under 80 columns where the language allows it.

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text:
• Keep individual procedures under 300-500 effective lines.
  • Separate statement blocks with blank lines or a marker character in column 1.
  • Indent consistently.
  • Module and subprogram names are lower case. The file is named after the contained module or subprogram, with .f90.

docs.title: Encouraged
docs.text:
• Separate argument declarations from local declarations visually.
  • Use descriptive unique names. Keep them under 12-15 characters.
  • Indent continuation lines so a multi-line expression lines up readably.
  • Comments start with a marker character (!). A standalone comment line starts the marker in column 1.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• SAS Coding Conventions
  • WRF Coding Conventions
  • USGS Coding Standards
Sources
  • doc/coding_conventions.md in the source repository.

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text:
• Model source: github.com/swat-model/swatplus, with issues, pull requests and releases.
  • This documentation: github.com/swat-model/swatplus-documentation.

Questions about using the model are best asked through the SWAT support page.

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text:
Open an issue with:

  • the SWAT+ version (shown in the banner at start-up and in the executable name);
  • the operating system and, for your own builds, the compiler;
  • a project that shows the problem, as small as possible (one of the refdata datasets with the changes that cause it is ideal);
  • simulation.out and diagnostics.out from the run.

docs.title: Contributing code
docs.text:
1. Fork swat-model/swatplus and create a branch from main with a descriptive name (fix-aquifer-init, add-soil-temp-output).
  2. Build and run your change on the reference datasets before opening a pull request. See Build with CMake and Testing.
  3. Open a pull request against main. Describe what the change does and why, which datasets you ran and how their outputs changed, and any change to input or output files.
  4. Answer review comments on the same branch.

Reviewers look for:

  • a clean build with gfortran and the Intel compilers;
  • unchanged outputs for parts of the model the change does not touch;
  • defaults for new parameters that keep existing results when the parameter is not set;
  • input file changes matched by a SWAT+ Editor change or a note on how to update existing projects;
  • code that follows the coding conventions.

docs.title: Contributing to the documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is a MkDocs site in the swatplus-documentation repository. Each page states the SWAT+ commit it was checked against in its front matter (verified_at_commit), and every statement about model behaviour should come from the source at that commit. Page bodies are written for model users; source file names and variable names go in the collapsed Sources block at the end of each page (??? quote "Sources").

To check a change locally:

pip install -r requirements.txt
mkdocs serve

The site is versioned with mike. Pushing a tag to the documentation repository, named after the SWAT+ version the pages describe (for example 62.0.1), publishes that version and moves the latest alias to it. Earlier versions stay available from the version selector.

Sources
  • CI: .github/workflows/test.yml and .github/workflows/build.yml in the source repository.
  • Documentation build and deployment: mkdocs.yml, requirements.txt and .github/workflows/deploy.yml in the documentation repository.

docs.title: Tagging and releases
docs.text: A SWAT+ version is a Git tag. No source file is edited to make a release: the build reads the tag and writes it into the executable's name and its start-up banner.

docs.title: Version numbers
docs.text:
Current tags have three parts, revision, minor and patch, for example 62.0.0 and 62.0.1. Older tags include 61.0, 61.0.2.61 and 60.5.7. List them with:

git tag --sort=-creatordate | head

At configure time CMake runs git describe --tags:

  • on a tagged commit the version is the tag, for example 62.0.1;
  • on a later commit it is the tag, the number of commits since, and the abbreviated commit name, for example 62.0.1-3-g1a2b3c4;
  • outside a Git clone it is unknown.

A version can also be given by hand with -D TAG=<version> when configuring.

docs.title: Version in the executable and outputs
docs.text:
The executable name, swatplus-<version>-<compiler>-<system>_<arch>[-Rel|-Dbg], for example swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-lin_x86_64-Rel.

The start-up banner, printed to the screen and to simulation.out:

                   SWAT+
             Revision 62.0.1
      Soil & Water Assessment Tool
GNU (13.3.0), 2026-10-19 22:51:37, Linux
    Program reading . . . executing

The title line of every output file, which contains the build date and Rev <year>.<version>:

 demo                      SWAT+ 2026-10-19        MODULAR Rev 2026.62.0.1

docs.title: Building a tagged version
docs.text:
git checkout 62.0.1
cmake -B build -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j 8

A tag on GitHub can be moved after it is first published (the 62.0.1 tag was replaced on 19 October 2026). Run git fetch --tags --force before checking out a tag in an existing clone, so that the local tag matches the one on GitHub.

docs.title: Making a release
docs.text:
1. Merge the changes for the release into main.

  2. Tag the merge commit and push the tag:

    git tag 62.0.2
git push origin 62.0.2

  3. Pushing a tag of the form x.y or x.y.z starts the release workflow, which builds the executables for Windows, Linux and macOS with gfortran and the Intel compilers and attaches the zipped executables to a GitHub release.

  4. Write the release notes on the GitHub release page, and archive the release on Zenodo (see Citing and license).
  5. Tag the documentation repository with the same version, which publishes a matching version of this site.
Sources
  • CMakeLists.txt: if(NOT TAG) block with git describe --tags, SWATPLUS_EXE, and configure_file of src/main.f90.in with ISO, TODAY and YEAR time stamps.
  • src/main.f90.in: prog = " SWAT+ @TODAY@ MODULAR Rev @YEAR@.@SWAT_VERSION@" and the banner format. The generated src/main.f90 is overwritten on every configure; edit main.f90.in.
  • doc/Tagging.md.
  • .github/workflows/build.yml: runs on tags matching *.* and *.*.*.
  • Banner and title line: output of the 62.0.1 gnu-lin_x86_64 release executable.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: SWAT+ has a scenario regression test: it runs the model on a reference dataset and compares chosen output files with copies kept in the repository. Differences outside a tolerance point to a change in results, which is then either a bug or an intended change that needs new reference outputs.

docs.title: Test script
docs.text:
test/spcheck.py (Python 3, standard library only) has three commands:

Command Use ctest <executable> <reference folder> <work folder> copy the reference folder into the work folder, run the executable there, and compare the files listed in the folder's .testfiles.txt with the reference copies; exit with code 1 if any value differs run <executable> <scenario> run build/<executable> on data/<scenario> in a new numbered folder under runs/<scenario>/ compare <scenario> <a> <b> compare two numbered runs of a scenario

Options --abserr and --relerr set the tolerances (defaults 1e-8 and 0.05), and --nlines and --nerrorlines limit how much of each file is checked and reported.

Two numbers are equal when

\[|v_1 - v_2| \le e_{abs} + e_{rel}\,|v_2|\]

Only real numbers are compared, value by value on matching lines; integers and text are skipped, as are the title lines with the build date (lines containing MODULAR).

docs.title: Running the test at 62.0.1
docs.text:
CMakeLists.txt registers one test, Ames_sub1, with tolerances of 1e-8 absolute and 1 % relative, and reference data in data/Ames_sub1. At 62.0.1 the repository has no data/ folder; the reference datasets are in refdata/. ctest therefore fails at once with data dir not found.

To run the comparison, call the script directly with the refdata folder:

cmake -B build -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j 8
python3 test/spcheck.py ctest build/swatplus-*-Rel refdata/Ames_sub1 build/test-runs --abserr 1e-8 --relerr 0.01

Notes on the reference dataset:

  • A full Ames_sub1 run writes about 9 GB, mostly daily carbon output, and takes a few minutes. Make sure the work folder has the space.
  • .testfiles.txt lists 42 files. With the shipped print.prt the model rewrites fewer than half of them; the rest (all basin_* files, hydin_aa.txt, ru_aa.txt and others) are copied from the reference folder and compared with themselves. The test therefore checks the HRU water and nutrient balances, plant and yield output and management output, and not channel, aquifer or basin output.

docs.title: Adding a scenario
docs.text:
1. Put a complete input set in a new folder under refdata/ (or data/).
  2. Run the model and check the outputs you want to fix as the reference.
  3. Commit the inputs and those outputs.
  4. Add a .testfiles.txt naming the output files to compare, one per line (# starts a comment).
  5. Add an add_test line to CMakeLists.txt pointing at the folder.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
.github/workflows/test.yml builds SWAT+ with Intel ifx on Ubuntu and runs ctest on pushes to branches whose name ends in main. With the data/ path above, the test step fails. The release workflow (build.yml) builds the release executables for each tag and does not run the tests.

Sources
  • test/spcheck.py: ctest_all, cmp_file and the run/compare commands.
  • CMakeLists.txt: set(ref_dir "${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}/data"), tolerances aerr = 1e-8, rerr = 0.01, and add_test(Ames_sub1 ...). The Ithaca_sub6 test is commented out.
  • refdata/Ames_sub1/.testfiles.txt.
  • .github/workflows/test.yml and .github/workflows/build.yml.
  • The 9 GB output size and the list of files rewritten are from a run of the 62.0.1 gnu-lin_x86_64 release executable on 20 October 2026.

docs.title: Visual Studio on Windows
docs.text:
Visual Studio 2022 on Windows can build, run and debug SWAT+ with the Intel Fortran compiler. The steps are: install the tools, clone the repository, configure the CMake build, and run a debug session against an input dataset.

The screenshots for these steps are in the doc/ folder of the SWAT+ source repository.

docs.title: Required software
docs.text:
Install in this order. The Intel compiler requires Visual Studio to be present first.

  1. Visual Studio Community 2022. During install, in the Workloads panel, check Desktop development with C++. That workload pulls in the CMake integration that SWAT+ needs.
  2. Intel Fortran Compiler for Windows. Use the standalone installer. The current Intel oneAPI release ships ifx. The older ifort was deprecated in 2024 and is gone from the 2025 release. SWAT+ produces the same results with either Intel compiler.
  3. Git for Windows. Visual Studio includes a copy of Git, but SWAT+ uses the standalone git during the CMake build to read the current tag for the version string.

Reboot after the three installs finish.

Optional: install Python (from the Microsoft Store) and the Python workload in Visual Studio if you want to run the integrated test suite from inside the IDE.

docs.title: Starting Visual Studio
docs.text:
The Intel compiler only works with the Visual Studio CMake integration if Visual Studio is launched from the Intel oneAPI command prompt. Follow these steps every time.

  1. Open the Windows Start Menu, type intel, and select Intel oneAPI command prompt for Intel 64 for Visual Studio 2022. Pin it if you use it often.
  2. The terminal opens and prints the oneAPI initialization output:
:: initializing oneAPI environment...
   Initializing Visual Studio command-line environment...
   Visual Studio version 17.13.0 environment configured.
   "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Community\"
   Visual Studio command-line environment initialized for: 'x64'
:  compiler -- latest
:  debugger -- latest
:: oneAPI environment initialized ::
  1. At the prompt, run:
devenv

This launches Visual Studio with the Intel environment variables set.

If you start Visual Studio by clicking the desktop icon directly, the Intel compiler will not be found and the build will fail.

docs.title: Cloning the repository
docs.text:
Visual Studio can clone the SWAT+ repository and open it as a CMake project in one step.

  1. On the Visual Studio start screen, click Clone a Repository.
  2. Click the GitHub icon (lower left) to browse your repositories. Sign in if prompted. Select your fork of swatplus and click Open. Adjust the local path if needed.
  3. Visual Studio clones the repository and loads it into Solution Explorer as a CMake project. It runs the CMake configure step against whichever Fortran compiler it finds (ifx, ifort, or gfortran). The 2025 Intel compiler only ships ifx, so any ifort configurations will fail on that version.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
SWAT+ is a CMake project. The Visual Studio toolbar exposes the available compiler and build-type combinations through a drop-down. Switching the selection triggers a reconfigure. The Output window prints the CMake settings used; check there which compiler was picked up.

To force a fresh configure, right-click CMakeLists.txt in Solution Explorer and select Delete Cache and Reconfigure.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Use Build > Build All or Build > Rebuild All. The executable name encodes the compiler, architecture, and version. The version is read from the latest Git tag automatically. See Tagging and releases.

The Intel-built Windows executable is dynamically linked. To run it on a machine without Visual Studio, ship the Intel redistributable libraries alongside it.

docs.title: Run and debug
docs.text:
You need to tell the project which folder contains the input dataset to run against.

  1. Right-click CMakeLists.txt in Solution Explorer and select Add Debug Configuration. If Co-Pilot is hiding Solution Explorer, close that pane first.
  2. In the dialog, pick Default and click Select. Visual Studio creates launch.vs.json if it does not exist and opens it for editing.

The default file looks like this:

{
  "version": "0.2.1",
  "defaults": {},
  "configurations": [
    {
      "type": "default",
      "project": "CMakeLists.txt",
      "projectTarget": "",
      "name": "CMakeLists.txt"
    }
  ]
}

Add a currentDir entry pointing at your input dataset. The path can be absolute or relative to the swatplus project root. The name field is what shows up in the toolbar.

{
  "version": "0.2.1",
  "defaults": {},
  "configurations": [
    {
      "type": "default",
      "project": "CMakeLists.txt",
      "projectTarget": "",
      "name": "Ames_testing",
      "currentDir": "C:/work/sp/Ames_testing"
    }
  ]
}

Do not change project or type. You can add more configurations by repeating Add Debug Configuration and editing the new block.

Pick your configuration from the toolbar drop-down and run Debug > Start Debugging or Debug > Start Without Debugging. Breakpoints, conditional watches, and step-through all work.

docs.text:
• Intel C++ and Fortran Compilers Redistributable Libraries by Version
  • Intel Fortran Compiler
  • Intel Fortran Compiler for oneAPI release notes

Sources
