docs.title: VS Code Codespaces
docs.text:
The SWAT+ repository ships a .devcontainer/ folder that lets GitHub Codespaces start a Visual Studio Code instance in the browser with the build tools installed, so no local Fortran compiler is needed.

When a Codespaces instance starts, it:

  • loads your fork into a remote working folder
  • installs the Intel ifx and gfortran compilers
  • configures VS Code to use the CMake build system
  • installs the VS Code extensions needed to debug Fortran, and the fortls Fortran language server
  • creates /workdata/my_data and copies the refdata/Ames_sub1 dataset into it

In 62.0.1 the /workdata/Ames_sub1 folder that the default Ames_sub1 debug configuration points to is not created. To use that configuration, create the folder and copy refdata/Ames_sub1 into it from the terminal:

mkdir -p workdata/Ames_sub1 && cp -r refdata/Ames_sub1/* workdata/Ames_sub1

The screenshots for these steps are in the doc/ folder of the SWAT+ source repository.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
GitHub gives every account 120 free CPU hours per month across all Codespaces instances. A 2-CPU instance running for 60 hours uses 120 hours of quota. Beyond that, you pay per active hour. A small per-hour storage fee applies whether the instance is running or stopped.

Instance states:

  • Active: the instance is in use (interactive or compiling). After 30 minutes of inactivity it goes to Inactive. The timeout is configurable.
  • Inactive: not running. Storage fee only.
  • Shutdown: you stopped it manually. Same as Inactive billing-wise.
  • Deleted: no further charges. A new instance has to be created from scratch to come back.

docs.title: Starting an instance
docs.text:
1. Sign in to GitHub and go to your swatplus fork.
  2. Open the hamburger menu (top left) and click Codespaces.
  3. Click New codespace (top right).
  4. Pick the repository, the branch, and the CPU count. Two CPUs is enough for SWAT+. Click Create codespace.

The instance takes a couple of minutes to come up. You should see an install progress bar in the lower right. When it disappears, a drop-down at the top of the editor asks which Fortran compiler to use. Pick one.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Click the CMake icon in the left sidebar (the triangle-with-wrench) to open the CMake pane.

  1. Under Project Status > Configure, check the Fortran compiler shown. To change it, hover and click the pencil icon, then pick another.
  2. Right-click CMakeLists.txt in the CMake pane and select Clean and Reconfigure. Do this every time you switch compilers, and any time you add or remove a Fortran source file.
  3. Right-click CMakeLists.txt again and select Build All Projects. The Output panel at the bottom should end with:
[build] Build finished with exit code 0

docs.title: Running and debugging
docs.text:
Click the debug icon in the left sidebar (the triangle with a bug). Pick Ames_sub1 from the drop-down and click the green triangle.

After a fresh build, VS Code may ask which executable to run. Any of the debug-build options works. A release build is not debuggable.

Watch model output in the Terminal tab at the bottom. Set breakpoints or conditional breakpoints, or let it run. On a runtime exception, the debugger stops at the failure point and you can inspect variable values.

docs.title: Using your own dataset
docs.text:
The /workdata/my_data folder starts with a copy of Ames_sub1. To use your own inputs, delete its contents and upload yours:

  1. In the VS Code Explorer, right-click /workdata/my_data and select Upload.
  2. Allow the cookie prompt if your browser shows one (GitHub needs it to open your local file picker).
  3. Select all the files in your input dataset and upload.
  4. Switch the debug drop-down to my_data and click the green triangle.

To add a third dataset, create a new folder under /workdata/, then edit .vscode/launch.json. The default file already has blocks for Ames_sub1 and my_data. Copy one block, change name and cwd, and add a comma between blocks.

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "Ames_sub1",
            "type": "cppdbg",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${command:cmake.launchTargetPath}",
            "args": [],
            "stopAtEntry": false,
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}/workdata/Ames_sub1",
            "environment": [
                {
                    "name": "PATH",
                    "value": "${env:PATH}:${command:cmake.getLaunchTargetDirectory}"
                }
            ],
            "externalConsole": false,
            "MIMode": "gdb",
            "setupCommands": [
                {
                    "description": "Enable pretty-printing for gdb",
                    "text": "-enable-pretty-printing",
                    "ignoreFailures": true
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            "name": "walnut_creek",
            "type": "cppdbg",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${command:cmake.launchTargetPath}",
            "args": [],
            "stopAtEntry": false,
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}/workdata/walnut_creek",
            "environment": [
                {
                    "name": "PATH",
                    "value": "${env:PATH}:${command:cmake.getLaunchTargetDirectory}"
                }
            ],
            "externalConsole": false,
            "MIMode": "gdb",
            "setupCommands": [
                {
                    "description": "Enable pretty-printing for gdb",
                    "text": "-enable-pretty-printing",
                    "ignoreFailures": true
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

docs.title: Stopping the instance
docs.text: To stop billing for active usage, click Codespaces in the bottom-left status bar and select Stop Current Codespace. It takes a minute or two.

docs.title: Deleting the instance
docs.text:
After stopping, go back to the browser tab where you created the instance (or open the Codespaces panel from your GitHub repository). Find the instance at the bottom, click the ellipsis on its row, and select Delete. Storage charges stop after deletion. A new instance has to be created from scratch the next time you want to work.

Sources
  • .devcontainer/devcontainer.json and .devcontainer/Dockerfile at 62.0.1. devcontainer.json contains two postCreateCommand keys; only the last one (the my_data copy) is used.
  • doc/VSCode_Codespace.md in the source repository, with the screenshots.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: These pages help when a SWAT+ run stops, completes with results that do not make sense, or takes too long. First runs and installation problems are covered in Getting started, and adjusting parameters to observations in Calibration.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
• Common runtime errors: the messages SWAT+ prints when a run stops or a name in the inputs is not matched, the names it matches without a message, files it creates when they are missing, and inputs in an older format.
  • Water balance issues: implausible precipitation, runoff, ET, percolation, lateral and tile flow, and basin totals that do not match the HRUs.
  • Performance tips: build type, time step, output volume and the size of the carbon output files.

docs.title: Checks after every run
docs.text:
1. simulation.out ends with Execution successfully completed, and success.fin exists. If not, the run stopped early: keep the screen output, since stop messages are not copied to the log files.
  2. Read diagnostics.out to the end. Every line after the first is a name that was not matched, and SWAT+ used a default or left the feature off.
  3. Check the names that are not reported when they do not match, above all the names in hru-data.hru, which fall back to the first record of each file. See Names matched without a message.
  4. Read checker.out: the soil group, rooting depth, field capacity, perco, latq_co and tile flag of each HRU show whether the intended soil and parameters were used.
  5. Compare the average annual water balance with regional estimates before calibrating.

The file layouts are in Checker and diagnostics. The revision of the executable is in the banner at the top of simulation.out (Revision 62.0.1); inputs written for an earlier revision can be misread without a message (see Old-format inputs).

Sources
  • diagnostics.out and files_out.out are opened in proc_bsn.f90; the banner and the completion message are written by main.f90.in.
  • Name lookup for HRUs: hru_read.f90.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This page lists the messages SWAT+ 62.0.1 writes when a run stops or when it cannot match a name in the inputs, and the input problems that change the results without any message. For each one it gives the cause and the fix.

docs.title: Message locations
docs.text:
Place Content the screen (standard output) errors that stop the run, written just before it stops diagnostics.out names that could not be matched while the inputs were read; the run continues simulation.out the revision banner and one line per simulated day, ending with Execution successfully completed gwflow_record messages from the gwflow module, including the ones that stop the run

Messages printed on the screen are not copied to simulation.out. When the model is started by a script or another program, keep the screen output, for example with swatplus > run.log 2>&1. The layout of the log files is described in Checker and diagnostics.

In the messages below, <name> stands for a name from the inputs and <n> for a number. SWAT+ pads names with spaces, so the gaps in a real message are wider.

docs.title: Missing object.cnt
docs.text:
Cannot find object.cnt input file

The file named on the simulation line of file.cio (normally object.cnt) does not exist, or the name is null. Usually the model was started outside the project folder. Change into the folder that contains file.cio and start it again. Started in an empty folder, SWAT+ also leaves a few files behind (see Files the model creates).

docs.title: Carbon input files
docs.text:
With carbon = 2 in codes.bsn, two files are required. SWAT+ stops with one of these messages, on the screen and in diagnostics.out:

 ERROR: <name> is required when carbon is enabled (codes.bsn carbon = 2)
 ERROR: <name> could not be opened
 ERROR: <name> data/values line is missing or could not be parsed (expected 28 values)
 ERROR: <name> provided <n> row(s); expected <n>

The first file is the one named in the third slot of the basin line of file.cio, normally carbon.bsn. The second has no slot: its name is the first name with _lyr added before the extension, normally carbon_lyr.bsn. Provide carbon.bsn with its 28 values and carbon_lyr.bsn with a row for each layer group, or set carbon to 0. The old carb_coefs.cbn is no longer read.

If the message names a file that is not a carbon file, such as ERROR: climate is required when carbon is enabled, the basin line of file.cio has only two names. See Old-format inputs.

docs.title: print.prt rows
docs.text:
Error: The output object <name> in the input file print.prt is not a valid object.
       and cannot be processed
Error: <name> print object is duplicated in the input file print.prt.  Aborting

These checks apply when use_obj_lbls is y in print.prt, so that the rows are read by name. A row name that SWAT+ does not know, or a row given twice, stops the run. The valid names, and the files each one opens, are listed in print.prt rows and files.

docs.title: Output folder
docs.text:
! ERROR: cannot create path specified in file.cio (out_path)
   > Windows-style path detected on Unix system: <name>
 ! ERROR: cannot create or access path specified in file.cio (out_path)
   > Path: <name>

The optional output folder line of file.cio names a folder SWAT+ cannot use. On Linux and macOS a folder name that contains : is taken as a Windows path and refused. The second message means the folder could not be created or opened, often because of file permissions. See Output folder.

docs.title: gwflow input files
docs.text:
The gwflow module writes its messages to gwflow_record in the run folder, so the screen shows only that the program stopped. These messages stop the run:

Message in gwflow_record Cause ERROR: gwflow.cells row has too few columns at i=<n> row n of cells.gw has fewer than the 14 required columns ERROR: gwflow.cells row out of order at i=<n> cell_id=<n> the cell IDs in cells.gw are not 1, 2, 3, ... in file order ERROR: gwflow.cellcons row has too few columns at i=<n> row n of cellcon.gw has fewer than 2 columns ERROR: gwflow.cellcons row out of order at i=<n> cell_id=<n> the cell IDs in cellcon.gw are not in file order neither gwflow.hrucell or gwflow.lsucell found; stop simulation conn_type in codes.gw is neither 1 nor 2

The messages use older file names: gwflow.cells is cells.gw and gwflow.cellcons is cellcon.gw. With conn_type 1 or 2 and neither hrucell.gw nor lsucell.gw present, the run does not stop. See gwflow inputs.

docs.title: Fortran run-time errors
docs.text:
Some readers do not check what they read. A missing line, a missing file or text where a number is expected then stops the run with a message from the Fortran run-time library instead of SWAT+. With gfortran builds it contains Fortran runtime error, and with Intel builds it starts with forrtl: severe. The message usually gives the file name or the unit number. Check that file for a missing or extra line or a wrong number of columns, and compare it with its page in the Input Reference.

Most readers do check, and do not stop. When a value in a row cannot be read, they stop reading that row without a message, and the columns after it keep their defaults. A row with a stray character or a missing value can therefore change the results silently.

docs.title: Messages in diagnostics.out
docs.text:
Line 1 of diagnostics.out is DIAGNOSTICS.OUT FILE. Each later line is written while the inputs are read, and the run continues. From a run of the Ames_sub1 reference dataset:

 agrr_lum                                AGRR_rot                                 not found in management.sch
 ames.tem                                          file not found (tgage)

docs.title: Land use names
docs.text:
Written for a row of landuse.lum that names a record that is not found. The line gives the land use name, the missing name and one of these endings:

Ending Column Result not found in plant.ini plnt_com no plants at the start not found in management.sch mgt no scheduled operations: no planting, fertilizer or harvest not found in cntable.lum cn2 built-in curve numbers 30, 55, 70 and 77 for soil groups A to D not found (landuse-consprac) cons_prac P factor 1.0 not found (landuse-tiledr) tile no tile drain not found (landuse-septic) sep no septic system not found (landuse-fstrip) vfs no filter strip not found (landuse-grassww) grww no grassed waterway not found (landuse-bmpuser) bmp no user BMP

Correct the name in landuse.lum, or add the missing record to the file it points to. See Name matching. Ames_sub1 writes four not found in management.sch lines, so the HRUs with those land uses have no management.

docs.title: Plant names
docs.text:
mgt schedule <n> op numb <n> <name> not found in plants.plt database
  plant com <n> plant numb <n> <name> not found in plants.plt database

The first is written for a plnt line of management.sch whose plant name is not in plants.plt; the numbers are the position of the schedule in the file and of the line in the schedule. The second is written for a plant in plant.ini that is not in plants.plt. Plant names are case-sensitive.

docs.title: Weather station names
docs.text:
<name> file not found (tgage)

A station in weather-sta.cli names a data file that is not listed in the matching index file. The ending gives the column: (pgage) precipitation and pcp.cli, (tgage) temperature and tmp.cli, (sgage) solar radiation, (hgage) humidity, (wgage) wind, (petgage) PET and (atmodep) atmospheric deposition. For the five weather variables, SWAT+ then generates that variable for the station on every day from its weather generator record. In Ames_sub1, weather-sta.cli names ames.tem while tmp.cli lists ames.tmp, so the temperatures are generated.

file not found (wgn) means the wgn name of the station is not in weather-wgn.cli. 62.0.1 has no record to fall back on in that case, and the generated weather of that station is undefined. Correct the name before running. See Unmatched names.

docs.title: Reservoir, wetland and other names
docs.text: Ending Name that was not found not found (res-init), (res-hyd), (res-release), (res-sed), (res-nut) a record named in reservoir.res not found (wet-init), (wet-hyd), (wet-release), (wet-sed), (wet-nut) a record named in wetland.wet not found (wetland.wet) the surf_stor name of an HRU in hru-data.hru; the HRU has no surface storage not found (field.fld) the field name of an HRU; the HRU uses the built-in field size not found (plants.plt) the plant of an HRU in hru-lte.hru entry in (hru-lte.hru) not found in (lum.dtl) a decision table named in hru-lte.hru not found (initial.cha), (hydrology.cha), (sediment.cha), (nutrients.cha) a record named in the legacy channel.cha, which 62.0.1 reads but does not route

docs.title: Carbon layer files
docs.text:
<name>: layer id <n> is out of range (1 to <n>); row ignored
 carbon_layers.prt: n_layers must be >= 1; got <n>; default <n> kept

The first means a row of carbon_lyr.bsn has a layer number other than 1 or 2, and the row is skipped. The second means the optional layer count file has a value below 1, and the per-layer carbon outputs use the largest layer count of any HRU.

docs.title: Names matched without a message
docs.text:
Several names are looked up without any report when they are not found. The run continues with the result in the table, so check these names by hand or in SWAT+ Editor.

Name Result when it is not found topo, hydro, soil, lu_mgt, soil_plant_init or snow in hru-data.hru the HRU uses the first record of the target file. The reader has messages for these names, but they are never written in 62.0.1. wst in a connection file such as hru.con the object uses the first station in weather-sta.cli. The stations must also be listed in ascending order of name for the lookup to work. See Weather station lookup. fertilizer name of a fert line in management.sch nothing is applied. The name is read from op_data1; see the management.sch example. harvest operation of a harv line nothing is harvested tillage name of a till line no soil is mixed transplant name of a plnt line or a decision table plant action the plant starts from seed. In 62.0.1 the file is transplant.ops, and a file named transplant.plt is not read. See transplant.ops. manure name of a manu line the manure is found by name in manure_db.frt, but its make-up comes from the row of manure_om.frt in the same position, whatever org_min names. See manure_om.frt. decision table named on an automatic operation line of management.sch the table is not applied. See Automatic operations. urban or ov_mann in landuse.lum the HRU is not urban, or keeps Manning's n of 0.05

docs.title: Files the model creates
docs.text:
For a number of input files, 62.0.1 opens the named file without checking that it exists, and the operating system then creates an empty file of that name. The run continues as if the file had no records. This happens for time.sim and print.prt, the place-of-use and point-of-diversion files of water allocation, wtps_wuses.wal, and the initial-condition files for pesticides, pathogens, metals, salts and constituents (pest_hru.ini, salt_hru.ini, cs_aqu.ini and others). For some of these slots a null name creates a file named null.

An empty file left behind changes the next run: an empty time.sim, for example, leaves the run without a valid simulation period. After a run that misbehaves, list the empty files in the project folder (find . -size 0 on Linux and macOS) and restore or delete them. If in doubt, write the inputs again from SWAT+ Editor.

docs.title: Old-format inputs
docs.text:
Files written for an earlier revision are read without a version check. These changes matter most for 62.0.1:

  • file.cio basin line. It now has three names, the third being the carbon file. With only two, every later line of file.cio is read one line too low and all later file names are wrong, with no message. With carbon = 2 the run stops with ERROR: climate is required when carbon is enabled. See Older file.cio files.
  • file.cio water_rights line. It now has two names. An old line with water_allocation.wro element.wro water_rights.wro makes SWAT+ read water_allocation.wro as the place-of-use file.
  • transplant.plt. Renamed to transplant.ops. A project that still has transplant.plt plants from seed.
  • pesticide.pes. Three columns were added after the existing 13 values. Older rows are still read, and the new columns keep their defaults, which means no plant uptake. See pesticide.pes.
  • print.prt. A file with dbout in place of use_obj_lbls is read by position, so an extra or missing row moves the switches of every later row to the wrong output group. See print.prt.
  • carb_coefs.cbn. No longer read. Its settings are in carbon.bsn and carbon_lyr.bsn.

Most input files start with a title line and a column header line, and SWAT+ skips both. A file that starts with the header loses its first data row, with no message. In the reference data, tillage.til of Ames_sub1 and puddle.ops of Osu_1hru have no title line, so their first entries are not read; see tillage.til and puddle.ops.

docs.title: Runs that stop without a message
docs.text:
Full disk. When the disk fills, the run stops with a Fortran run-time error about writing a file, or with no message at all, and the last output files are cut short. Other programs that use the same disk start to fail as well. Daily output is the usual cause: a full 46-year run of the Ames_sub1 reference dataset writes about 9 GB, almost all of it the daily carbon files switched on by its hru_cb and hru_cb_vars rows. Check the free space before long runs (df -h . on Linux and macOS) and switch off the daily outputs you do not need; see Output volume.

The last day. The last daily line in simulation.out is the last day that finished, so the problem occurred on the next day. Climate records that are shorter than the simulation do not stop the run: SWAT+ generates the missing days (see Weather outside the observed record).

A run that never gets past its first day. Earlier revisions could repeat the operations of a management schedule without end when every operation had the same month and day. 62.0.1 runs each operation at most once per pass on a given day, so a run that hangs at the start with 62.0.1 has another cause. A debug build with run-time checks usually stops with a message that points to it.

docs.title: Performance tips
docs.text: title: Performance tips description: What sets the run time and disk use of a SWAT+ 62.0.1 run, and how to reduce them: build type, time step, output volume and the carbon output files. status: review verified_against: - CMakeLists.txt - CMakePresets.json - src/command.f90 - src/basin_print_codes_read.f90 - src/output_landscape_init.f90 - src/carbon_layers_read.f90 - src/soil_nutcarb_write.f90 - src/soil_carbvar_write.f90 verified_at_commit: 6f515368525e7d84089ae0f9d33f4c9115de5679

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The run time of SWAT+ depends on the length of the simulation, the number of objects (HRUs, channels, aquifers, reservoirs), the time step and the amount of output. The disk space a run needs depends almost entirely on the output switched on in print.prt. This page covers what can be changed.

docs.title: One run per processor core
docs.text: SWAT+ is a serial program: the source has no OpenMP or MPI code, and one run uses one processor core. To use several cores, run several scenarios or calibration samples at the same time, each in a separate copy of the project folder. Output file names are fixed, so two runs in the same folder overwrite each other's files.

docs.title: Build type
docs.text:
The executables on the releases page are optimized builds (Rel in the file name; see Install). When building from source, set the build type:

cmake -B build -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j 8

-j 8 only speeds up the compilation. Without a build type, CMake adds no optimization flag and the executable name has no -Rel or -Dbg suffix. A Debug build adds run-time checks (array bounds and floating-point traps with gfortran) and runs much slower; use it to track down a crash and switch back afterwards. With gfortran on Windows, the 62.0.1 CMake setup adds the gfortran run-time checks to every build type, including Release. See Building from source.

docs.title: Time step
docs.text: step in time.sim sets the number of time steps per day. With a value above 1, precipitation, infiltration, surface runoff and channel and reservoir routing are calculated for every time step, while plant growth, soil water and nutrient cycling still run once a day. Run time grows with the number of steps. Use a sub-daily step only when the question needs it, for example Green-Ampt infiltration or sub-daily peak flows.

docs.title: Output volume
docs.text:
Each y in the daily column of a print.prt row writes one row per object per day, so daily output is about 365 times the size of yearly output and 30 times the size of monthly output. Average annual output adds one row per object. Ways to reduce it:

  • Switch daily output on only for the rows you will use, and use monthly, yearly or average annual output for the rest.
  • Limit the daily rows to the period you need with the print period on line 3 of print.prt (day_start, yrc_start, day_end, yrc_end and interval), and skip warm-up years with nyskip. See Print period.
  • Leave csvout at n unless you need the .csv files: with y, every output file is written twice, once as text and once as .csv.
  • With gwflow, check the gwflow rows of print.prt. Several gwflow output groups are on unless a row switches them off; see gwflow outputs.

files_out.out lists every output file a run opened. Check it after a short first run to see what a long run will write.

docs.title: Carbon output files
docs.text:
The carbon files are the largest outputs, because the per-layer files have a value for every soil layer and variable.

  • Legacy carbon rows. The hru_cb and hru_cb_vars rows with l in the daily column write per-layer diagnostics for every HRU on every day. The Ames_sub1 reference dataset has this setting, and a full 46-year run of its 12 HRUs writes about 9 GB, almost all of it these files. Set the daily column of these rows to n unless you need the daily layer values. See Legacy CSU carbon outputs.
  • Per-layer carbon rows. In 62.0.1 the files of the hru_cb_lyr, hru_cb_cpool, hru_cb_npool, hru_cb_plt, hru_cb_flux, hru_cb_drv, hru_cb_dyn and hru_cb_snap rows repeat their block of HRU rows once per HRU. Their size grows with the square of the number of HRUs: 100 HRUs give 100 times the rows they should. Use yearly or average annual output for these rows in models with many HRUs. See Repeated rows.
  • Number of layers. The per-layer files have as many columns per variable as the HRU with the most soil layers. An optional carbon_layers.prt file sets a smaller number, for example to write only the top three layers. See Layer count file.

Check the free disk space before a long run with daily output (df -h . on Linux and macOS). A disk that fills during a run stops it, often without a clear message; see Runs that stop without a message.

docs.title: Object count and storage
docs.text:
Run time grows roughly in proportion to the number of HRUs, channels, aquifers and routing units. When testing inputs, use a short simulation period or a small part of the watershed, and run the full model once the inputs are settled.

SWAT+ reads its inputs at the start and writes the outputs during the run. With many daily outputs, a project folder on a local disk runs noticeably faster than one on a network share.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Change Effect CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release optimized code; a Debug build runs much slower step 0 or 1 in time.sim daily calculation, fastest daily output only where needed smaller files, faster runs print period and nyskip in print.prt fewer daily rows csvout = n half the output files no l in the daily column of hru_cb and hru_cb_vars avoids the largest carbon files yearly or average annual per-layer carbon files avoids the repeated HRU rows growing with the square of the HRU count several runs in separate folders uses several processor cores Sources
  • Build flags: CMakeLists.txt and CMakePresets.json
  • Output switches: basin_print_codes_read.f90, file opening in output_landscape_init.f90
  • Carbon writers and their calls: command.f90, soil_nutcarb_write.f90, soil_carbvar_write.f90, layer count in carbon_layers_read.f90

docs.title: Water balance issues
docs.text: title: Water balance issues description: Causes of an implausible SWAT+ 62.0.1 water balance, by term: precipitation, runoff, ET, management, percolation, lateral and tile flow, and basin totals. status: review verified_against: - src/climate_control.f90 - src/cli_precip_control.f90 - src/cli_staread.f90 - src/hru_read.f90 - src/hru_module.f90 - src/landuse_read.f90 - src/basin_output.f90 - src/lsu_output.f90 - src/read_mgtops.f90 - src/mgt_sched.f90 - src/topohyd_init.f90 - src/swr_percmicro.f90 - src/hru_output.f90 verified_at_commit: 6f515368525e7d84089ae0f9d33f4c9115de5679

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
When a run completes but basin_wb_aa.txt or hru_wb_aa.txt looks wrong, the cause is usually in the climate inputs, the curve numbers, the management, the soil and hydrology parameters, or the way the basin totals are weighted. This page goes through the water balance term by term. Many of the causes leave no message, so the checks below name the file and column to look at.

Before changing parameters, read diagnostics.out and checker.out (see Checker and diagnostics) and the list of names matched without a message. An HRU that silently uses the first record of landuse.lum, soils.sol or hydrology.hyd gives a water balance that no parameter change will fix.

docs.title: Balance check
docs.text:
For an HRU, landscape unit or the basin, the average annual water balance should close:

\[P + I + Q_{\mathrm{runon}} \approx ET + WYLD + PERC + \Delta SW + \Delta SNO\]

where \(P\) is precip, \(I\) is irr, \(Q_{\mathrm{runon}}\) is surq_runon + latq_runon, \(ET\) is et, \(WYLD\) is wateryld (surq_gen + latq + qtile), \(PERC\) is perc, and \(\Delta SW\) and \(\Delta SNO\) are the changes in soil water and snow over the period. The columns are described in Water balance outputs. A large gap points to wetland storage, gwflow exchange or water held in the surface runoff lag. A term that is far from what the climate and land cover suggest points to one of the sections below.

docs.title: Precipitation
docs.text:
The precip column does not match the observed rainfall.

  • Weather station of the HRU. Each HRU takes its station from the wst column of hru.con. A name that is not in weather-sta.cli, or a weather-sta.cli whose stations are not in ascending order of name, gives the HRU the first station in the file, with no message. See Weather station lookup.
  • Data file of the station. A line file not found (pgage) in diagnostics.out means the station names a precipitation file that is not listed in pcp.cli, and SWAT+ generates the rainfall from the weather generator on every day. See Weather station names.
  • Simulation period. Days before the start or after the end of the record, and days flagged as missing, are generated. See Weather outside the observed record.
  • Sub-daily runs. With step above 1 in time.sim, a station with daily precipitation records gets no rainfall in its time steps. A sub-daily run needs sub-daily records or generated precipitation. See Time step.

hru_pw files and the precip column of hru_wb show what each HRU received, so compare a few HRUs with the station file before looking further.

docs.title: Surface runoff
docs.text:
surq_gen is too high or too low.

  • Curve numbers. The cn2 column of landuse.lum names a record in cntable.lum, and the soil group in soils.sol picks one of its four values. A name that is not found is reported as not found in cntable.lum, and the HRU uses the built-in values 30, 55, 70 and 77 for groups A to D. The hydgrp column of checker.out shows the soil group each HRU uses.
  • Moisture adjustment. cn3_swf in hydrology.hyd places the curve number for wet conditions between field capacity (0) and saturation (1). See Curve number soil water factor.
  • Runoff method. gampt in codes.bsn selects the curve number method (0) or Green-Ampt (1), which is meant for sub-daily runs. See Runoff method.
  • Lag. surq_gen is the runoff after the surface runoff lag and surq_cont the runoff generated on the day. A large difference between them in yearly totals means water is held in the lag.

docs.title: Evapotranspiration
docs.text:
et is too high or too low.

  • PET method. pet in codes.bsn: 0 Priestley-Taylor, 1 Penman-Monteith, 2 Hargreaves, 3 the PET file of the station. Penman-Monteith uses solar radiation, humidity and wind, which are generated when the station has no records for them. Compare the pet column of the water balance file with a regional estimate.
  • Compensation factors. esco and epco in hydrology.hyd set how far down the profile soil evaporation and plant uptake can reach. checker.out lists the values each HRU uses. See Soil evaporation.
  • Plant cover. If plants do not grow, eplant stays low and more water leaves as soil evaporation, runoff and percolation. Check biomass and LAI in the hru_pw files and yields in crop_yld_aa.txt (see Plant and weather).

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Crops do not grow, or grow without fertilizer or harvest.

  • A land use whose mgt schedule is not in management.sch is reported as not found in management.sch, and its HRUs get no operations. The Ames_sub1 reference dataset has four such land uses.
  • Several operation names are not reported when they are not found: a fertilizer name gives no fertilizer, a harvest operation no harvest, a tillage name no mixing, and a transplant name a plant started from seed. In the Ames_sub1 reference dataset, the fertilizer names of every fert line are in the wrong column, so the dataset applies no mineral fertilizer in 62.0.1. See the management.sch example.
  • Set mgtout to y in print.prt to write mgt_out.txt, the log of every operation and decision table action that ran. An operation missing from the log did not happen.

docs.title: Percolation
docs.text:
perc is close to zero.

perco in hydrology.hyd limits percolation out of the bottom of the soil profile, and the relation is strongly non-linear: 0.5 lets about 0.5 % of the potential percolation through, 0.9 about 3 %, and only values close to 1 allow free drainage. The value 0.5, used for every HRU in Ames_sub1, therefore leaves almost nothing to percolate. See Percolation from the soil profile.

Also check sumfc and sumul in checker.out, the water held at field capacity and saturation over the profile. Values that are the same for every HRU can mean the HRUs all use the first record of soils.sol because their soil names did not match.

docs.title: Lateral and tile flow
docs.text:
latq or qtile is out of range.

  • Lateral flow. latq_co and lat_ttime in hydrology.hyd scale and delay lateral flow. See Lateral flow.
  • Tile drains. An HRU has a tile drain when the tile column of its land use names a record in tiledrain.str. The tiledrain column of checker.out shows 1 for those HRUs. A decision table tile_install action has no effect on an HRU whose land use had no tile record at the start. A tile lag of 0.01 h or less keeps tile water in the lag store, so qtile stays at zero. See Tile flow methods.
  • Septic systems. In 62.0.1 a septic system adds no water or nutrients to the soil. See Septic simulation in 62.0.1.

docs.title: Basin totals
docs.text:
The basin or landscape unit values do not match the HRU values.

Basin rows are sums of the HRU values weighted by the BSN_FRAC column of ls_unit.ele, and landscape unit rows by RU_FRAC. 62.0.1 uses these fractions as given, without scaling them to add up to 1. In the Ames_sub1 reference dataset the 12 BSN_FRAC values add up to 2, so every basin water balance, nutrient balance, losses and plant file shows twice the area-weighted HRU average. Set each fraction to the HRU area divided by the basin area, and check that they add up to 1. The basin sum also assumes ls_unit.ele lists one element per HRU, in HRU order. See Aggregation and Nutrient balance and losses.

Routing unit hydrograph files (ru_*) add up every hydrograph type of every element: total flow plus the recharge, surface, lateral and tile parts. Their flo is therefore larger than the routing unit's outflow, which is in the hydout files. See ru files.

flo in the hydrograph files is a volume in m³ per print step, although the units row gives m³/s. Divide a daily value by 86,400 to compare it with a gauge record. See Hydrograph columns.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
This section gets you from a fresh machine to a running SWAT+ simulation.

If you have never run the model before, follow the pages in order:

  1. Install. Get the SWAT+ executable on your machine.
  2. Quick start: Ames_sub1. Run the small reference dataset shipped with the source repository.
  3. Project folder anatomy. Understand what is in a SWAT+ project directory and what each group of files does.
  4. Your first watershed. Build a project for a new area using QSWAT+ and run it.

If you only want to read about the model first, skip ahead to Model theory.

docs.title: Your first watershed
docs.text: The steps below build a SWAT+ project for an area of your choice, run it and look at the output, with what each step produces. They do not go through QSWAT+ screen by screen.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Data:

  • A digital elevation model (DEM) covering your area, in a projected coordinate system, with no holes.
  • A soil map, either SSURGO (US), HWSD (global), or a custom raster paired with a soil property lookup table.
  • A land use map, either NLCD (US), ESA WorldCover (global), or a custom raster paired with a SWAT+ land use lookup table.
  • A daily climate record (precipitation and temperature at minimum, optionally solar radiation, wind, humidity) from one or more stations covering the simulation period.
  • An outlet point (the gauge or stream location you want to drain to).

Software:

  • QGIS with the QSWAT+ plugin, SWAT+ Editor and, for calibration, SWAT+ Toolbox. See Install.

docs.title: Step 1: Delineate the watershed (QSWAT+)
docs.text:
In QGIS, create a new QSWAT+ project and load the DEM. QSWAT+ will:

  1. Fill sinks in the DEM.
  2. Compute flow direction and accumulation.
  3. Build the stream network at a threshold drainage area you choose.
  4. Subdivide the watershed into subbasins at stream junctions.
  5. Snap your outlet point to the stream network.

Output: a polygon layer of subbasins and a polyline layer of channels (reaches).

docs.title: Step 2: Create HRUs
docs.text:
Overlay the land use map, soil map, and a slope class layer on the subbasins. Each unique combination of (subbasin, land use, soil, slope class) is a candidate HRU. QSWAT+ writes the HRUs and the connectivity files.

You can keep all candidate HRUs (high spatial detail, slow run) or filter by area threshold (faster, less detail).

Output: HRU definitions and *.con connectivity files.

docs.title: Step 3: Build the input files (SWAT+ Editor)
docs.text:
Open the project in SWAT+ Editor. The editor will:

  1. Import climate station data and write the .cli, .pcp, .tmp, and weather-wgn.cli files. Stations without data get filled by the weather generator.
  2. Populate soil layer parameters from the soil property table.
  3. Populate plant, fertiliser, tillage, and pesticide databases.
  4. Let you assign management schedules to each land use.
  5. Write the final input folder.

Set the simulation period and choose the outputs. Start the simulation one to three years before the period you want to analyse, and set the number of warm-up years in nyskip of print.prt so they are left out of the outputs.

Output: a folder of plain-text SWAT+ inputs, ready to run.

docs.title: Step 4: Run
docs.text:
Run the model from SWAT+ Editor, or from a terminal inside the project's TxtInOut folder:

cd path/to/your/project/Scenarios/Default/TxtInOut
path/to/swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-lin_x86_64-Rel

Watch for the Execution successfully completed message. Then read diagnostics.out: it lists every name that could not be matched (a management schedule, a weather station, a plant) and every missing file. Fix those before looking at results.

docs.title: Step 5: Look at output
docs.text:
Start with the basin water balance:

basin_wb_aa.txt

The annual-average precipitation, evapotranspiration, surface runoff, lateral flow, percolation, and water yield should be in the range you expect for your climate. If precipitation is far from the expected value, the weather stations are probably assigned wrongly. If ET takes up nearly all of the precipitation, check land use and plant parameters.

Then look at the channel output (basin_sd_cha_aa.txt or the per-channel channel_sd_aa.txt) for streamflow.

If you have measured streamflow at the outlet, compare to channel_sd_day.txt for the gauge channel.

docs.title: Step 6: Calibrate
docs.text: The first run is rarely a good match to observed data. Move on to Calibration to adjust parameters and improve the fit.

docs.title: Common first-run problems
docs.text:
• No precipitation anywhere: the climate station coordinates are outside the watershed extent, so QSWAT+ assigned every HRU to the weather generator instead of the station. Check weather-sta.cli.
  • Crops never grow: the management schedule is not assigned, or the planting date is outside the simulation period.
  • All flow is surface runoff: curve numbers are too high. Check cntable.lum and the soil hydrologic group.
  • Streamflow is zero downstream: a channel object has no upstream connection in chandeg.con or hru.con. Inspect the connectivity.
Sources
  • File names and groups: src/input_file_module.f90. Completion message: src/main.f90.in.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: SWAT+ has two parts: the model itself, a command-line program, and the tools used to build and edit projects (QSWAT+, SWAT+ Editor and SWAT+ Toolbox). Most users install the tools and let SWAT+ Editor run the model. The model can also be downloaded or built without the tools.

docs.title: SWAT+ tools
docs.text:
install.swat.tamu.edu has one-line installers for Windows, Linux and macOS. Each installer can be run again at any time to update.

Install all three tools at once:

# Linux and macOS
curl -fsSL https://install.swat.tamu.edu/all.sh | bash

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://install.swat.tamu.edu/all.ps1 | iex

Or one at a time:

Tool Purpose Linux and macOS Windows (PowerShell) QSWAT+ QGIS plugin that delineates the watershed, creates HRUs and writes the project database. Also installs the SWAT+ support data and TauDEM. Needs QGIS. curl -fsSL https://install.swat.tamu.edu/qsp.sh \| bash irm https://install.swat.tamu.edu/qsp.ps1 \| iex SWAT+ Editor Edits project inputs, writes the input files and runs the model. curl -fsSL https://install.swat.tamu.edu/spe.sh \| bash irm https://install.swat.tamu.edu/spe.ps1 \| iex SWAT+ Toolbox Sensitivity analysis, calibration and other tasks on a finished project. curl -fsSL https://install.swat.tamu.edu/spt.sh \| bash irm https://install.swat.tamu.edu/spt.ps1 \| iex

On Linux and macOS the tools go to ~/.local/share/SWATPlus/, and on Windows to %USERPROFILE%\SWATPlus\.

docs.title: Model executable
docs.text:
Every release on the GitHub releases page has prebuilt executables. For 62.0.1:

File System swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-win_amd64-Rel.zip Windows, 64-bit (gfortran build) swatplus-62.0.1-ifo-win_amd64-Rel.zip Windows, 64-bit (Intel Fortran build) swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-lin_x86_64-Rel.zip Linux, x86-64 (gfortran build) swatplus-62.0.1-ifx-lin_x86_64-Rel.zip Linux, x86-64 (Intel Fortran build) swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-lin_aarch64-Rel.zip Linux, ARM64 swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-mac_arm64-Rel.zip macOS, Apple silicon swatplus-62.0.1-ifo-mac_x86_64-Rel.zip macOS, Intel

Each zip contains a single executable with the same name (plus .exe on Windows). The name tells you the version, the compiler (gnu for gfortran, ifo for Intel Fortran Classic, ifx for Intel Fortran), the system and architecture, and Rel for an optimized release build. The gfortran and Intel builds give results that can differ slightly in the last digits.

Unzip the file and put the executable next to your project folder or in a folder on your PATH. On Linux and macOS, make it executable:

chmod +x swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-lin_x86_64-Rel

On macOS the first start of a downloaded program may be blocked; allow it under System Settings, Privacy and Security, or remove the quarantine flag with xattr -d com.apple.quarantine <file>.

To check the download, run it in an empty folder:

mkdir empty && cd empty
../swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-lin_x86_64-Rel

It prints a banner with the revision number and stops because there is no project:

                   SWAT+
             Revision 62.0.1
      Soil & Water Assessment Tool
GNU (13.3.0), 2026-10-19 22:51:37, Linux
    Program reading . . . executing

 Cannot find object.cnt input file

It also writes a few files (diagnostics.out, simulation.out, codes.bsn and others) into the folder. Run the model from inside a project folder; it reads its inputs from the current folder and writes the outputs there.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
Build from source to change the model or to use a development version. You need git, CMake 3.22 or newer, a Fortran compiler (gfortran, Intel ifx or ifort) and make or ninja.

git clone https://github.com/swat-model/swatplus.git
cd swatplus
git checkout 62.0.1
cmake -B build -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j 8

The executable is written to build/ with a name of the form swatplus-<version>-<compiler>-<system>_<arch>-Rel (-Dbg for a Debug build, no suffix when no build type is given). Builds from a commit between tags have a version such as 62.0.1-3-g1a2b3c4. The Developer Guide has instructions for Visual Studio, VS Code and Codespaces.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Run the reference dataset to check the executable from start to finish: Quick start: Ames_sub1.

Sources
  • Release files: SWAT+ 62.0.1 on GitHub, checked 20 October 2026; the banner above is from the gnu-lin_x86_64 executable.
  • Installers: install.swat.tamu.edu, checked 20 October 2026.
  • Executable naming: set(SWATPLUS_EXE "swatplus-${SWAT_VERSION}-${FFC}-${AR}${TY}") in CMakeLists.txt, with SWAT_VERSION from git describe --tags.
  • Build instructions: doc/Building.md.

docs.title: Project folder anatomy
docs.text: A SWAT+ project is one folder of plain-text files, usually called TxtInOut. The model reads every input from that folder and writes its outputs back into it. Weather data files can be kept in separate folders named in file.cio; everything else is in the one folder.

docs.title: The master file
docs.text:
file.cio is the index of the project. Each line names a group of inputs and the files to read for it, in a fixed order. null means that the file is not used. Read this file first when you open a project. The full description is on file.cio.

file.cio of the Ames_sub1 reference dataset at 62.0.1 (spacing shortened):

Output files end in _day, _mon, _yr or _aa (average annual) and .txt, or .csv when CSV output is switched on in print.prt. The first part of the name gives the object (basin_, lsunit_, hru_, channel_sd_, aquifer_, reservoir_, ...) and the next part the variables:

Code Variables wb water balance nb nutrient balance ls sediment and nutrient losses pw plant growth and stress aqu, sd_cha, res aquifer, channel, reservoir

The Output Reference describes each file.

Check simulation.out and diagnostics.out after every first run of a new or changed project.

Sources

  • Example: refdata/Ames_sub1/file.cio. The aquifer line contains nbull, a typing error in the shipped file; the dataset has no aquifers, so the name is never used.

docs.title: Quick start: Ames_sub1
docs.text: Run a complete SWAT+ simulation with the small reference dataset that comes with the source code.

docs.title: The dataset
docs.text: Ames_sub1 is a test dataset of 12 HRUs near Ames, Iowa, with no channels, aquifers or reservoirs. It simulates 1 January 1975 to 31 December 2020 on a daily time step. It is used to test the model and has not been calibrated. The folder is in the SWAT+ source repository at refdata/Ames_sub1.

docs.title: Before running
docs.text:
You need:

  • the SWAT+ executable (see Install);
  • a copy of the Ames_sub1 folder, either from a clone of the source repository or downloaded from the link above;
  • about 10 GB of free disk space. With the shipped print.prt the run writes daily carbon output for every HRU, about 9 GB in 62.0.1. To keep the output small, change the daily column of the hru_cb and hru_cb_vars rows in print.prt from l to n before running.

The shipped folder already contains output files from earlier model versions (for example basin_wb_aa.txt, written in 2024). A run with the shipped print.prt does not rewrite them, so check the date in the first line of an output file, or delete the old outputs (*_aa.txt, *_yr.txt, *_day.txt, *.out) from your copy before running.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
From a terminal, change into your copy of the folder and run the executable from there:

# Linux and macOS
cd path/to/Ames_sub1
path/to/swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-lin_x86_64-Rel

:: Windows
cd path\to\Ames_sub1
path\to\swatplus-62.0.1-gnu-win_amd64-Rel.exe

SWAT+ reads its inputs from the current folder, so always start it from inside the project folder. The run takes a few minutes; on a recent Linux workstation it took 4 minutes 20 seconds, most of it writing the daily carbon output.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
While it runs, SWAT+ prints the simulation date to the screen:

  Original Simulation            1  14  1994 Yr   20 of   46 Time  12:37:36

At the end, the screen and simulation.out show:

 Execution successfully completed

and the same line is written to success.fin.

With the shipped print.prt, a 62.0.1 run writes:

Files Content hru_wb_day.txt, hru_wb_aa.txt HRU water balance, daily and average annual hru_nb_day.txt, hru_nb_aa.txt, hru_ncycle_day.txt, hru_ncycle_aa.txt HRU nutrient balance and nitrogen cycle hru_ls_aa.txt HRU sediment and nutrient losses, average annual hru_pw_day.txt, hru_pw_aa.txt HRU plant growth and stress crop_yld_yr.txt, crop_yld_aa.txt, basin_crop_yld_yr.txt, basin_crop_yld_aa.txt crop yields hru_carbvars.txt, hru_cbn_lyr.txt, hru_seq_lyr.txt, hru_cflux_stat.txt, hru_cpool_stat.txt, hru_n_p_pool_stat.txt, hru_org_*_vars.txt, hru_plc_stat.txt, basin_carbon_all.txt, hru_begsim_soil_prop.txt, hru_endsim_soil_prop.txt carbon and soil organic matter mgt_out.txt, lu_change_out.txt management operations performed, land use changes simulation.out, diagnostics.out, checker.out, erosion.out, files_out.out, co2.out run log, warnings, input summaries

A few other files appear as well: paddy_test.csv (a rice paddy test output written on every run), wtps_wuses.wal and an empty file named null.

Open hru_wb_aa.txt to see the average annual water balance of each HRU. For the first HRU in this run:

precip surq_gen latq perc et 952.6 mm 34.7 mm 0.1 mm 0.0 mm 932.5 mm

The columns are described in Water balance outputs.

docs.title: Warnings in diagnostics.out
docs.text:
diagnostics.out lists anything the model could not match while reading the inputs. For Ames_sub1 at 62.0.1 it contains:

 agrr_lum      AGRR_rot      not found in management.sch
 soyb_lum      SOYB_rot      not found in management.sch
 oats_lum      OATS_rot      not found in management.sch
 wwht_lum      WWHT_rot      not found in management.sch
 ames.tem                    file not found (tgage)

The first four are land uses in landuse.lum that name management schedules missing from management.sch; no HRU uses those land uses. The last line means the station's temperature file, ames.tem in weather-sta.cli, is not in the list in tmp.cli (which names ames.tmp), so the model generates daily temperatures from the weather generator statistics in weather-wgn.cli. The Ames_sub1 walkthrough explains both. Check this file after every first run of a new project.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Cannot find object.cnt input file: SWAT+ was started outside the project folder. Change into the folder first.
  • Permission denied on Linux or macOS: run chmod +x on the executable.
  • A command or the model stops with no message: check free disk space.
  • The run stops early: read simulation.out, diagnostics.out and checker.out for the last message before the stop.

See FAQ and troubleshooting for other errors.

docs.title: Input reference
docs.text:
This section describes the SWAT+ input files for revision 62.0.1. Each page gives the purpose of a file, its columns with units and defaults, how the model uses the values, an example from the reference datasets, and the files it is linked to. Where the code behaves in a way a user would not expect (a column that is read but has no effect, a default that differs from the one SWAT+ Editor writes), the page says so.

Every page was checked against the SWAT+ source at the commit recorded as verified_at_commit in its front matter. Where the source and older documentation disagree, the pages follow the source. The last section of each page, Sources, links to the Fortran routines and lists the variable names for developers.

file.cio names every other input file, so it is the place to start.

docs.title: Older projects
docs.text:
A project set up for an earlier revision needs these changes before it runs correctly with 62.0.1:

  • The basin line of file.cio now has three file names, and the water_rights line has two. An old basin line shifts every later line of file.cio by one without a message. See older file.cio files.
  • The dynamic carbon model is now carbon = 2 in codes.bsn. With carbon = 1 no organic matter routine runs. See carbon model.
  • carb_coefs.cbn is no longer read. Its settings moved to carbon.bsn and carbon_lyr.bsn, and its output switch to print.prt.

docs.title: Simulation control
docs.text:
• file.cio: master index. Names the input file for every category, the weather data folders and the output folder.
  • time.sim: simulation period and number of time steps per day.
  • print.prt: warm-up years, daily print window and the output files written at each interval.
  • object.cnt: basin name, areas and the number of spatial objects of each type.

docs.title: Basin parameters
docs.text:
• codes.bsn: basin-wide method codes (PET method, channel routing, carbon model, runoff method and others).
  • parameters.bsn: basin-wide coefficients for runoff, peak rate, nutrients, pesticides, routing, lapse rates, erosion and CO₂.
  • carbon.bsn: parameters of the dynamic soil carbon model.
  • carbon_lyr.bsn: decomposition rates and CO₂ fractions of the dynamic soil carbon model, for the surface layer and the deeper layers.

docs.title: Spatial objects and connectivity
docs.text:
• Connect files: hru.con, rout_unit.con, chandeg.con, aquifer.con, reservoir.con, recall.con and the other connect files, which place each object, assign its weather station and route its outflow.
  • hru-data.hru: the records each HRU uses for topography, hydrology, soil, land use, initial conditions, surface storage, snow and field geometry.
  • Hydrology and topography: hydrology.hyd, topography.hyd, field.fld and shade_factor.shf.
  • Recall: point sources and inlets given as time series.
  • hru-lte.hru: the simplified HRU-lte objects.
  • Routing and landscape units: rout_unit.def, rout_unit.ele, rout_unit.rtu, ls_unit.def, ls_unit.ele and aqu_catunit.ele.
  • Link files: chan-surf.lin for overbank flow to floodplain HRUs and aqu_cha.lin for aquifer return flow to several channels.

docs.title: Climate
docs.text:
• Climate files: weather stations (weather-sta.cli), weather generator statistics (weather-wgn.cli), the lists of observed data files and atmospheric deposition.
  • *.pcp: measured daily or sub-daily precipitation for one gauge.
  • *.tmp: measured daily maximum and minimum air temperature for one gauge.
  • *.tem: temperature files with the .tem extension, read like .tmp files.
  • snow.sno: snowfall, snowmelt and snow cover parameters.

docs.title: Soils and land use
docs.text:
• soils.sol: soil profiles and layer properties.
  • landuse.lum: land use and management records used by HRUs.
  • Land use tables: curve number, conservation practice and overland flow Manning's n tables named in landuse.lum.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
• Channel group: the channel line of file.cio and which of its files are used, initial channel contents, stream temperature and the legacy channel files.
  • Chandeg channel files: channel-lte.cha, hyd-sed-lte.cha, sed_nut.cha and nutrients.cha, with the geometry, hydraulic, sediment and water quality parameters of the channels SWAT+ routes.

docs.title: Aquifers, reservoirs and wetlands
docs.text:
• Aquifer files: aquifer.aqu and its initial conditions.
  • Reservoir files: reservoir.res and its initial condition, hydrology, sediment, nutrient and weir databases.
  • Wetland files: wetland.wet and hydrology.wet, for HRUs with ponded water including rice paddies.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
• Operation databases: harvest, grazing, irrigation, chemical application, fire and street sweeping.
  • Decision tables: lum.dtl, res_rel.dtl, scen_lu.dtl and flo_con.dtl.
  • plants.plt: plant parameter database.
  • fertilizer.frt: fertilizer and manure databases.
  • tillage.til: tillage implements and biological mixing.
  • carb_coefs.cbn: no longer read in 62.0.1.
  • treatment.trt: placeholder file, not read.
  • Manure allocation: manure sources and the HRUs that draw from them.
  • Management schedules and other inputs: management.sch, puddle.ops, transplant.ops, co2_yr.dat and object.prt.

docs.title: Initial conditions
docs.text: • Initialization files: plant.ini, soil_plant.ini, nutrients.sol and om_water.ini. Pesticide, pathogen, salt and constituent initial conditions are on the pages for those modules.

docs.title: Structural practices
docs.text: • Structural practice files: tile drains, septic systems, filter strips, grassed waterways, user-defined practices, the septic and urban databases, and saturated buffers.

docs.title: Pollutants
docs.text:
• Pesticides: pesticide.pes, initial pesticide amounts and the metabolite chain.
  • Pathogens: pathogens.pth and initial pathogen amounts.
  • Heavy metals: heavy metal inputs.

docs.title: Groundwater
docs.text: • gwflow: the cell-based groundwater module, used in place of the lumped aquifers when gwflow = 1 in codes.bsn.

docs.title: Salts and constituents
docs.text:
• Salt module: inputs for the eight major salt ions.
  • Constituent module: constituents.cs and the inputs for selenate, selenite and boron.

docs.title: Water allocation
docs.text:
• Water allocation: places of use, points of diversion and return, and the treatment, use, tower, canal, pipe and outside-basin files.
Sources
  • File names and their order in file.cio: readcio_read.f90 and input_file_module.f90.
  • Each page lists the readers and the routines that use its inputs in its Sources section.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
aquifer.aqu contains the properties of the one-dimensional aquifers: initial water table, specific yield, baseflow recession, deep seepage, revap and groundwater nitrate and phosphorus. Each aquifer object in aquifer.con selects a row by number in its aqu column. The aquifer line of file.cio names two files, initial.aqu and aquifer.aqu (in that order); either can be null.

A model has one aquifer object per row of aquifer.con. Usually there is a shallow aquifer for each land area and one or more deep aquifers that receive the seepage of the shallow ones. Models that simulate groundwater with the gwflow grid model use gwflow.con instead of these aquifers.

initial.aqu lists named sets of initial-condition files. In 62.0.1 its rows are read but not used; initial pesticides, pathogens, salts and constituents of aquifers come from initial.aqu_cs, described below.

docs.title: aquifer.aqu
docs.text:
Free format, whitespace-separated. Line 1 is a title and line 2 the column header; both are skipped. Each later line is one aquifer property set with 18 values in this order. The reader does not match columns by header name.

# Column Units Built-in value Typical range Description 1 id - - - Number of the property set. The aqu column of aquifer.con refers to the row by this number. 2 name - - - Name of the aquifer. Not used by the model. 3 init - - - Name of an initial-condition set, matched against initial.aqu_cs. See initial.aqu_cs. 4 gw_flo mm 0.05 0 to 2 Return flow on the day before the simulation starts. It starts the recession, and sets the water volume for the initial nitrate mass. 5 dep_bot m 0 0 to 10 Depth from the mid-slope surface to the bottom of the aquifer. Must be larger than dep_wt. 6 dep_wt m 0 0 to 10 Initial depth from the mid-slope surface to the water table. 7 no3_n mg N/L 0 0 to 1000 Initial nitrate-N concentration. 8 sol_p mg P/L 0 0 to 1000 Mineral P concentration of the water entering the stream, constant through the run. 9 carbon % 0.5 0 to 15 Organic carbon content. Reported in the aquifer output; not used in any calculation in 62.0.1. 10 flo_dist m 50 0 to 1000 Average flow distance to the stream. Not used. 11 bf_max mm 0 0 to 2 Return flow at which all channels linked to the aquifer receive groundwater. Used only when aquifer flow is distributed to channels with aqu_cha.lin. 12 alpha_bf 1/day 0 0 to 1 Baseflow recession constant. 13 revap - 0 0 to 1 Revap coefficient: revap as a fraction of potential evapotranspiration. 14 rchg_dp fraction 0 0 to 1 Fraction of the day's recharge that leaves the aquifer as deep seepage. 15 spec_yld m³/m³ 0 0 to 0.4 Specific yield: the volume of water drained by gravity per volume of aquifer. Must be above 0. 16 hl_no3n days 30 0 to 200 Half-life of nitrate in the aquifer. 17 flo_min m 0 0 to 10 Water table depth for return flow: the aquifer sends return flow only while the water table is at this depth below the surface or shallower. 18 revap_min m 0 0 to 10 Water table depth for revap: revap occurs only while the water table is shallower than this depth.

The built-in values apply when aquifer.con points to a number between 1 and the largest id that has no row in the file. They are not filled in for missing columns.

Give every row an id, and keep the ids unique. The ids do not have to be consecutive.

docs.title: Aquifer water balance
docs.text: Each day, for each aquifer, in this order. Depths of water are in mm over the aquifer area (the area column of aquifer.con).

docs.title: Storage and water table
docs.text:
At the start of the run the stored water is

\[S_0 = 1000\,(\mathrm{dep\_bot} - \mathrm{dep\_wt})\;\mathrm{spec\_yld}\]

Each day the recharge \(R\), all water routed into the aquifer from HRUs, routing units and other aquifers, is added to storage, and withdrawals for water allocation are then taken. Irrigation drawn from the aquifer by decision tables is removed from storage when it is applied. The water table depth follows from the storage:

\[h = \max\!\left(0,\ \mathrm{dep\_bot} - \frac{S}{1000\;\mathrm{spec\_yld}}\right)\]

The aquifer calculation in 62.0.1 has no recharge delay: recharge is added on the day it arrives.

docs.title: Return flow
docs.text:
When \(h \le\) flo_min, return flow follows the baseflow recession

\[Q_d = Q_{d-1}\,e^{-\alpha} + R_d\,\left(1 - e^{-\alpha}\right)\]

limited to between zero and the storage, where \(\alpha\) is alpha_bf. When \(h >\) flo_min, \(Q_d = 0\), and the next day's recession starts from zero.

The recession constant is a direct index of how fast groundwater flow responds to recharge (Smedema and Rycroft, 1983). Values are about 0.1 to 0.3 for land with a slow response and 0.9 to 1.0 for land with a rapid response. It is best estimated from measured streamflow during periods without recharge. When the number of baseflow days \(BFD\) (the days for baseflow to decline through one log cycle) is known,

\[\alpha = \frac{1}{BFD}\,\ln 10 = \frac{2.3}{BFD}\]

Return flow leaves through the outflows of type tot in aquifer.con.

docs.title: Deep seepage
docs.text:
\[\mathrm{seep}_d = \mathrm{rchg\_dp}\;R_d\]

limited to the storage. Seepage leaves through the outflows of type rhg in aquifer.con, usually to a deep aquifer. Without such an outflow it leaves the model.

docs.title: Revap
docs.text:
When \(h <\) revap_min,

\[\mathrm{revap}_d = \mathrm{revap}\;PET_d\]

limited to the storage, where \(PET_d\) is the potential evapotranspiration at the aquifer's weather station (mm). Revap represents water that moves from the aquifer into the unsaturated zone above it when that zone is dry, and uptake by deep-rooted plants. It is removed from the aquifer and not added to the soil. As revap approaches 0, the transfer is restricted; as it approaches 1, revap approaches the potential evapotranspiration.

docs.title: Nitrate and phosphorus
docs.text:
Nitrate recharge is added to the stored nitrate \(N\) (kg/ha). The concentration is \(c = N/S\), and the nitrate leaving with return flow and seepage is \(c\,Q\) and \(c\,\mathrm{seep}\). Each day the remaining nitrate decays by

\[N \leftarrow N\,\exp\!\left(\frac{-0.693}{\mathrm{hl\_no3n} + 0.1}\right)\]

The decay represents uptake by bacteria and chemical conversion where the aquifer is depleted of oxygen; it is the net loss from all processes.

The initial nitrate mass is \(10\,\mathrm{gw\_flo}\,A\,\mathrm{no3\_n}/1000\), the concentration times the volume of one day's initial return flow (\(A\) in ha). This is a mass in kg for the whole aquifer, but the daily calculation treats the store as kg/ha, so the initial store scales with the aquifer area. It does not use the stored water \(S_0\).

Soluble P in the return flow is \(\mathrm{sol\_p}\) times the day's recharge volume (m³), divided by 1000, in kg. The load therefore follows the recharge. It appears on days with recharge even when there is no return flow, and is zero on days without recharge. The aquifer stores no phosphorus between days.

docs.title: Pesticides, salts and constituents
docs.text:
Pesticides entering with recharge are added to the aquifer store and decay with the aquifer half-life of pesticide.pes (adjusted to temperature when the temperature decay option is on). The concentration is the stored mass divided by \(f\,S + Q + \mathrm{revap} + \mathrm{seep}\), where \(f\) is the pesticide groundwater mixing factor of parameters.bsn. Return flow and seepage take pesticide out at that concentration, all of it dissolved. Revap takes none.

Salts and other constituents (see salt and cs) are mixed in the stored water and leave with return flow and seepage at the stored concentration.

docs.title: Aquifer flow to channels with aqu_cha.lin
docs.text: When aqu_cha.lin links aquifers to channels (see file.cio), the return flow is spread over the linked channels as each channel is routed: on the same day when the aquifer comes before the channel in the routing order, otherwise on the next day. The length of channel that receives flow is the total linked channel length times \(Q/\mathrm{bf\_max}\); when \(Q \ge\) bf_max all linked channels receive flow, and when it is lower only part of the channel length does, each channel in proportion to its length. Set bf_max to a value above zero whenever aqu_cha.lin is used.

docs.title: Calibration and decision tables
docs.text:
These parameters can be changed during calibration through calibration.cal (see parameter change files): flo_init_mm (gw_flo), dep_bot, dep_wt_init (dep_wt), no3_init (no3_n), minp_init (sol_p), cbn_init (carbon), flo_dist, bf_max, alpha (alpha_bf), revap_co (revap), deep_seep (rchg_dp), sp_yld (spec_yld), hlife_n (hl_no3n), flo_min and revap_min.

Calibration changes are applied after the aquifers are initialised. A change to sp_yld recalculates the storage from the current water table, and a change to no3_init recalculates the nitrate mass. Changes to flo_init_mm and dep_wt_init come too late to change the initial state and have no effect. A change to dep_bot does not change the stored water; it moves the water table that is calculated from it.

The decision table condition aqu_dep tests the water table depth of an aquifer (m). See decision tables.

docs.title: initial.aqu
docs.text:
Named sets of initial-condition files, in the same layout as initial.cha. Two header lines are skipped, then one set per line. The Editor adds a trailing description value, which the reader ignores.

# Column Description 1 name Name of the set. 2 org_min Name of an organic-mineral initial record. 3 pest Name of a pesticide initial record. 4 path Name of a pathogen initial record. 5 hmet Name of a heavy metal initial record. 6 salt Name of a salt initial record.

In 62.0.1 the rows are read and nothing is done with them: the init column of aquifer.aqu is not matched against this file, and the aquifer's initial water and nitrate come from aquifer.aqu.

docs.title: initial.aqu_cs
docs.text:
An optional file with a fixed name, read when present. Two header lines are skipped, then one row per line with six names: name, pest, path, hmet, salt and cs.

  • pest names a row in pest_water.ini. The initial pesticide in the aquifer (kg/ha) is the water concentration (mg/kg) times an assumed bulk density of 2.0 t/m³ times dep_bot times 10.
  • path names a row in path_water.ini.
  • hmet is read but not used.
  • salt names a row in salt_aqu.ini: initial salt ion concentrations (g/m³) and salt mineral fractions.
  • cs names a row in cs_aqu.ini: initial constituent concentrations (g/m³) and sorbed concentrations (mg/kg).

Pesticide and pathogen rows are selected by matching name with the init column of aquifer.aqu. Salt and constituent rows are selected by position instead: aquifer 3 (the third row of aquifer.con) uses row 3 of initial.aqu_cs, whatever its name. Salt and constituent masses are the concentrations times the initial stored water.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
refdata/Osu_1hru in the SWAT+ repository:

(three of the 21 rows)

The shallow aquifers start with the water table 6 m below a 10 m deep aquifer, so they contain \(1000 \times (10 - 6) \times 0.05 = 200\) mm of water. Return flow and revap both need the water table within 5 m of the surface, so neither occurs until recharge raises it by 1 m (50 mm of storage). The recession constant of 0.95 1/day gives a fast response. One percent of recharge goes to deep seepage. hl_no3n is 0, which gives a daily nitrate decay factor of \(e^{-6.93}\), so nearly all nitrate entering the aquifer is lost on the day it arrives.

The deep aquifer aqu_deep010 has dep_wt = 20 m, below its dep_bot of 10 m, so its initial storage is negative (\(1000 \times (10 - 20) \times 0.03 = -300\) mm) and the water table starts 20 m down. It is recharged by the seepage the shallow aquifers send to it. With flo_min = 0 it sends return flow only when the water table reaches the surface, and with revap_min = 0 it has no revap.
