docs.title: water allocation
docs.text:
Warning

In revision 62.0.1 the water allocation calculation follows these inputs only for a network with a single place of use, other than an irrigation district, whose POD lines are listed in POD-number order. Other layouts can take the wrong amounts or stop the run, and several columns are read but have no effect. See Limitations in 62.0.1 before setting up a network.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Water allocation moves water from where it is taken to where it is used: irrigation districts, towns, industry, treatment plants, reservoirs, canals and places outside the basin. Revision 62.0.1 describes the network with three kinds of object:

  • A place of use (POU) is where water goes: an irrigation district, a water treatment plant, a water use, a water tower, a canal, a channel, a reservoir, an aquifer or a receiver outside the basin. Each POU has a daily demand (its duty).
  • A point of diversion (POD) is where water is taken: a channel, reservoir, aquifer, canal, water tower, outside-basin source or an unlimited source. A POD can supply several POUs, and a POU can draw on several PODs.
  • A point of return (POR) is where a POU sends water after it has been used or treated: back to a channel, reservoir or aquifer, on to another treatment plant or use, or out of the basin.

Two files define the network: place_of_use.wro lists every POU with its PODs and PORs, and point_of_diver.wro lists every POD with the POUs it serves. The .wal files describe the objects between them: treatment plants, water uses, water towers, canals, pipes, irrigation districts and outside-basin sources.

This structure replaces the water_allocation.wro transfer file of earlier revisions, whose columns in earlier documentation (rule_typ, srcs, ob_typ, withdr, limit_mon, cha_ob, rcv_ob, rcv_num) have no counterpart in 62.0.1. water_allocation.wro, element.wro and water_rights.wro are no longer read.

docs.title: Files and activation
docs.text:
File Name set by Contents place_of_use.wro water_rights line of file.cio, first name Places of use, with their PODs and PORs point_of_diver.wro water_rights line of file.cio, second name Points of diversion and the POUs each serves water_hru_irr.wal fixed name HRUs in each irrigation district wtps_wuses.wal fixed name Numbers of treatment plants and water uses water_treat.wal fixed name Water treatment plants water_use.wal fixed name Water uses (domestic, industrial, commercial) outside_src.wal fixed name Sources outside the basin om_treat.wal, om_use.wal, om_osrc.wal fixed names Water quality sets for treated water, used water and outside sources water_tower.wal fixed name Water towers (storage) water_canal.wal fixed name Canals water_pipe.wal fixed name Pipes outside_rcv.wal fixed name Receivers outside the basin (not read)

The water_rights line of file.cio now takes two file names, the POU file and the POD file, with defaults place_of_use.wro and point_of_diver.wro. A file.cio written for an earlier revision has water_allocation.wro element.wro water_rights.wro on that line, and SWAT+ 62.0.1 then reads water_allocation.wro as the POU file and element.wro as the POD file. Update the line before running an older project; older file.cio files explains how the old line is read.

Water allocation runs when the POU file has at least one place of use. If a .wro file or wtps_wuses.wal is missing, or the line in file.cio says null, SWAT+ creates an empty file of that name in the run folder (a file called null in the second case) and reads nothing from it. The empty file does no harm.

All files have a title on line 1. The .wro files and most .wal files then give the number of records on line 2 and a column header on line 3. Records are read as free-format values separated by spaces, by position, so the header text is not checked.

docs.title: Daily sequence
docs.text:
Each day, before any object is simulated:

  1. The day's POD and POR totals are set to zero.
  2. Outside-basin source PODs, water tower PODs and unlimited PODs give water to their POUs.
  3. POUs with no PODs (a treatment plant or use fed only by returns from other POUs) treat or use the water they have stored and pass it to their PORs.
  4. The demand of every POU is set, from rate_max or from its decision table, and split among its PODs by frac (or by a decision table).

During the day, natural PODs give water when their object is simulated: a channel POD after the channel is routed (the water comes out of the channel's outflow for the day), a reservoir POD after the day's inflow is added, an aquifer POD after recharge is added. A canal POD gives water when the canal receives water.

Each time a POD gives water, every POU whose PODs have all given water for the day receives it. Water delivered to a POU that is a treatment plant, use or canal is processed at once (treated, used, or routed through the canal), and the POU's outflow is passed to its PORs.

Because step 2 runs before step 4, outside-source, water tower and unlimited PODs work with the previous day's demand, and with zero demand on the first day.

docs.title: place_of_use.wro
docs.text: Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of POUs, line 3 a header. Each POU then takes one line, followed by one line for each of its PODs and one line for each of its PORs.

docs.title: POU line
docs.text: # Column Units Description 1 num - POU number, 1 to the number on line 2. The record is stored under this number. 2 name - POU name. 3 typ - POU type, from the table below. 4 typ_num - Number of the object of that type that receives the water (for example the channel number, or the record number in water_treat.wal). For irr, the record number in water_hru_irr.wal. 5 pods - Number of POD lines that follow. 0 for a POU fed only by returns from other POUs. 6 pors - Number of POR lines that follow. 7 dtbl_mx - Name of a flow control decision table (flo_con.dtl) that sets the daily demand, or null. 8 rate_max m³/s Maximum demand rate. Without a decision table the POU demands \(\mathrm{rate\_max} \times 86400\) m³ every day. With a decision table, its demand is capped at that amount. 9 dtbl_pod_fr - Name of a flow control decision table that sets the fraction taken from each POD, or null to use the frac column of the POD lines. 10 dtbl_por_fr - Name of a flow control decision table that sets the fraction sent to each POR, or null to use the frac column of the POR lines. POU type Water goes to irr The HRUs of an irrigation district in water_hru_irr.wal cha A channel (added to the channel's inflow) res A reservoir aqu An aquifer wtp A water treatment plant in water_treat.wal use A water use in water_use.wal wtow A water tower in water_tower.wal can A canal in water_canal.wal orcv A receiver outside the basin in outside_rcv.wal

docs.title: POD lines
docs.text:
One line per POD, starting with the word POD.

# Column Units Description 1 kind - The word POD. 2 num - Not used (overwritten by column 5). 3 name - POD name, for reference. 4 typ - POD type, for reference. The type used is the one in point_of_diver.wro. 5 typ_num - Object number, for reference. 6 conv_typ - Conveyance type, pipe or pump. Read but not used. 7 conv_num - Conveyance number. Read but not used. 8 dtbl_min - Decision table for the minimum level. Read but not used. 9 const_min depends on POD type Minimum level below which the POD gives no water. See the POD type table under point_of_diver.wro. 10 dtbl_wdraw - Name of a flow control decision table that manages the annual withdrawal limit, or null. When a name is given, the limit is not reset at the start of each year; the duty_reset decision table action resets it instead. 11 ann_max m³/s Annual withdrawal limit for this POD and POU. Once the volume taken during the year reaches \(\mathrm{ann\_max} \times 86400\) m³, the POD gives this POU no more water until the limit is reset. 12 frac fraction Fraction of the POU's daily demand taken from this POD. The fractions of a POU's PODs normally add up to 1. 13 comp - y to let this POD make up a shortfall when the POU's PODs together delivered less than its demand, n otherwise. Channel PODs cannot make up a shortfall.

docs.title: POR lines
docs.text:
One line per POR, starting with the word POR.

# Column Units Description 1 kind - The word POR. 2 num - Not used (overwritten by column 5). 3 name - POR name, for reference. 4 typ - Receiving object type: cha, res, aqu, wtp, use, wtow, can or orcv. hru is accepted but receives nothing. 5 typ_num - Number of the receiving object of that type. 6 conv_typ - Conveyance type. Read but not used. 7 conv_num - Conveyance number. Read but not used. 8 dtbl_max - Read but not used. 9 const_max - Read but not used. 10 ann_max - Read but not used. 11 frac fraction Fraction of the POU's outflow sent to this POR.

A water treatment plant POU sends each POR its frac of the treated water, and a water use POU sends each POR its frac of its effluent. For the other POU types, canals included, each POR receives its frac of the water withdrawn for the POU, in addition to the delivery to the POU itself.

docs.title: point_of_diver.wro
docs.text:
Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of PODs, line 3 a header. Each POD takes one line: five fixed columns, then six columns for each POU it serves.

# Column Units Description 1 num - POD number. 2 name - POD name. 3 typ - POD type, from the table below. 4 typ_num - Number of the object of that type (channel number, reservoir number, record number in outside_src.wal, and so on). 5 pous - Number of POUs served. 6 to 11 pou_num, pou_name, pod_num, pou_typ, pou_typ_num, right - Repeated for each POU: the POU number in place_of_use.wro, its name, the position of this POD among that POU's POD lines, the POU type and object number, and the water right (sr senior, jr junior).

The right column is read but does not change the order of withdrawals in 62.0.1.

POD type Water taken from Meaning of const_min cha Channel outflow for the day Minimum daily flow volume (m³). No water is taken on days when the channel outflow is at or below it. res Reservoir storage Fraction of the principal spillway volume. No water is taken when storage is at or below it. aqu Aquifer storage Water table depth (m). Water is taken only while the water table is shallower than this depth. can Canal storage Fraction of the current canal storage, so values up to 1 set no limit. wtow Water tower storage Fraction of the current tower storage, so values below 1 set no limit. osrc Outside-basin source Not used. unl Unlimited source with no water quality Not used. hru Accepted, gives no water - gwf Accepted, gives no water -

The amount taken is the POD's duty (its frac of the POU demand), limited by the water the object has above the minimum. Withdrawals from channels, reservoirs, canals and towers take sediment and nutrients with the water in proportion. Aquifer withdrawals take water, nitrate and mineral P.

Two types do not follow this rule:

  • An osrc POD gives its frac of the daily volume available from the outside source, whatever the POU demand. The available volume is the flo value of the om_osrc.wal record with the same number as the source. The water has no sediment or nutrients.
  • A unl POD gives \(\mathrm{frac}\) times its duty, which is \(\mathrm{frac}^2\) times the POU demand.

docs.title: water_hru_irr.wal
docs.text:
Irrigation districts for irr POUs. Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of districts, line 3 a header. Each district takes one line with its name and number of HRUs, followed by one line per HRU.

Line Columns Description District name, num_hrus District name and the number of HRU lines that follow. HRU hru, dtbl_lum HRU number and the name of the decision table in lum.dtl that sets its irrigation demand.

The demand of an irrigation POU is meant to be the sum of the demands of its HRUs, set by their decision tables. See Limitations in 62.0.1 for how 62.0.1 handles it.

docs.title: wtps_wuses.wal
docs.text:
Sets up storage for treatment plants and water uses. It is needed whenever water_treat.wal or water_use.wal is used.

Line Contents 1 Title 2 Number of treatment plants, number of water uses 3 Header (skipped) 4 Names of the treatment plants 5 Names of the water uses

The two numbers must match the number of records in water_treat.wal and water_use.wal. Lines 4 and 5 must both be present, even when one of the numbers is 0. The names are read but not used.

docs.title: water_treat.wal
docs.text:
Water treatment plants. Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of plants, line 3 a header. Each plant takes one line, followed by one line per treatment level.

Plant line:

# Column Units Description 1 name - Plant name. 2 stor_mx m³ Maximum storage. Read but not used. 3 lag_days days Treatment time. Read but not used: treated water leaves the same day. 4 loss_fr fraction Water loss during treatment. Read but not used; the loss comes from the flo value of the quality set. 5 num_treats - Number of treatment level lines that follow.

Treatment level line:

# Column Description 1 org_min_typ How the quality of the treated water is set: const (a record in om_treat.wal), dtbl (a decision table) or recall (a recall record). 2 org_min_name Name of the om_treat.wal record, decision table or recall record. 3, 4 pests_typ, pests_name Same pair for pesticides. Read but not used. 5, 6 paths_typ, paths_name Same pair for pathogens. Read but not used. 7, 8 salts_typ, salts_name Same pair for salt ions. Read but not used. 9, 10 constit_typ, constit_name Same pair for other constituents. Read but not used. 11 description Text.

If the project has pesticides, each treatment level line is followed by a header line and a line of pesticide concentrations in the treated water, one value per pesticide. If it has pathogens, a header line and a line of pathogen concentrations follow in the same way.

When a plant has more than one treatment level, the last level sets the quality of the outflow.

Treated outflow to each POR is

\[Q_{out} = V_{stor}\; f_{\mathrm{om}}\; \mathrm{frac}_{POR}\]

where \(V_{stor}\) is the water delivered to the plant that day (m³), \(f_{\mathrm{om}}\) is the flo value of the quality set (the fraction of water that leaves the plant after treatment losses) and \(\mathrm{frac}_{POR}\) is the POR's fraction. Sediment and nutrient loads are the quality set's concentrations times \(Q_{out}\), limited to the loads that came into the plant. The difference between incoming and outgoing loads is reported as the amount removed by treatment.

docs.title: water_use.wal
docs.text:
Water uses (domestic, industrial, commercial). Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of uses, line 3 a header. Each use takes one line, followed by the optional pesticide and pathogen lines described for water_treat.wal.

# Column Units Description 1 name - Use name. 2 stor_mx m³ Maximum storage. Read but not used. 3 lag_days days Read but not used. 4 loss_fr fraction Read but not used. 5 to 14 org_min_typ, org_min_name, ... constit_typ, constit_name - Quality pairs as in a water_treat.wal treatment level. org_min_name names a record in om_use.wal when the type is const. 15 description - Text.

The outflow of a use is the water delivered that day times the flo value of its om_use.wal record (the fraction returned as effluent), with the record's concentrations. Each POR receives its frac of the outflow.

docs.title: outside_src.wal
docs.text:
Sources outside the basin, used by osrc PODs. Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of sources, line 3 a header. Each source takes one line, followed by the optional pesticide and pathogen lines described for water_treat.wal.

# Column Description 1 name Source name. 2 to 11 org_min_typ, org_min_name, ... constit_typ, constit_name Quality pairs as in a water_treat.wal treatment level. org_min_name names a record in om_osrc.wal when the type is const. 12 description Text.

docs.title: om_treat.wal, om_use.wal and om_osrc.wal
docs.text:
Water quality sets for treated water, used water (effluent) and outside sources. Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of records, line 3 a header. Each record is a name followed by 18 values.

# Column Units Description 1 name - Record name. 2 flo see text In om_treat.wal and om_use.wal, the fraction of the incoming water that leaves the plant or use. In om_osrc.wal, the volume available from the source each day (m³). 3 sed mg/L Sediment. 4 orgn mg N/L Organic nitrogen. 5 sedp mg P/L Organic phosphorus. 6 no3 mg N/L Nitrate nitrogen. 7 solp mg P/L Soluble (mineral) phosphorus. 8 chla mg/L Chlorophyll a. 9 nh3 mg N/L Ammonia nitrogen. 10 no2 mg N/L Nitrite nitrogen. 11 cbod mg/L Carbonaceous biological oxygen demand. 12 dox mg/L Dissolved oxygen. 13 to 18 san, sil, cla, sag, lag, grv mg/L Sand, silt, clay, small aggregates, large aggregates and gravel. 19 temp °C Water temperature.

docs.title: water_tower.wal
docs.text:
Water towers: storage between a source and its users. Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of towers, line 3 a header, then one line per tower.

# Column Units Description 1 id - Tower number. 2 name - Tower name. 3 stor_mx m³ Storage capacity. Used by the wtow_vol decision table condition and the fill_wtow action. 4 ddown_days days Read but not used. 5 loss_fr fraction Read but not used.

A tower is filled by a wtow POU and emptied by a wtow POD. Its water quality does not change in storage.

docs.title: water_canal.wal
docs.text:
Canals. Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of canals, line 3 a header, then one line per canal.

# Column Units Description 1 id - Canal number. 2 name - Canal name. 3 w_sta - Nearby weather station. Read but not used. 4 init - Initial concentrations. Read but not used. 5 dtbl - Decision table for canal outflow. Must be null in 62.0.1: with any other name the canal releases no water. 6 ddown_days days Days to draw the storage down. Each day the canal releases its storage divided by ddown_days. 7 w m Bottom width. 8 d m Depth. 9 l km Length. 10 s m/m Slope. Read but not used. 11 ss m/m Side slope (horizontal to vertical) of the trapezoidal section. 12 sat_con mm/day Seepage rate from the canal bed to groundwater. 13 evap_co fraction Fraction of the canal storage kept after evaporation each day. 1 means no evaporation loss; 0 empties the canal. 14 num_aqu - Number of aquifers that receive seepage. 15 onward aqu_fr fraction One value per aquifer: the fraction of the seepage that goes to aquifer 1, aquifer 2, and so on. The aquifers are always the first num_aqu aquifers of the model, in order.

The canal capacity is computed from its shape as \(V_{max} = (w + ss\,d)\,d\,l \times 1000\) m³ (with \(l\) in km), and is used by the fill_can decision table action.

When a canal receives water, it first supplies any POUs for which it is a POD. Evaporation is then applied, and seepage of \(\mathrm{sat\_con} \times d \times l\) m³ is divided among the aquifers by their fractions, with nitrate and soluble P in proportion. Finally the canal releases its storage divided by ddown_days. In 62.0.1 this release is removed from the canal but is not passed on; the PORs of a canal POU receive their share of the water withdrawn for the canal instead.

When gwflow canal seepage is switched on, gwflow takes canal width, depth and sat_con from this file. It also expects a bed thickness, a diversion ID and start and end days for each canal, which water_canal.wal does not supply in 62.0.1, so gwflow treats every canal as connected to a channel.

docs.title: water_pipe.wal
docs.text:
Pipes. In 62.0.1 pipes are read but have no effect: water moves from PODs to POUs and from POUs to PORs without conveyance losses.

Line 1 is a title, line 2 the number of pipes, line 3 a header. For each pipe the reader then takes a header line and two record lines: the first gives the number of aquifers, and the second is read as the full record. Both record lines have the same layout:

# Column Units Description 1 id - Pipe number. 2 name - Pipe name. 3 stor_mx m³ Maximum storage. 4 ddown_days days Drawdown time. 5 loss_fr fraction Water lost along the pipe. 6 num_aqu - Number of aquifers that receive the loss. 7 onward aqu_fr fraction One value per aquifer: fraction of the loss to that aquifer.

docs.title: outside_rcv.wal
docs.text: Receivers outside the basin, with columns id, name and filename (an output file for the receiver). SWAT+ 62.0.1 does not read this file, so orcv POUs and PORs have no receiving object.

docs.title: Decision tables
docs.text:
Water allocation uses flow control decision tables (flo_con.dtl) and land use decision tables (lum.dtl). See decision tables for the file format.

Item Kind Effect wallo_dmd with option set_dmd action Sets the POU demand to the action's constant (m³). wallo_dmd with option irr_dmd action Adds the current demand of the POU named by the action's object number. wallo_dmd with option fill_res, fill_wtow or fill_can action Sets the demand to the volume needed to fill a reservoir (to a fraction of its principal or emergency volume), a water tower or a canal (to a fraction of capacity), times a second constant. duty_reset action Sets a new annual withdrawal limit for one POD of one POU and resets the volume taken so far. irr_pou_dmd condition Tests the current demand of a POU. wtow_vol condition Tests water tower storage as a fraction of stor_mx.

docs.title: Limitations in 62.0.1
docs.text:
Several parts of the daily calculation do not follow the input structure above:

  • The duty used for a withdrawal is looked up with the POD's number and the position of the POU in that POD's list, in place of the POU's number and the POD's position in that POU. Results follow the input only when these coincide: POD number \(n\) is the \(n\)-th POD line of every POU it serves, and the \(k\)-th POU listed for a POD in point_of_diver.wro is POU number \(k\). A network with one POU whose POD lines are listed in POD-number order meets this. Other layouts take the wrong duty or fail.
  • For an irrigation district (irr POU), the HRU demands from the district's decision tables are summed and then replaced by \(\mathrm{rate\_max} \times 86400\), so the POU always demands its maximum rate. Delivery to the district does not step through the listed HRUs.
  • No decision table action sets the POD and POR fractions, so naming a table in dtbl_pod_fr or dtbl_por_fr sets all fractions to zero.
  • For an aquifer POD, the water delivered is computed after the aquifer storage has been reduced, so it is smaller than the water removed from the aquifer by the factor \((1 - r)\), where \(r\) is the fraction of storage withdrawn.
  • Projects with pesticides or pathogens fail when water_treat.wal, water_use.wal or outside_src.wal is read, because the storage for the treated-water concentrations is not set up.
  • Water taken by start-of-day PODs (outside sources, towers, unlimited sources) is not counted in the day's delivered totals, which are reset when the day's demand is set.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A town water use that draws on a channel and an aquifer and returns its effluent to another channel. The single POU lists its PODs in POD-number order, which keeps POD numbers and POU positions aligned as 62.0.1 requires.

place_of_use.wro:

place_of_use.wro: town supply
1
num  name   typ  typ_num  pods  pors  dtbl_mx  rate_max  dtbl_pod_fr  dtbl_por_fr
1    town   use  1        2     1     null     0.05      null         null
POD  1  river   cha  12  pipe  0  null  20000.0  null  20.0  0.7  n

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A wetland in SWAT+ is an HRU that can store ponded water on its surface. The same mechanism simulates rice paddies. Two files are specific to wetlands, named in slots 7 and 8 of the reservoir line of file.cio:

  • wetland.wet: one row per wetland, naming its initial conditions, hydrology, release rule, sediment and nutrient records.
  • hydrology.wet: wetland hydrology records. Depths and areas are relative to the HRU.

Wetlands also use four reservoir files, described on the reservoir page: initial.res, sediment.res, nutrients.res and weir.res. Release rules are decision tables in res_rel.dtl (see decision tables).

An HRU becomes a wetland when the surf_stor column of hru-data.hru names a row of wetland.wet. With null there, the HRU has no ponded storage.

Both files are free format and whitespace-separated. Line 1 is a title and line 2 is the column header; both are skipped. The readers do not match columns by header name, so every row needs all of its values in the order given below. Columns after the last one listed are ignored. Names must match, including case. A slot in file.cio set to null, or a file that does not exist, leaves the table empty.

docs.title: wetland.wet
docs.text:
One row per wetland.

# Column Units Description 1 id - Wetland number. Read; not used. Rows are used in the order they appear. 2 name - Wetland name, matched against surf_stor in hru-data.hru. 3 init - Name of a row in initial.res. 4 hyd - Name of a row in hydrology.wet. The name paddy switches on rice paddy behaviour; see Outflow. 5 rel - Name of a release decision table in res_rel.dtl. Not used for paddies. 6 sed - Name of a row in sediment.res. 7 nut - Name of a row in nutrients.res.

Several HRUs can use the same row. A name that is not found is reported in diagnostics.out as <name> not found (wet-init), (wet-hyd), (wet-release), (wet-sed) or (wet-nut), and a surf_stor name that is not in wetland.wet as <name>not found (wetland.wet). A wetland whose hyd is not found uses the built-in hydrology values (zero depths and areas). A non-paddy wetland whose rel is not found releases no water through its rule.

Some files, such as the example below, have an eighth column naming a weir record. 62.0.1 does not read it; how a wetland gets its weir record is described under Storage volumes and weir height.

docs.title: hydrology.wet
docs.text:
One row per wetland hydrology record.

# Column Units Built-in value Description 1 name - - Name of the hydrology record, matched against hyd in wetland.wet. 2 hru_ps fraction 0 Fraction of the HRU area covered at the principal spillway (when flow over the surface inlet riser starts). Used only in the surface area set up before the first day, which the daily calculation replaces. 3 dp_ps mm 0 Average water depth at the principal spillway. Sets the principal volume and, without weir records, the weir height. 4 hru_es fraction 0 Fraction of the HRU area covered at the emergency spillway (when water starts to spill into the ditch). Not used in the daily simulation. 5 dp_es mm 0 Average water depth at the emergency spillway. Sets the emergency volume. 6 k mm/hr 0.01 Hydraulic conductivity of the wetland bottom. Sets the seepage rate. 7 evap - 0.7 Evaporation coefficient, a multiplier on potential evapotranspiration for ponded water. 8 vol_area_co - 1 Coefficient \(a\) of the volume–area relation. 9 vol_dp_a - 1 Coefficient \(b\) of the volume–depth relation. 10 vol_dp_b - 1 Coefficient \(c\) of the volume–depth relation. 11 hru_frac fraction 0.5 Fraction of the HRU that drains into the wetland. Read but not used.

The built-in values apply to wetlands whose hyd name is not found. In rows of the file, the reader replaces zero or negative values in four columns:

  • evap becomes 0.6.
  • k becomes the saturated hydraulic conductivity of the top soil layer of the HRU whose number equals the row number of the record in hydrology.wet (HRU 1 for the first row, and so on), which is not in general an HRU that uses the record.
  • hru_ps and hru_es are set to 0.08 × and 1.5 × values that are still zero when the file is read, so they stay at 0.

docs.title: Storage volumes and weir height
docs.text:
At the start of the run, and again when a decision table switches the wetland on, the storage limits are set from the HRU area \(A_{hru}\) (ha) on the assumption that the whole HRU is ponded:

\[V_p = 10\,A_{hru}\,\mathrm{dp\_ps}, \qquad V_e = 10\,A_{hru}\,\mathrm{dp\_es}\]

in m³. hru_ps and hru_es do not enter the volumes.

If weir.res has at least one record, every wetland starts with the first record of weir.res as its weir: the weir height is that record's height (m), the principal volume becomes \(V_p = 10^4\,A_{hru}\,\mathrm{height}\), and \(V_e\) is raised to at least \(1.2\,V_p\). Without weir records the weir height is dp_ps / 1000 m. A weir operation in the management schedule can later change the height and select another weir.res record by name (see Management and decision tables).

The initial water volume is the flo fraction of the om_water.ini row named in initial.res, multiplied by \(V_p\), with concentrations from the same row.

docs.title: Daily water balance
docs.text:
For an HRU with a wetland, the daily HRU routines change as follows:

  • Surface run-on from upstream objects (with tile flow) is added to the wetland storage.
  • The HRU generates no surface runoff. The day's precipitation, over the whole HRU area (\(10\,R\,A_{hru}\) m³), and any irrigation water are added to the wetland storage.
  • Evaporation from the ponded water is taken before soil evaporation; while water is ponded there is no soil evaporation (see Evaporation).
  • Seepage from the ponded water is the infiltration into the soil.
  • Water above saturation in the soil profile is returned to the wetland storage. If the weir height is below 1 mm it becomes surface runoff instead.
  • The wetland outflow is the surface runoff of the HRU.

Water depth is storage divided by the HRU area: \(d = V / (10\,A_{hru})\) mm.

docs.title: Surface area
docs.text:
For wetlands that are not paddies, the water surface area \(A_w\) follows the storage \(V\) relative to the principal volume \(V_p\):

\[x = b^2 + 4c\left(1 - \frac{V}{V_p}\right), \qquad h = \frac{-b - \sqrt{x}}{2c} + b, \qquad A_w = A_{hru}\,\min\!\left(1, \max(0.01,\; 1 + a\,h)\right)\]

with \(a\) = vol_area_co, \(b\) = vol_dp_a and \(c\) = vol_dp_b. When \(x\) is below \(10^{-6}\), \(h\) is 0. With the built-in values (\(a = b = c = 1\)) the whole HRU is covered at \(V = V_p\), and 63% at \(V = 0.5\,V_p\). The area set up before the first day also multiplies the fraction by hru_ps.

For paddies the surface area is always the HRU area.

The surface area sets seepage and the weir flow. Precipitation, evaporation and the water depth are always calculated over the whole HRU.

docs.title: Evaporation
docs.text:
When the HRU has ponded water and its leaf area index is 4 or less, the maximum evaporation is

\[E_{max} = \mathrm{evap}\;\left(1 - \frac{LAI}{4}\right) PET\]

With a leaf area index above 4 there is no evaporation from the ponded water. Evaporation is taken from the ponded water first, and from the soil only when no ponded water remains.

In 62.0.1 the evap value is looked up through the record's row number in hydrology.wet used as an HRU number: the coefficient applied is that of the wetland on the HRU with that number, or 0.7 if that HRU has no wetland. In a model where HRU 1 uses the first hydrology.wet record, HRU 2 the second and so on, this gives the intended value.

docs.title: Seepage
docs.text:
Daily seepage is

\[S = \min\left(V,\; 240\,k\,A_w\right)\]

in m³, with \(k\) in mm/hr. When the seepage is more than 0.1 mm over the HRU, it is reduced by the amount the soil profile cannot take before it becomes saturated. Nitrate, ammonium, soluble phosphorus, organic nitrogen and organic phosphorus move with the seepage into the top soil layer in proportion to the water. A puddling operation can replace k during the run. When gwflow is active, the exchange with groundwater is calculated by the groundwater model (see gwflow).

docs.title: Outflow
docs.text:
A wetland whose hyd name in wetland.wet is paddy is a rice paddy. Its outflow is weir flow from the weir.res record selected for it, and rel is not used:

  • If the storage exceeds \(V_e\), the water above \(V_e\) is released.
  • While the water depth is above the weir height, flow over the weir is \(Q = 0.45\,A\,c\,w\,H^{k}\) (m³/s), with the weir.res coefficients, the HRU area \(A\) (ha) and the depth above the weir \(H\) (m). It is applied hour by hour for up to 24 hours in a daily run, each hour limited to the water above the weir.
  • With the weir height at zero the whole water depth acts as head, so the ponded water drains over the weir.

Other wetlands release through the decision table named in rel. The conditions and release options are those of reservoirs (release rules), evaluated against the wetland's storage, principal and emergency volumes, water depth and weir height. The outflow is not smoothed.

Paddy HRUs also write a daily line to paddy_test.csv with precipitation, irrigation, seepage, evapotranspiration terms, weir height, water depth, weir outflow, soil water, sediment and nitrate.

docs.title: Sediment and nutrients
docs.text: Sediment settling and nutrient losses in the ponded water follow the reservoir equations with the wetland's sediment.res and nutrients.res records (see sediment settling and nutrient losses), using the HRU's weather. When the wetland was empty at the start of the day and releases water, the sediment yield of the outflow is calculated with a MUSLE-type equation from the HRU's cover and erosion factors, as for a flushed field.

docs.title: Management and decision tables
docs.text:
These operations and decision-table entries act on wetlands and paddies:

  • Decision table conditions vol_wet (storage against the principal or emergency volume), wet_depth (water depth, mm) and weirh (weir height, mm). See decision tables.
  • Decision table action weir_height with option wet: sets the weir height to const mm, sets \(V_p\) to the HRU area times that height, and raises \(V_e\) to at least \(1.2\,V_p\). It does not change the weir record.
  • Management operation weir: sets the weir height to its third data value (mm), sets \(V_p\) the same way with \(V_e\) raised to at least \(1.1\,V_p\), and selects the weir.res record named in its first data field.
  • Decision table actions impound_off and impound_on: impound_off removes the wetland and its stored water from the HRU. impound_on sets the wetland up again from the surf_stor row of hru-data.hru; the name given in the action's file pointer is not matched in 62.0.1.
  • Puddling (puddle action, with puddle.ops): replaces the wetland bottom conductivity and raises the sediment concentration of the ponded water.
  • Fertilizer applied to an HRU with ponded water goes into the water when carbon in codes.bsn is 2. With other carbon values it is counted in the fertilizer output but added to neither the water nor the soil.
  • Tillage when the water depth is above 1 mm mixes the soil layers with the ponded-water routine, including pesticides in the soil.

See management schedules and operations for the operation formats.

When gwflow is active and gwflow.wetland exists, the wetland bed thickness (m) for each wetland HRU is read from it: two header lines, then one line per wetland with a name and a thickness, where the digits in the name give the HRU number (for example wet019 for HRU 19).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
refdata/Osu_1hru in the SWAT+ repository is a single rice paddy HRU. hru-data.hru names paddy0001 in surf_stor.

wetland.wet:

wetland.       wet: written by SWAT+ edi############for SWAT+ rev.60.5.4
     id                name        init         hyd         rel         sed         nut        WEIR
       1          paddy0001    initwet1       paddy        weir     sedwet1     nutwet1       weir1

The title line is damaged but is skipped. The hydrology record is paddy, so the HRU is a paddy and the weir decision table named in rel is not used. The WEIR column is not read.

hydrology.wet:

hydrology.wet: written by SWAT+ editor v2.2.0 on 2023-03-22 04:25 for SWAT+ rev.60.5.4
name                    hru_ps         dp_ps        hru_es         dp_es             k          evap   vol_area_co      vol_dp_a      vol_dp_b      hru_frac
paddy                     1.00        150.00         1.00        150.00           0.5           0.75          1.00         1.00         1.00          1.0

The emergency volume is 150 mm of water over the HRU. Seepage is at most 0.5 × 24 = 12 mm per day. Ponded water evaporates at 0.75 × PET while the rice canopy is sparse, falling to zero as the leaf area index reaches 4.

weir.res has one record, weir1, with a height of 0 m, so the paddy starts with a weir height of zero and a principal volume of zero, and any ponded water drains over the weir. During the season weir_height actions in lum.dtl raise the weir to 60 mm and lower it to 0 again. While water stands above 60 mm it flows over the 5 m weir at \(Q = 0.45\,A \times 1.83 \times 5 \times H^{1.5}\) m³/s.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
SWAT+ is a watershed model. It simulates water, sediment, nutrient, pesticide, and crop yield response to climate and management at scales from a single field up to a large river basin.

This section covers what the model is, how it differs from the original SWAT, how to cite it, and how releases are numbered.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
• What is SWAT+
  • SWAT vs SWAT+
  • Citing and license
  • Release notes

docs.title: License
docs.text: SWAT+ is released under the GNU Lesser General Public License, version 2.1 (LGPL-2.1). The full text is in the LICENSE file of the source repository.

docs.title: Citing the software
docs.text:
Cite the model release used in the study, with its version and DOI. The author list below is the one in the repository's citation file at 62.0.1:

Arnold, J. G., Čerkasova, N., White, M. J., Bailey, R., Thorp, K., Jeong, J., Zhang, X., Ugraskan, T., van Griensven, A., Rathjens, H., Raj, C., Cai, X., Geter, W. F., David, O., Carlson, J. R., and Chawanda, C. J. Soil and Water Assessment Tool Plus (SWAT+), version 62.0.1. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14983533

Releases are archived on Zenodo:

DOI Points to 10.5281/zenodo.14983533 all versions; resolves to the newest archived release 10.5281/zenodo.22919722 release 62.0.0 10.5281/zenodo.14983534 release 61.0.2

When a release has a version DOI, cite that DOI so the exact code can be found again.

GitHub shows a "Cite this repository" button on the repository page, built from the same citation file, with APA and BibTeX forms.

docs.title: Citing the documentation
docs.text: When a statement comes from this site, cite the page and the documentation version shown in the version selector at the top of the page, for example "SWAT+ Documentation, revision 62.0.1, Soft calibration, https://docs.swat.tamu.edu/62.0.1/calibration/soft-calibration/".

docs.title: Older versions
docs.text:
Revisions before the move to GitHub are in the modular_swatplus repository on Bitbucket.

Sources
  • CITATION.cff, LICENSE and README.md at 62.0.1.
  • Zenodo records 14983533 (concept), 22919722 and 14983534, checked 20 October 2026.

docs.title: Release notes
docs.text:
SWAT+ releases are listed on the GitHub releases page, with prebuilt executables and the merged pull requests of each release. Version numbers are explained in Tagging and releases.

This page lists the changes in each release that affect model users: input files, outputs and results. Each version of this documentation describes one release; use the version selector at the top of the page for earlier ones.
Released 19 October 2026.

docs.title: Input files
docs.text:
• file.cio, water_rights line: now names two files, the places of use (place_of_use.wro) and the points of diversion (point_of_diver.wro), in place of the three water rights files. The water allocation input files were reorganized around places of use, points of diversion and return; see Water allocation. A file.cio written for 62.0.0 or earlier must be updated; see Older file.cio files.
  • parameters.bsn: two columns that were unused are now read as the pesticide groundwater mixing factor and a switch for temperature-dependent pesticide decay. SWAT+ Editor still labels them lin_sed and exp_sed; a value of 1 in the second turns temperature-dependent decay on. See parameters.bsn.
  • pesticide.pes: three new columns for plant uptake. Files in the older layout are still read, with no plant uptake. See pesticide.pes.
  • Recall: the recall file named in file.cio is read (instead of a fixed name), and empty recall files are no longer created. See recall.
  • exco.exc and exco_om.exc: the original layout is restored.
  • Manure: a manure database (manure_db.frt, manure_om.frt) and manure allocation inputs were added. See manure allocation.
  • Transplanting: transplant data are read from transplant.ops; transplant.plt is no longer read.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• Water allocation outputs were replaced by place-of-use based files.
  • New sediment budget outputs for channels, stream orders and the basin, with corrected average annual values.
  • Rice paddy output, and paddy water included in the ET reports.
  • gwflow outputs now follow their print.prt and gwflow switches, and the average annual storage change is computed correctly.
  • The legacy carbon output no longer writes duplicate rows for each HRU.

See the Output Reference for the files.

docs.title: Model changes
docs.text:
• Rice paddies: seepage, weir spill volume and the impoundment switch day were revised, and soil evaporation is skipped while paddy water remains.
  • Canopy interception is applied for all runoff methods.
  • Pesticides: temperature-dependent decay, plant uptake and mass balance corrections.
  • Water allocation and irrigation were reworked; the irrigation days of an unlimited source are reset correctly.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
• aquifer_delay (gwflow) is changed in days.
  • New object types gwf_riv and gwf_sgl for gwflow channel and single-value parameters.
  • nperco_lchtile changes the right parameter.

See Parameter change files.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• A crash in tillage mixing for plant communities with more than 12 plants.
  • An endless loop when all operations of a management schedule share one date.
  • Root depth of perennials stuck at 25.4 mm at a cold start.
  • Release executables built with gfortran no longer stop with a floating-point trap on macOS, and the macOS executable no longer needs Homebrew's gcc libraries.

docs.title: Documentation for 62.0.1
docs.text:
This version of the documentation was rewritten against the 62.0.1 source. Pages now describe what the model does, including inputs that are read but have no effect and behaviour that differs from the input file labels, so that results can be interpreted correctly. Examples:

  • Measured PET is replaced by the Hargreaves estimate within the same day, so pet 3 in codes.bsn gives Hargreaves results (codes.bsn).
  • Name lookups between files fall back to the first entry without a message when a name does not match; check diagnostics.out and the names themselves (weather-sta.cli, hru-data.hru).
  • Several basin parameters cannot be changed through calibration.cal (Parameter change files).
  • Manure allocation, street sweeping and the pathogen simulation have no effect, and water allocation behaves as its inputs describe only for a single place of use (Water allocation).

Each page states these points where they apply.

Sources

docs.title: SWAT vs SWAT+
docs.text: SWAT+ is the restructured successor to SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool). Most of the process equations are the same. The code structure, the input files and the way parts of a watershed are connected are different. The SWAT column below refers to SWAT2012, the last release of the original model (swat-model/swat2012).

docs.title: Spatial structure
docs.text:
SWAT2012 SWAT+ Units subbasins, each with HRUs and one main channel landscape units, routing units, HRUs, channels, aquifers, reservoirs, wetlands, point sources, each a separate object Connections fixed: HRUs drain to their subbasin's channel, subbasins drain downstream in numbered order defined in connection files (*.con): any object can send any part of its flow (surface runoff, lateral flow, tile flow, recharge) to any other object Floodplain and upland not separated landscape units can separate upland and floodplain areas

The connection files make it possible, for example, to route upland runoff across a floodplain before it reaches the channel, to send tile flow from one HRU to a wetland, or to divide a reservoir's outflow between two channels.

docs.title: Input files
docs.text:
SWAT2012 used one set of files per subbasin and HRU (.sub, .hru, .mgt, .gw, .rte, .sol, ...), each repeating the full parameter list.

SWAT+ uses relational input files grouped by purpose. A parameter set is written once, given a name, and referenced by name from every object that uses it. For example, one row of hydrology.hyd can serve hundreds of HRUs. The master file file.cio lists every input file by group:

  • simulation: time.sim, print.prt, object.cnt
  • basin: codes.bsn, parameters.bsn, carbon.bsn
  • climate: weather-sta.cli, weather-wgn.cli, pcp.cli, tmp.cli and the station files
  • connections: hru.con, rout_unit.con, aquifer.con, chandeg.con, reservoir.con, recall.con, ...
  • HRUs, land use and management: hru-data.hru, landuse.lum, management.sch, cntable.lum, decision tables (*.dtl)
  • hydrology: hydrology.hyd, topography.hyd, field.fld
  • soils and plants: soils.sol, nutrients.sol, plants.plt, plant.ini
  • databases: fertilizer, tillage, pesticide, urban and other parameter tables

The Input Reference describes each file.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
SWAT2012 scheduled operations in the .mgt file of each HRU, by date or by fraction of heat units.

SWAT+ management schedules (management.sch) are shared between HRUs, and can combine dated operations with decision tables (*.dtl). A decision table checks conditions every day (soil water, plant growth stage, date, crop rotation year, reservoir level, and so on) and applies an action when they are met. Decision tables also drive reservoir releases, flow control and land use change. See Decision tables.

docs.title: Groundwater
docs.text:
SWAT2012 had a shallow and a deep aquifer for each HRU, with the shallow aquifer feeding the main channel of its subbasin.

SWAT+ aquifers are separate objects, usually one per landscape unit or group of HRUs, connected to channels through aquifer.con. SWAT+ also includes gwflow, a gridded groundwater module that simulates water table heads and exchanges with channels, soils, tile drains, reservoirs and wells cell by cell. See Aquifers.

docs.title: Additional processes
docs.text: SWAT+ adds or extends: a carbon module with soil organic matter pools, water allocation between sources and users, salts and other constituents, rice paddies, and a sediment budget for channels. Each is described in the Model Theory section.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
SWAT2012 wrote a fixed set of files (output.hru, output.sub, output.rch, output.std).

SWAT+ writes one file per object type, process and time step, switched on and off in print.prt. Examples from the Ames_sub1 reference dataset:

basin_wb_aa.txt        basin water balance, average annual
hru_wb_aa.txt          HRU water balance, average annual
channel_sd_day.txt     channel flow and loads, daily
basin_aqu_aa.txt       aquifer, average annual

The suffix gives the time step: _day, _mon, _yr or _aa. Each row of print.prt switches the four time steps on or off. See the Output Reference.

docs.title: Code
docs.text: SWAT2012 SWAT+ Language Fortran, fixed form Fortran, free form Organization shared common blocks modules grouped by process and object Source released as archives public on GitHub, LGPL-2.1 Build hand-written makefiles CMake

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
There is no automatic converter from a SWAT2012 project to SWAT+. Rebuild the project in QSWAT+ from the same DEM, soil, land use and climate data, then transfer calibrated parameter values by hand, checking each against the SWAT+ units and meaning.

Sources
  • Connection and input file names: type input_con and the other input_* types in src/input_file_module.f90.
  • Aquifer objects: src/aquifer_module.f90, read by aqu_read.f90. Gridded groundwater: gwflow_*.f90. Spatial aquifer connections (aquifer2d.con): aqu2d_read.f90, aqu2d_init.f90.
  • Build: CMakeLists.txt compiles src/*.f90 free form (-free for Intel, -ffree-line-length-none for GNU) into one executable.
  • SWAT2012: swat-model/swat2012.

docs.title: What is SWAT+
docs.text:
The Soil and Water Assessment Tool Plus (SWAT+) is an open-source watershed model developed jointly by the USDA Agricultural Research Service (USDA-ARS) and Texas A&M AgriLife Research, with contributions from Colorado State University, the USDA-ARS Hydrology and Remote Sensing Laboratory and other institutions.

SWAT+ simulates the quantity and quality of surface water and groundwater, from small watersheds to large river basins. It is used to evaluate the effects of land use, land management, soils and climate change on water resources.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Over more than two decades the original Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) became one of the most widely used watershed models in the world. Its many applications showed limits in how a watershed could be represented, and the additions made over the years left a code base that was hard to maintain and extend. SWAT+ is a restructured version of SWAT. Most of the process equations are the same, but the code is organized around objects and the input files are relational, which makes the model easier to maintain and lets new science be added as separate modules. SWAT+ also allows a more flexible spatial representation: landscape units, HRUs, aquifers, channels and reservoirs can be connected in any arrangement through connection files. The main differences are listed on SWAT vs SWAT+.

docs.title: Processes simulated
docs.text:
For each HRU, channel, aquifer, reservoir and wetland, SWAT+ keeps a daily mass balance of:

  • water: precipitation, snow, evapotranspiration, surface runoff, lateral flow, percolation, groundwater flow and channel routing
  • sediment: detachment, transport and deposition on the landscape and in channels
  • nutrients: nitrogen and phosphorus cycling in the soil, plant uptake, transport with runoff and subsurface flow, and in-stream transformations
  • carbon: soil organic carbon and residue pools
  • pesticides and pathogens: application, decay and transport
  • salts and other constituents
  • plant growth: biomass, leaf area, yield, and water, nutrient and temperature stress

Management (planting, tillage, fertilizer and manure, irrigation, harvest, grazing) can follow fixed schedules or rules in decision tables. Water can be allocated between sources and users, and structural practices such as tile drains, filter strips and terraces can be represented.

Output can be written daily, monthly, yearly and as average annual values. The Model Theory section describes each process.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• effects of management practices on water yield and water quality
  • soil erosion and non-point source pollution
  • crop yield response to climate and management
  • watershed planning and total maximum daily load (TMDL) studies
  • climate change impacts on water resources
  • irrigation and water allocation

docs.title: Running the model
docs.text:
SWAT+ is a command-line program. It reads a folder of plain-text input files that describe the watershed, climate, soils, land use, management and simulation period, and writes plain-text (and optionally CSV) output files to the same folder.

Most users do not write the input files by hand. They use the supporting tools:

  • QSWAT+, a QGIS plugin, delineates the watershed from a DEM, creates HRUs from soil, land use and slope maps, and writes the project database.
  • SWAT+ Editor edits the inputs of a project, writes the input files and runs the model.
  • SWAT+ Toolbox runs sensitivity analysis, calibration and other tasks on a finished project.

All three can be installed from install.swat.tamu.edu. See Install.

docs.title: Source and license
docs.text:
The source code is at github.com/swat-model/swatplus and is released under the GNU Lesser General Public License 2.1. See Citing and license.

Sources
  • README.md and CITATION.cff in the source repository at 62.0.1.
  • Input file groups: src/input_file_module.f90.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
These pages describe how SWAT+ represents the processes that move water, sediment, nutrients and other constituents through a watershed. Each page covers one group of processes: the equations the model solves, the input files and columns that control them, and where SWAT+ 62.0.1 differs from the SWAT 2009 theoretical documentation.

The landscape processes run once per day for every hydrologic response unit (HRU): weather, snow, evapotranspiration, surface runoff, soil water, erosion, plant growth and the soil nutrient cycles. Their results leave the HRU as surface runoff, lateral flow, tile flow and percolation, and pass to the routing objects: channels, aquifers, reservoirs and wetlands, and recall points. Decision tables apply management and reservoir release rules across both groups.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Group Page Contents Landscape water Overview and water balance HRU water balance, the order of daily calculations, where each term is reported Landscape water Climate and weather Measured and generated weather, day length, sub-daily precipitation, elevation lapse, potential evapotranspiration Landscape water Hydrology Canopy interception, surface runoff, lateral flow, percolation, tile flow, lag to the channel Landscape water Soil water and temperature Soil layers, water retention, initial soil water, soil evaporation, soil temperature Landscape water Erosion and sediment Peak runoff rate, MUSLE, sub-daily erosion, sediment in lateral flow, urban loads, filter strips, grassed waterways and user BMPs Routing Channels Channel routing, sediment transport and in-stream water quality Routing Aquifers Aquifer objects and the gwflow groundwater module Routing Reservoirs and wetlands Reservoir water balance and release rules, wetlands Routing Recall and point sources Recall time series and point source loads Routing Decision tables Condition evaluation and actions Plants and chemistry Plant growth and land use management Heat units, biomass, leaf area, stresses, harvest, scheduled management Plants and chemistry Nutrient cycling Soil nitrogen and phosphorus pools, transformations, losses; algae, CBOD and oxygen in runoff; septic systems Plants and chemistry Carbon Static and CENTURY-based soil carbon Plants and chemistry Pesticides Application, partitioning, decay and transport Plants and chemistry Salts and constituents Salt ion chemistry, other constituents, pathogens and heavy metals

docs.title: SWAT 2009 processes not in SWAT+ 62.0.1
docs.text:
The SWAT 2009 theoretical documentation describes some processes that SWAT+ 62.0.1 does not simulate, or simulates in a different way:

  • Elevation bands within a subbasin. SWAT+ corrects precipitation and temperature for the elevation of each object instead (see Climate and weather).
  • Monthly climate change adjustments of precipitation, temperature, solar radiation and humidity. SWAT+ 62.0.1 has no input for them; adjust the weather files instead.
  • Hourly air temperature and the distribution of solar radiation over the hours of the day.
  • The adjustment of the curve number for slope.
  • Transmission losses from tributary channels within a subbasin. SWAT+ has no tributary channels; losses are computed for each channel object.
  • Bank storage in the main channel.
  • The SWAT 2009 channel sediment routing (simplified Bagnold stream power equation, channel erodibility and cover factors, downcutting and widening). SWAT+ uses the channel sediment model described in Channels.
  • Potholes and other depressional areas, replaced by wetlands and paddies in HRUs (see Reservoirs and wetlands).
  • Reservoir release from measured monthly outflow or a target storage. SWAT+ uses release decision tables and measured releases from recall files.
  • Chlorophyll-a and Secchi depth relations for lakes and reservoirs.
  • The stream and dam reaeration formulas of QUAL2E; SWAT+ uses the reaeration rate given in nutrients.cha.
  • The two-population bacteria model (persistent and less persistent bacteria), replaced by the pathogen routines described in Salts and constituents.
  • Continuous fertilization and automatic fertilization by nitrogen stress. Decision tables can fertilize in response to conditions instead (see Decision tables).
  • Consumptive water use and water transfer between objects, replaced by water allocation (see Water allocation).

docs.title: Page layout
docs.text:
Every symbol is defined under its equation. Where a symbol is a user input, the input file and the column header the SWAT+ Editor writes are named with it, and the basin switches and parameters that change the result are listed together on each page.

The last section of every page, Sources, is for developers. It links to the Fortran routines at the 62.0.1 tag, maps symbols and columns to Fortran variable names, and records implementation details.

Sources
  • Daily HRU sequence: hru_control.f90
  • Object loop that calls HRUs, channels, aquifers and reservoirs: command.f90

The pages in this section were checked against SWAT+ 62.0.1 (commit 6f51536). Where a page and the Fortran source disagree, the source describes what the model does.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Water that percolates below the soil profile recharges groundwater. Groundwater returns to the stream network as baseflow, moves up toward the root zone in dry periods ("revap"), and leaks downward out of the shallow system as deep seepage. SWAT+ offers two ways to simulate this:

  • 1D aquifer objects (the default): each aquifer is a lumped storage defined in aquifer.aqu and connected to channels, reservoirs or other aquifers through aquifer.con. Recharge, baseflow, revap and seepage are computed once a day from a few parameters.
  • gwflow (gwflow = 1 in codes.bsn): the aquifer is replaced by a grid of cells. Each cell has a groundwater head, and water moves between cells by Darcy's law and exchanges with channels, reservoirs, wetlands, tile drains, canals and pumping wells.

In SWAT, every subbasin had a shallow and a deep aquifer. In SWAT+ an aquifer is an independent spatial object. A watershed can have one aquifer or many, and deep seepage from a shallow aquifer can be routed to a second (deep) aquifer object or allowed to leave the system.

docs.title: Recharge
docs.text:
Recharge is the water an aquifer receives from the objects routed to it: percolation from HRUs, routing units or other aquifers, and any channel or reservoir seepage directed to it in the connection files. The daily recharge depth is

\[ w_{rchg} = \frac{V_{in}}{10\,A} \] Symbol Meaning Units \(w_{rchg}\) recharge to the aquifer mm \(V_{in}\) volume of water entering the aquifer on the day m³ \(A\) aquifer area ha

SWAT delayed recharge with an exponential lag (GW_DELAY). The SWAT+ 1D aquifer has no recharge delay: water leaving the soil profile is added to aquifer storage on the day it arrives. Recharge is added to storage first, and all outflows on the day are then computed from the new storage.

docs.title: Water table depth
docs.text:
Storage is converted to a water table depth using the specific yield:

\[ d_{wt} = d_{bot} - \frac{S}{1000\,S_y}, \qquad d_{wt} \ge 0 \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(d_{wt}\) depth from the land surface to the water table m initial value dep_wt \(d_{bot}\) depth from the land surface to the bottom of the aquifer m dep_bot \(S\) water stored in the aquifer mm \(S_y\) specific yield m³/m³ spec_yld

At the start of the simulation storage is set from the initial water table depth, \(S = 1000\,(d_{bot} - d_{wt})\,S_y\).

docs.title: Baseflow
docs.text:
Baseflow (return flow) occurs only while the water table is at or above the threshold depth flo_min. It follows the recession equation used in SWAT:

\[ Q_{gw,i} = \begin{cases} Q_{gw,i-1}\,e^{-\alpha} + w_{rchg}\left(1 - e^{-\alpha}\right) & d_{wt} \le d_{flo} \\ 0 & d_{wt} > d_{flo} \end{cases} \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(Q_{gw,i}\) baseflow on day \(i\) mm initial value gw_flo \(\alpha\) baseflow recession constant 1/day alpha_bf \(d_{flo}\) water table depth at or above which baseflow occurs m flo_min

Baseflow is limited to the water in storage. Because the threshold is a depth, a larger flo_min allows baseflow from a deeper water table. In SWAT the equivalent threshold GWQMN was a storage in mm.

The baseflow hydrograph goes to every object listed in aquifer.con with hydrograph type tot, split by the fractions given there. When channels are linked to the aquifer through the aquifer-channel link file, baseflow is spread over the linked channels from the outlet upward. The contributing channel length grows with the ratio of baseflow to bf_max, so bf_max is the baseflow at which every linked channel receives water.

docs.title: Deep seepage
docs.text:
A fixed fraction of the day's recharge leaves the aquifer through its bottom:

\[ w_{seep} = \beta_{deep}\, w_{rchg} \]

where \(\beta_{deep}\) is rchg_dp (fraction). Seepage is limited to the water left in storage after baseflow. It leaves the aquifer as its second hydrograph; routing it in aquifer.con with hydrograph type rhg sends it to another object, usually a deep aquifer.

docs.title: Revap
docs.text:
When the water table is shallower than revap_min, water is removed from the aquifer in response to evaporative demand:

\[ w_{revap} = \begin{cases} \beta_{rev}\,E_o & d_{wt} < d_{rev} \\ 0 & d_{wt} \ge d_{rev} \end{cases} \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(w_{revap}\) revap mm \(\beta_{rev}\) revap coefficient - revap \(E_o\) potential evapotranspiration at the aquifer's weather station mm \(d_{rev}\) water table depth above which revap occurs m revap_min

Revap is limited to the water left in storage. In SWAT the revap threshold REVAPMN was a storage in mm and revap tapered off as storage approached it. In SWAT+ the threshold is a depth and revap is either on or off. Revap is removed from the aquifer and is not added back to the soil profile.

The daily order is recharge, water table depth, baseflow, seepage, then revap. When the aquifer is a point of diversion in the water allocation inputs, withdrawals are taken after recharge and before baseflow.

docs.title: Nitrate and phosphorus
docs.text:
Nitrate in recharge water is added to the aquifer nitrate pool. Baseflow and seepage remove nitrate at the concentration of the aquifer water, \(C_{NO3} = N_{aq}/S\). The pool also decays with half-life hl_no3n:

\[ N_{aq,i} = N_{aq,i-1}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{-0.693}{t_{1/2} + 0.1}\right) \]

where \(t_{1/2}\) is hl_no3n (days). A half-life of 0 removes almost all aquifer nitrate each day.

Soluble phosphorus in baseflow is the volume of water entering the aquifer on the day multiplied by the concentration sol_p (mg/L). It is a fixed concentration and does not draw on a phosphorus pool.

docs.title: Pesticides, salts and constituents
docs.text:
Pesticides entering with recharge decay with the aquatic half-life of the pesticide. The concentration available for transport is the pesticide mass divided by a mixing volume made of baseflow, seepage, revap and a fraction of storage set by the pesticide groundwater mixing factor in parameters.bsn. Baseflow and seepage remove pesticide at that concentration. All aquifer pesticide is soluble.

Salt ions and other constituents are mixed through the aquifer water. Their concentration is mass divided by the groundwater volume, and baseflow and seepage remove mass at that concentration. See Salts and constituents.

docs.title: Activation
docs.text: Setting gwflow = 1 in codes.bsn turns on gwflow. SWAT+ then reads the gwflow input files (codes.gw, zones.gw, cells.gw, cellcon.gw, chancell.gw and the optional files for tiles, reservoirs, floodplains, canals, pumping and phreatophytes), and the 1D aquifer objects are switched off. If chancell.gw is missing, gwflow is switched off and the 1D aquifers are used.

docs.title: Cell water balance
docs.text:
Each active cell has a head \(h\), a bottom elevation, a land surface elevation, a hydraulic conductivity \(K\), a specific yield \(S_y\), an ET extinction depth and an area \(A_{c}\). The day is divided into flow time steps of length \(\Delta t\) (time_step in codes.gw). On each step the change in cell storage is the sum of lateral flows from neighbouring cells and the sources and sinks of the day:

\[ \Delta V = \left(\sum_k Q_k + Q_{ss}\right)\Delta t, \qquad h^{new} = h + \frac{\Delta V}{S_y\,A_{c}} \]

The solution is explicit: all heads are updated from the heads at the start of the step.

docs.title: Lateral flow between cells
docs.text:
Flow between a cell and each connected neighbour follows Darcy's law:

\[ Q_k = K_f\,\frac{h_k - h}{L}\,b_f\,w \] Symbol Meaning Units \(Q_k\) flow from neighbour \(k\) into the cell m³/day \(K_f\) face conductivity, the harmonic mean of the two cells' \(K\) m/day \(L\) distance between the cell centroids m \(b_f\) mean saturated thickness of the two cells m \(w\) face width, the square root of the smaller cell's area m

Inactive cells and no-flow boundary cells pass no water. Constant-head boundary cells exchange water with their neighbours but keep their initial head.

docs.title: Sources and sinks
docs.text:
• Recharge: percolation from each HRU or landscape unit is delayed and passed to the cells it overlaps: \(R_i = (1 - \delta)\,w_{perc,i} + \delta\,R_{i-1}\), with \(\delta = e^{-1/\tau}\) and \(\tau\) the recharge delay (days) of the cell's zone.
  • Groundwater ET: ET demand not met by the soil profile is taken from the cell: all of it when the head is at or above the land surface, none when the head is below the extinction depth, and a linearly varying share in between.
  • Channel exchange: each channel cell exchanges water with the stream through the streambed, \(Q = K_{bed}\,(\Delta h / b_{bed})\,W\,L_{ch}\), where \(W\) is channel width, \(L_{ch}\) the channel length in the cell and \(b_{bed}\) the bed thickness. When the head is above the channel stage, groundwater discharges to the channel and \(\Delta h\) is head minus stage. When the head is between the bed and the stage, the channel leaks to the aquifer and \(\Delta h\) is stage minus head. When the head is below the bed, leakage uses the flow depth as \(\Delta h\).
  • Other exchanges: reservoirs, ponds, wetlands, floodplains, tile drains, canals, pumping (from water allocation or an external schedule) and phreatophyte transpiration are added when their input files are present.
  • Saturation excess: when the head rises above the land surface, the excess water goes to the nearest channel.

gwflow can also transport heat and solutes (nitrate, phosphorus, salt ions and constituents) between cells and can track groundwater travel time. Inputs are described in gwflow inputs and outputs in gwflow outputs.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter File Effect gwflow codes.bsn 0 = 1D aquifer objects; 1 = gwflow grid model gw_flo aquifer.aqu Initial baseflow (mm) dep_bot aquifer.aqu Depth to the aquifer bottom (m) dep_wt aquifer.aqu Initial water table depth (m) no3_n aquifer.aqu Initial nitrate-N concentration (mg/L) sol_p aquifer.aqu Soluble P concentration of baseflow (mg/L) bf_max aquifer.aqu Baseflow at which all linked channels receive flow (mm) alpha_bf aquifer.aqu Baseflow recession constant (1/day) revap aquifer.aqu Revap coefficient rchg_dp aquifer.aqu Fraction of recharge lost to deep seepage spec_yld aquifer.aqu Specific yield (m³/m³) hl_no3n aquifer.aqu Half-life of nitrate in the aquifer (days) flo_min aquifer.aqu Water table depth at or above which baseflow occurs (m) revap_min aquifer.aqu Water table depth above which revap occurs (m)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The carbon column of codes.bsn selects how SWAT+ handles soil organic matter:

carbon Model 0 Static model. Residue decomposes and organic N and P mineralise as in SWAT; soil carbon is not tracked as a state. See Nutrient cycling. 1 Reserved for C-FARM, which is not implemented. 2 Carbon model based on CENTURY (Parton et al., 1993, 1994) as implemented in SWAT-C by Zhang (2018). Carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus move through litter and soil organic matter pools in every soil layer.

The carbon model is switched on by carbon = 2; earlier revisions used 1. With carbon = 1 neither model runs, so residue does not decompose and organic N and P are not mineralised. Set the column to 0 or 2.

When carbon = 2, the files carbon.bsn (basin-wide settings) and carbon_lyr.bsn (rates and CO₂ fractions) are required, and the run stops if either is missing. The legacy carb_coefs.cbn file is no longer read.

docs.title: Pools
docs.text:
Each soil layer has three litter pools and three soil organic matter pools. Every pool contains mass, carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus.

Pool Content Metabolic litter Easily decomposed part of residue and manure Structural litter Resistant part of residue, of which a share is lignin Lignin Lignin within structural litter Microbial biomass Active microbes and their products Slow humus Organic matter with turnover times of years to decades Passive humus Stabilised organic matter with turnover times of centuries

Surface residue is kept separately for each plant until it decomposes into the litter pools of the top soil layer.

Carbon moves between pools as follows. Each transfer releases part of the carbon as CO₂.

  • structural litter (non-lignin part) and metabolic litter to microbial biomass
  • lignin to slow humus (70 %; the other 30 % is respired)
  • microbial biomass to slow humus and passive humus
  • slow humus to microbial biomass and passive humus
  • passive humus to microbial biomass

docs.title: Surface residue
docs.text:
Each plant's surface residue decomposes when the top soil layer is above 0 °C:

\[ \Delta R = \delta\,R, \qquad \delta = \min\left(1,\;\max\left(\delta_{min},\;k_{rsd}\;\gamma_{nut}\;\sqrt{\gamma_{tmp}\,\gamma_{sw}}\right)\right) \] \[ \gamma_{tmp} = \max\left(0.1,\;0.9\,\frac{T}{T + e^{9.93 - 0.312\,T}} + 0.1\right), \qquad \gamma_{sw} = \max\left(0.05,\;0.1 + 0.9\sqrt{SW/FC}\right) \] \[ \gamma_{nut} = \min\left(1,\;e^{-0.693\,(CN - CN_{ref})/CN_{ref}},\;e^{-0.693\,(CP - CP_{ref})/CP_{ref}}\right) \] Symbol Meaning Input \(R\) surface residue of a plant (mass, C, N, P) \(k_{rsd}\) residue decomposition coefficient of the plant plnt_decomp in plants.plt \(\delta_{min}\) minimum daily decomposition fraction rsd_decay in parameters.bsn \(T\), \(SW\), \(FC\) top layer temperature (°C), soil water and field capacity (mm) \(CN\), \(CP\) residue C:N and C:P ratios, capped at cnr_cap and cpr_cap carbon.bsn \(CN_{ref}\), \(CP_{ref}\) ratios at which the factor is 1 cnr_ref, cpr_ref in carbon.bsn

The decomposed residue is added to the litter pools of the top soil layer. The plant's above-ground lignin fraction (ab_lig_frac in plants.plt) goes to lignin, the lignin fraction divided by 0.8 goes to structural litter (lignin included), and the rest goes to metabolic litter.

Before decomposition, a fraction sfc_rsd_photodeg (carbon.bsn) of each plant's surface residue is lost each day to photodegradation and counted as emitted carbon.

docs.title: Roots and incorporated residue
docs.text:
Residue in the soil (dead roots and residue mixed in by tillage) is moved to the litter pools of its layer on each day the layer is above 0 °C, using the plant's below-ground lignin fraction (bg_lig_frac in plants.plt) in the same way.

Manure adds to the litter pools according to the manure partitioning settings in carbon.bsn.

docs.title: Environmental controls
docs.text:
The daily rate of every transformation in a layer is the optimal rate times a combined control factor:

\[ c_s = \min\left(15,\;0.9\,\sqrt{f_{tmp}\,f_{sw}}\;f_{ox}\;f_{till}\right) \]

Temperature \(f_{tmp}\) is chosen with tmpf_eqn in carbon.bsn:

tmpf_eqn Function of layer temperature \(T\) (°C) 1 \(T/(T + e^{5.058 - 0.2504T})\) up to 35 °C, then \(1 - 0.04(T - 35)\) up to 60 °C, then 0 2 \(\dfrac{(T - T_n)^{q}\,(T_x - T)}{(T_o - T_n)^{q}\,(T_x - T_o)}\) with \(q = (T_n - T_o)/(T_o - T_x)\), and 0 outside \(T_n < T < T_x\); \(T_n\), \(T_o\), \(T_x\) are t_cbn_min, t_cbn_opt, t_cbn_max 3 \(0.9\,T/(T + e^{9.93 - 0.312T}) + 0.1\)

Soil water \(f_{sw}\) is chosen with watf_eqn:

watf_eqn Function 1 \(0.1 + 0.9\sqrt{SW/FC}\), limited to 0.05 to 1 2 Product of a water factor (rising from 0 at no water to 1 at field capacity) and an aeration factor based on the air-filled pore space; reduces activity in both dry and waterlogged soil

Oxygen decreases with the depth \(z\) (mm) of the middle of the layer:

\[ f_{ox} = 1 - \frac{0.8\,z}{z + e^{18.40961 - 0.023683632\,z}} \]

Tillage \(f_{till}\) depends on idc_till in codes.bsn:

idc_till Effect 1 \(f_{till} = 1.6\) in layers within the tillage depth for till_eff_days days after tillage (partly in the layer containing the tillage depth), otherwise 1 2, 4 No effect (\(f_{till} = 1\)) 3 (default) \(f_{till}\) is 1 plus the layer tillage factor, which rises with each tillage operation and decays afterwards (Kemanian method)

docs.title: Rates
docs.text:
Potential daily transformation of each pool is its carbon (and nitrogen) content times an optimal rate from carbon_lyr.bsn, times \(c_s\):

Pool Daily fraction transformed Rate column Structural litter \(k_{str}\,c_s\,e^{-3\,L}\), where \(L\) is the lignin share of structural litter (at most 0.8) str_rate Metabolic litter \(k_{meta}\,c_s\) meta_rate Microbial biomass \(k_{mic}\,c_s\,x_{bm}\), with \(x_{bm} = 1\) in the top layer and \(0.25 + 0.0075\,\text{sand}\) below microb_top_rate (top layer), microb_rate Slow humus \(k_{hs}\,c_s\) hs_rate Passive humus \(k_{hp}\,c_s\) hp_rate

carbon_lyr.bsn has two rows: row 1 applies to the top soil layer and row 2 to all other layers.

docs.title: Allocation and CO₂
docs.text:
Transfer Fraction respired as CO₂ Remainder goes to Metabolic and non-lignin structural litter a1co2 microbial biomass Lignin 0.3 slow humus Microbial biomass abco2 in the top layer; \(0.17 + 0.0068\,\text{sand}\) below passive humus (\(0.003 + 0.00032\,\text{clay}\)), rest to slow humus Slow humus asco2 passive humus (the larger of 0.001 and hs_hp minus 0.00009 × clay), rest to microbial biomass Passive humus apco2 microbial biomass

Sand and clay are in percent.

docs.title: Nitrogen
docs.text:
Each receiving pool has a target N:C ratio. In the top layer these depend on the N content of the residue; in deeper layers they depend on the mineral N concentration of the layer. When the N released by the decomposing pools is less than the N needed to build the receiving pools, the difference is immobilised from soil nitrate and ammonium. If mineral N cannot cover it, the transformations that need N are reduced in proportion. Surplus N is mineralised to ammonium.

Before the transformations, denitrification removes nitrate when the soil water factor exceeds denit_frac in parameters.bsn, at a rate set by denit_exp, the temperature factor and the layer organic carbon.

docs.title: Phosphorus
docs.text: Phosphorus is mineralised from passive humus at 1.4 times the fraction of humus N that was transformed on the day, and goes to the labile mineral pool. Phosphorus in decomposing litter is released in proportion to the litter carbon transformed: 80 % to labile mineral P and 20 % to passive humus.

docs.title: Carbon in water and sediment
docs.text:
• Sediment: eroded soil removes organic carbon from the top layer in proportion to the share of the layer mass eroded (at most 90 %).
  • Dissolved carbon from microbial biomass: in the top layer, microbial carbon is lost to water leaving the layer with \(1 - \exp\left(-w/(SAT + 10^{-4}\,K_{oc}\,C)\right)\), where \(w\) is runoff plus lateral flow plus percolation, \(K_{oc}\) is koc_c and \(C\) the layer organic carbon. The concentration in surface runoff and lateral flow is solc_ratio times the concentration in percolation. In deeper layers, carbon moving with percolation and lateral flow is removed with \(1 - \exp(-w/(\phi z - WP))\).
  • Carbon leaving the bottom of the profile is reported as percolated carbon.

docs.title: Initial pools
docs.text: At the start of the run, the organic carbon of each layer (from soils.sol) is split into pools. A share init_seq is humus and microbial carbon, divided between microbial biomass (init_microb), slow humus (init_slow) and passive humus (init_passive). Humus pools start with C:N of 10 and C:P of 80; microbial biomass with C:N of 8 and C:P of 80. With mathers_method = 1, slow humus is initialised with the Mathers relation based on clay plus silt content.
