docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Channels move water, sediment and dissolved and particulate constituents from upstream objects to the watershed outlet. A SWAT+ channel is defined by its geometry (width, depth, slope, length, side slope, Manning's n) in hyd-sed-lte.cha, from which a rating curve of depth, area, wetted perimeter, top width, velocity and travel time against flow rate is built at the start of the run.

Each day a channel:

  1. adds rain falling on the channel surface to the inflow;
  2. checks for overbank flow, traps sediment on the floodplain and fills floodplain wetlands;
  3. computes bank and bed erosion;
  4. routes the water through channel and floodplain storage;
  5. removes transmission losses and evaporation;
  6. runs in-stream water quality, pesticides, pathogens, salts and constituents;
  7. computes water temperature.

When gwflow is active, the channel also exchanges water with the groundwater cells it crosses (see Aquifers).

docs.title: Rating curve
docs.text: The rating curve is computed for a trapezoidal main channel with a floodplain above bankfull. For a given flow rate it gives flow depth, cross-section area, wetted perimeter, hydraulic radius, velocity (Manning's equation), and travel time \(TT = L / (3.6\,v)\) in hours, with \(L\) the channel length (km) and \(v\) the velocity (m/s).

docs.title: Flow routing
docs.text: Inflow is added to channel storage on each routing step. The routing method is set by rte_cha in codes.bsn.

docs.title: Variable storage (rte_cha = 0, default)
docs.text:
\[ q_{out} = \min\left(1,\;\frac{2\,\Delta t\;C_{st}}{2\,TT + \Delta t}\right) V_{stor} \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(q_{out}\) outflow during the step m³ \(\Delta t\) routing step h \(TT\) travel time at the previous step's outflow rate h \(C_{st}\) storage coefficient multiplier - scoef in parameters.bsn \(V_{stor}\) water in channel and floodplain storage m³

With a daily time step there is one routing step per day.

docs.title: Muskingum (rte_cha = 1)
docs.text:
\[ O_2 = C_1 I_2 + C_2 I_1 + C_3 O_1 \] \[ C_1 = \frac{\Delta t - 2KX}{2K(1 - X) + \Delta t}, \quad C_2 = \frac{\Delta t + 2KX}{2K(1 - X) + \Delta t}, \quad C_3 = \frac{2K(1 - X) - \Delta t}{2K(1 - X) + \Delta t} \]

\(C_1\) is not allowed to fall below 0, and the three coefficients are scaled to sum to 1. The storage time constant is a weighted mean of the travel times at bankfull depth and at 0.1 × bankfull depth (using the kinematic wave celerity, 5/3 of the velocity):

\[ K = \frac{c_1\,K_{bf} + c_2\,K_{0.1bf}}{c_1 + c_2} \] Symbol Meaning Input \(I\), \(O\) inflow and outflow volumes at the start (1) and end (2) of the step \(K\) storage time constant (h) \(X\) weighting factor msk_x in parameters.bsn \(c_1\), \(c_2\) weights for bankfull and low flow msk_co1, msk_co2 in parameters.bsn

When \(\Delta t\) exceeds \(2K(1 - X)\), the step is divided into sub-steps so that the method stays stable.

docs.title: Floodplain storage
docs.text: After each routing step, the part of storage above the bankfull channel volume becomes floodplain storage and the rest stays as channel storage. Both drain through the routing equation.

docs.title: Transmission losses and evaporation
docs.text:
Once a day, after routing, water is removed from channel storage:

\[ TL = 24\,K_{ch}\,L\,W, \qquad E_{ch} = \eta\,E_o\,L\,W \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(TL\) transmission loss m³ \(K_{ch}\) effective hydraulic conductivity of the channel bed mm/h k in hyd-sed-lte.cha \(L\), \(W\) channel length and bankfull width km, m len, wd \(E_{ch}\) evaporation from the channel m³ \(\eta\) evaporation coefficient - evap_adj in parameters.bsn \(E_o\) potential evapotranspiration mm

Both are limited to the water in channel storage and use the full bankfull width, whatever the flow. Transmission losses are reported as channel seepage. In SWAT, transmission losses used the wetted perimeter and could recharge the shallow aquifer; in SWAT+ the loss leaves channel storage and is not routed anywhere unless gwflow is used.

docs.title: Overbank flow and floodplain deposition
docs.text:
The daily peak flow is estimated from the mean daily inflow with a peak rate factor that decreases with drainage area:

\[ q_{pk} = r_{pk}\left[1 + 2.66\left(\frac{A}{100}\right)^{-0.3}\right]\frac{Q_{day}}{86400} \]

where \(r_{pk}\) is pk_rto in sed_nut.cha (default 1) and \(A\) the drainage area (ha). When the peak exceeds 1.5 times the bankfull flow rate, part of the sediment, organic N and particulate P is trapped on the floodplain:

\[ \varepsilon_{fp} = \min\left(1,\;\frac{q_{pk}}{\bar{q}}\left[1 - \exp\left(-10^{-4}\,\frac{A_{fp}}{q_{pk}}\right)\right]\right) \]

with \(\bar q\) the mean daily flow rate and \(A_{fp}\) a floodplain area of five channel widths times the channel length (m²). Organic N and particulate P are trapped with the enrichment ratios n_dep_enr and p_dep_enr. Overbank water also fills the wetlands of HRUs that lie on the floodplain.

docs.title: Bank erosion
docs.text:
Banks erode when the reach velocity, raised to account for flow around bends, exceeds a critical velocity that depends on bank cohesion (from clay content), vegetation cover and bulk density:

\[ v_{cr} = c_{vcr}\,\log_{10}(2200\,D)\,\sqrt{0.0004\,(f_{bd} + 0.021\,\tau_{coh} + f_{veg})} \] \[ f_{veg} = 4500\,c_{cov}\,e^{-5D}, \qquad \tau_{coh} = \max\left(1000,\;-87.1 + 42.82\,cl - 0.261\,cl^2 + 0.029\,cl^3\right) \]

The bank retreat rate (m/day) follows a logistic function of \(v/v_{cr}\), scaled by channel width and a duration factor that decreases with drainage area, and limited by an exhaustion rate of \(0.0002\,W\). Eroded bank mass is retreat × depth × a quarter of the channel length × bulk density. Bank material adds organic N and P at the concentrations n_conc and p_conc, with a share p_bio of the P as soluble P. A fraction wash_bed_fr of the eroded bank material is deposited in the channel; the rest moves downstream.

Symbol Meaning Input \(D\) bankfull depth (m) dp \(c_{cov}\) bank cover factor cov_fact \(cl\) bank clay content (%) clay \(f_{bd}\) bulk density factor, \(\max(0.001,\;39.24\,\rho_b - 1000)\) dry_bd \(c_{vcr}\) critical velocity coefficient 12th value, labelled eq_slp in Editor files

docs.title: Bed erosion
docs.text: Bed erosion is computed when the velocity exceeds \(0.293\sqrt{d_{50}}\) m/s, as \(10^{-4}(v/v_{cr})\) m/day of bed lowering. It is reported in the channel morphology output but is not added to the sediment in the flow.

docs.title: Water quality
docs.text: In-stream nitrogen, phosphorus, algae, dissolved oxygen and carbonaceous BOD follow the QUAL2E kinetics (Brown and Barnwell, 1987), with rate constants from nutrients.cha. The calculation runs once a day for every channel with inflow, on the concentrations of the day's inflow.

docs.title: Temperature and solution method
docs.text:
Every rate is given for 20 °C and corrected to the water temperature \(T_w\):

\[k_T = k_{20}\,\theta^{\,T_w - 20}, \qquad T_w = 5 + 0.75\,\bar{T}_{air}\]

with \(T_w\) at least 0.1 °C and \(\bar{T}_{air}\) the day's mean air temperature at the channel's weather station.

Process \(\theta\) Algal growth and respiration; organic N hydrolysis; nitrite oxidation; organic P mineralisation; CBOD decay 1.047 Algal, organic N and organic P settling; CBOD settling; reaeration (also used for ammonium oxidation) 1.024 Benthic P and ammonium sources 1.074

The channel is treated as a mixed reach with a residence time \(\tau\), the travel time through the channel in days (at most 1). For each constituent with inflow concentration \(C_{in}\), a constant source or sink \(M\) (mg/L/day) and a first-order rate \(K\) (1/day), the outflow concentration is

\[C_{out} = C_{in}\,e^{-a} + \frac{C_{in}/\tau + M}{1/\tau - K}\left(1 - e^{-a}\right), \qquad a = \left(\frac{1}{\tau} - K\right)\Delta t\]

with \(\Delta t\) = 1 day.

A first-order transformation from one constituent to another (for example organic N to ammonium) is converted into the equivalent constant term, so the mass removed from one constituent is added to the next.

docs.title: Algae
docs.text:
Algal biomass \(A\) (mg/L) is computed from chlorophyll-a with chla_alg. The growth rate combines light and nutrient limitation:

\[\mu = \mu_{max}\,f_L\,f_{NP}, \qquad f_N = \frac{N}{N + K_N}, \qquad f_P = \frac{P_{sol}}{P_{sol} + K_P}\]

where \(f_{NP}\) is \(f_N f_P\), \(\min(f_N, f_P)\) or \(2/(1/f_N + 1/f_P)\) for q2e_alg 1, 2 or 3. The light factor averages light over the water depth \(d\):

\[f_L = 0.92\,\frac{T_L}{24}\,\frac{1}{\lambda\,d}\,\ln\!\left(\frac{K_L + I}{K_L + I\,e^{-\lambda d}}\right), \qquad I = \frac{f_{PAR}\,H_{day}}{T_L}\] Symbol Meaning Input \(\mu_{max}\) Maximum specific growth rate (1/day) alg_grow \(\rho\) Respiration rate (1/day) alg_resp \(\sigma_1\) Settling rate (m/day) alg_stl \(K_N\), \(K_P\) Half-saturation constants for N and P (mg/L) const_n, const_p \(K_L\) Half-saturation constant for light (MJ/m²/h) lt_co × 0.06 \(\lambda\) Light extinction coefficient (1/m) lt_nonalg \(f_{PAR}\) Fraction of solar radiation that is photosynthetically active slr_act \(H_{day}\) Solar radiation of the day (MJ/m²) weather \(N\) Ammonium plus nitrate in the channel storage (mg/L) \(T_L\) Hours used as the day length (see the list below)

The net growth \(\mu - \rho\) is the source term for algae and settling at \(\sigma_1/d\) the first-order loss. Biomass is kept between 0 and 5000 mg/L. Algal growth takes up soluble P at alg_p per unit of biomass.

docs.title: Nitrogen, phosphorus, CBOD and oxygen
docs.text:
Constituent Sources and sinks Inputs CBOD decay at \(\kappa_1\); settling at \(\kappa_3/d\) cbn_bod_co, cbn_bod_stl Organic N hydrolysis to ammonium at \(2\beta_3\); settling at \(\sigma_4/d\) ptln_nh3n, ptln_stl Ammonium gain from organic N hydrolysis; oxidation to nitrite at \(\kappa_2\) air_rt Nitrite gain from ammonium oxidation; oxidation to nitrate at \(\beta_2\) no2n_no3n Nitrate gain from nitrite oxidation Organic P mineralisation to soluble P at \(\beta_4\); settling at \(\sigma_5/d\) ptlp_solp, ptlp_stl Soluble P gain \(\beta_4 P_{org} + \sigma_2/d_{ch}\); loss to algal growth ben_disp Dissolved oxygen reaeration \(\kappa_2 (O_{sat} - O)\); CBOD decay; \(\alpha_5\) per unit of ammonium and \(\alpha_6\) per unit of nitrite oxidised; a loss of \(\sigma_4/d\) air_rt, o2_nh3n, o2_no2n

Soluble P is updated directly, \(P_{out} = P_{in} + (\beta_4 P_{org} + \sigma_2/d_{ch} - \alpha_2\,\mu\,A)\,\tau\), with \(d_{ch}\) the bankfull depth of the channel and \(\alpha_2\) = alg_p. The oxygen saturation concentration (mg/L) depends on the water temperature \(T_K\) in kelvin:

\[\ln O_{sat} = -139.34410 + \frac{1.575701\times10^{5}}{T_K} - \frac{6.642308\times10^{7}}{T_K^2} + \frac{1.243800\times10^{10}}{T_K^3} - \frac{8.621949\times10^{11}}{T_K^4}\]

Reaeration uses air_rt directly; the stream reaeration formulas of QUAL2E and reaeration over dams are not computed. The inflow oxygen concentration is limited to between 0.001 and 30 mg/L before the calculation.

docs.title: Behaviour in 62.0.1
docs.text:
Several parts of the in-stream calculation differ from QUAL2E:

  • \(T_L\) is the day-length threshold for plant dormancy (dorm_hr in parameters.bsn, or a value of at most 1 hour derived from latitude), not the day length. At latitudes below 20° with dorm_hr = 0 it is zero or negative, the light intensity is set to almost zero, and algae do not grow.
  • The extinction coefficient never exceeds lt_nonalg, so algal self-shading (alg_shd_l, alg_shd_nl) has no effect.
  • Ammonium is oxidised at the reaeration rate air_rt; nh3n_no2n has no effect. Organic N hydrolysis uses twice ptln_nh3n.
  • Algal uptake of ammonium and nitrate and algal oxygen production and respiration are computed but not applied.
  • Sediment oxygen demand (ben_bod) is not taken from dissolved oxygen; the organic N settling term \(\sigma_4/d\) is subtracted instead. The benthic ammonium source (ben_nh3n) only enters the inflow concentration used to compute ammonium oxidation.
  • The benthic P source is added as ben_disp (mg/m²/day) divided by the depth in m, which gives mg/m³ per day, but is added to a concentration in mg/L.

When the 24th value of codes.bsn is 1 (the column Editor files label i_fpwet; the wq_cha column is not used), a simplified exchange replaces the QUAL2E results for nitrate, organic N, soluble P and particulate P. Over the travel time \(TT\) (h), soluble N and P are converted to particulate forms:

\[ \Delta N = \min\left(NO_3,\;\left[1 - e^{-k_N TT}\right] N_{org}\right), \qquad \Delta P = \min\left(P_{sol},\;\left[1 - e^{-k_P TT}\right] P_{sed}\right) \]

with \(k_N\) and \(k_P\) from n_sol_part and p_sol_part in sed_nut.cha (default 0.01).

docs.title: Water temperature
docs.text:
When the channel's weather station has measured temperatures, water temperature is built from:

  • the flow-weighted temperature of upstream channels;
  • local inflows from the routing units draining to the channel (snowmelt, surface runoff and lateral flow) and groundwater, each given the mean air temperature over its lag period (sno_lag, surf_lag, lat_lag, gw_lag days) times a coefficient;
  • heat exchange with the air, using dew point, wind speed and optional shading factors, over the travel time.

Parameters are in temperature.cha. Without measured air temperature, water temperature is \(5 + 0.75\,T_{air}\).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Climate supplies the moisture and energy that drive the water balance and sets the relative size of its parts. SWAT+ needs daily precipitation, maximum and minimum air temperature, solar radiation, relative humidity and wind speed. Each weather station in weather-sta.cli takes each variable either from a measured data file or from the weather generator, and every HRU, channel and other spatial object uses the station assigned to it in its connection file. Potential evapotranspiration (PET) is computed in the model by one of three methods. A fourth option is meant to read PET from a file, but in 62.0.1 it returns the Hargreaves estimate.

docs.title: Measured and generated data
docs.text:
Each row of weather-sta.cli names a weather generator station from weather-wgn.cli and one data set for each variable: precipitation, temperature, solar radiation, relative humidity and wind speed, followed by a PET data set and an atmospheric deposition station. The value sim tells SWAT+ to generate that variable from the weather generator statistics.

Measured values come from the files listed in pcp.cli, tmp.cli, slr.cli, hmd.cli, wnd.cli and pet.cli (see *.cli, *.pcp, *.tmp and *.tem). The names in weather-sta.cli are matched to these lists with a search that assumes the lists are sorted by name; the *.cli page describes what happens when they are not. A value of -97 or less (for example -99) marks a missing record, and SWAT+ fills that day with a generated value. Days outside the period covered by a measured file are also generated.

docs.title: Weather generator
docs.text:
The generator produces daily weather from the monthly statistics of a station in weather-wgn.cli. Precipitation is generated first, because temperature, radiation and humidity are adjusted for wet and dry days.

Whether a day is wet follows a first-order Markov chain. The probability of rain is pr_wd (a wet day following a dry day) or pr_ww (a wet day following a wet day) for the month. On a wet day the amount comes from a skewed distribution:

\[R_{day} = \mu_{mon} + 2\,\sigma_{mon}\left(\frac{\left[\left(SND_{day} - \frac{g_{mon}}{6}\right)\frac{g_{mon}}{6} + 1\right]^3 - 1}{g_{mon}}\right)\] Symbol Meaning Input \(R_{day}\) Generated precipitation, at least 0.1 mm mm H2O \(\mu_{mon}\) Mean daily precipitation on wet days in the month from pcpmm and pcpd in weather-wgn.cli \(\sigma_{mon}\) Standard deviation of daily precipitation pcpstd, mm \(g_{mon}\) Skew coefficient of daily precipitation pcpskw \(SND_{day}\) Standard normal deviate for the day generated

The result is scaled by a monthly correction factor so that the long-term mean of generated wet-day amounts equals \(\mu_{mon}\).

Maximum and minimum temperature are drawn around the monthly means tmpmx and tmpmn with standard deviations tmpstdmx and tmpstdmn. The maximum is lowered on wet days and raised on dry days by half the monthly temperature range, weighted by the fraction of wet days. Relative humidity is drawn from a triangular distribution around the monthly mean, which comes from the dew point (dewpt) and mean temperature, and is raised on wet days. Wind speed follows a modified exponential distribution around the monthly mean windav.

The generator in 62.0.1 returns the monthly mean solar radiation solarav for every generated day. The wet and dry day adjustment is computed but then replaced by the monthly mean, so generated radiation does not vary from day to day within a month.

igen in parameters.bsn sets the random number seeds. With igen = 0 every run uses the same seeds and the same generated weather. Any other value offsets the seeds, so different values give different weather sequences.

docs.title: Maximum half-hour rainfall
docs.text: The fraction of daily rain that falls in the wettest half hour, \(\alpha_{0.5}\), is used by the peak runoff rate and erosivity calculations (see Erosion and sediment). It is generated every day from a triangular distribution between 0.02083 and \(1 - \exp(-125/(R_{day} + 5))\), with its mode set from the monthly maximum half-hour rainfall rainhmx in weather-wgn.cli. The mode is multiplied by adj_pkrt in parameters.bsn and limited to between 0.1 and 0.95.

docs.title: Day length and maximum radiation
docs.text:
Each day SWAT+ computes the day length and the maximum possible solar radiation for every weather generator station from its latitude. The solar declination \(\delta\) and the relative distance between the earth and the sun \(d_r\) on day of year \(d\) are

\[\delta = \sin^{-1}\!\left[0.4\,\sin\!\left(\frac{d - 82}{58.09}\right)\right], \qquad d_r = 1 + 0.033\,\cos\!\left(\frac{d}{58.09}\right)\]

and the hour angle of sunset \(h\), the day length \(T_{DL}\) and the maximum solar radiation \(H_{max}\) are

\[h = \cos^{-1}\!\left(-\tan\delta\,\tan\phi\right), \qquad T_{DL} = 7.6394\,h, \qquad H_{max} = 30\,d_r\left(h\,\sin\phi\,\sin\delta + \cos\phi\,\cos\delta\,\sin h\right)\] Symbol Meaning Units \(\phi\) Latitude of the weather generator station, lat in weather-wgn.cli radians \(h\) Hour angle of sunset; 0 during polar night and \(\pi\) during polar day radians \(T_{DL}\) Day length h \(H_{max}\) Maximum possible solar radiation reaching the ground on a cloudless day MJ/m²/day

\(H_{max}\) is used by net radiation and Hargreaves PET. The day length controls plant dormancy (see Plant growth and land use management). SWAT+ also computes how the day's radiation is spread over the hours of the day, but no process in 62.0.1 uses that distribution.

docs.title: Sub-daily precipitation
docs.text:
With more than one time step per day (step in time.sim), a day of generated precipitation is spread over the day's time steps with a double exponential intensity curve. The peak rate is

\[i_{pk} = 2\,R_{day}\,\alpha_{0.5}\]

where \(R_{day}\) is the day's precipitation (mm) and \(\alpha_{0.5}\) the fraction falling in the wettest half hour, so \(i_{pk}\) is in mm/h. The time to the peak, as a fraction \(v\) of the storm duration, is drawn from a triangular distribution between 0.05 and 0.95 with a mode of 0.25. The storm duration is

\[T_{dur} = \frac{R_{day}}{i_{pk}\,(k_1 + k_2)}, \qquad k_1 = \frac{v}{4.605}, \qquad k_2 = \frac{1 - v}{4.605}\]

limited to 24 hours, with \(i_{pk}\) recomputed when the limit applies. The cumulative rainfall at time \(t\) (h) from the start of the storm is

\[R(t) = R_{pk} - i_{pk}\,T_{dur}\,k_1\left[1 - \exp\!\left(\frac{t - t_{pk}}{T_{dur}\,k_1}\right)\right] \qquad (t \le t_{pk})\] \[R(t) = R_{pk} + i_{pk}\,T_{dur}\,k_2\left[1 - \exp\!\left(\frac{t_{pk} - t}{T_{dur}\,k_2}\right)\right] \qquad (t > t_{pk})\]

with \(R_{pk} = v\,R_{day}\) and \(t_{pk} = v\,T_{dur}\). The storm starts at the beginning of the day, the rainfall of each time step is the increase of \(R(t)\) over the step, and any amount left at the end is added to the last step that received rain.

The same curve fills a day of a measured sub-daily record that contains a missing value. Daily precipitation records are not split into time steps: in a sub-daily run a station with daily records gives no rainfall in its time steps. Use sub-daily records, or generated precipitation, for sub-daily runs.

docs.title: Elevation lapse
docs.text:
When lapse is 1 in codes.bsn, precipitation and temperature are corrected for the difference in elevation between each object and the gauge (or the weather generator station, for generated data) that supplies it:

\[R_{obj} = \max\left(0,\; R_{gage} + \frac{\mathrm{plaps}\,(z_{obj} - z_{gage})}{1000}\right)\] \[T_{obj} = T_{gage} + \frac{\mathrm{tlaps}\,(z_{gage} - z_{obj})}{1000}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(\mathrm{plaps}\) Precipitation lapse rate, plaps in parameters.bsn mm/km \(\mathrm{tlaps}\) Temperature lapse rate, tlaps in parameters.bsn °C/km \(z_{obj}\), \(z_{gage}\) Elevation of the object and of the gauge or generator station m

The temperature correction is applied to the maximum, minimum and mean temperature. A positive tlaps makes objects above the gauge cooler. The precipitation correction is a fixed depth per day, added on dry days as well as wet ones, and the result is never negative.

docs.title: Carbon dioxide
docs.text: The CO2 concentration used by plant growth and Penman-Monteith PET is set for each year of the run. If the file co2_yr.dat is present, yearly values are read from it; years before the record use the first value and years after it the last. Without the file every year uses co2 from parameters.bsn. The values used are written to co2.out.

docs.title: Snow
docs.text: On days when the mean air temperature is at or below fall_tmp, precipitation that passes the canopy is added to the snowpack. Snow melts on days when the maximum temperature is above melt_tmp, at a rate that varies through the year between melt_min and melt_max and is reduced by the fraction of the HRU covered by snow. The equations and the parameters are on the snow.sno page. Snow sublimation is taken from the soil evaporation demand (see Soil water and temperature).

docs.title: Potential evapotranspiration
docs.text:
Potential evapotranspiration is the rate of evapotranspiration from a large area covered completely by a short, actively growing crop with plenty of water. The method is chosen with pet in codes.bsn:

pet Method 0 Priestley-Taylor 1 Penman-Monteith 2 Hargreaves 3 Station PET (see PET read from file)

The three computed methods share these terms:

Symbol Meaning Calculation \(\bar{T}\) Mean air temperature, °C from the weather inputs \(P\) Atmospheric pressure, kPa \(101.3 - z\,(0.01152 - 0.544\times10^{-6}\,z)\) with HRU elevation \(z\) in m \(\lambda\) Latent heat of vaporization, MJ/kg \(2.501 - 2.361\times10^{-3}\,\bar{T}\) \(\gamma\) Psychrometric constant, kPa/°C \(1.013\times10^{-3}\,P/(0.622\,\lambda)\) \(e^0\), \(e\) Saturation and actual vapour pressure, kPa \(e = e^0 \times\) relative humidity \(\Delta\) Slope of the saturation vapour pressure curve, kPa/°C \(4098\,e^0/(\bar{T} + 237.3)^2\)

docs.title: Net radiation
docs.text:
Priestley-Taylor and Penman-Monteith use net radiation for a reference crop:

\[H_{net} = (1 - \alpha)\,H_{day} - \left(0.34 - 0.139\sqrt{e}\right)\left(0.9\,\frac{H_{day}}{H_{max}} + 0.1\right)\sigma\,T_K^4\]

where \(H_{day}\) is the solar radiation reaching the ground (MJ/m²/day), \(H_{max}\) the maximum possible solar radiation for the day, \(\sigma = 4.903\times10^{-9}\) MJ m\(^{-2}\) K\(^{-4}\) day\(^{-1}\), \(T_K\) the mean air temperature in kelvin, and \(\alpha\) the albedo: 0.23 for the reference crop, or 0.8 when the snowpack contains more than 0.5 mm of water.

docs.title: Priestley-Taylor
docs.text:
\[PET = 1.28\,\frac{\Delta}{\Delta + \gamma}\,\frac{H_{net}}{\lambda}\]

Priestley and Taylor (1972) replaced the aerodynamic term of Penman's equation with the coefficient 1.28, which suits humid areas. The method tends to underestimate PET in arid and semi-arid areas, where advection is a large part of the energy balance.

docs.title: Penman-Monteith
docs.text:
\[PET = \frac{\Delta\,H_{net} + \gamma\,\rho_K\,(e^0 - e)/r_a}{\lambda\left[\Delta + \gamma\,(1 + r_c/r_a)\right]}\]

For the reference crop SWAT+ uses the aerodynamic resistance \(r_a = 114/u_{1.7}\) (s/m), where \(u_{1.7} = u_{10}\,(0.17)^{0.2}\) is the wind speed at 1.7 m estimated from the input wind speed \(u_{10}\) (taken as measured at 10 m), and a canopy resistance that responds to CO2:

\[r_c = \frac{49}{1.4 - 0.4\,CO_2/330}\]

\(\rho_K\) combines air density, the latent heat of vaporization and unit conversions, and is computed as \(1710 - 6.85\,\bar{T}\). The method needs measured or generated relative humidity and wind speed.

Penman-Monteith also computes a crop-specific maximum transpiration from the plant canopy height, leaf area and stomatal conductance (stcon_max, vpd and frac_stcon in plants.plt). In 62.0.1 that value is replaced in the actual evapotranspiration step by the leaf area based estimate used with the other methods (see Soil water and temperature), so the choice of PET method changes PET but not the way PET is split into transpiration and soil evaporation.

docs.title: Hargreaves
docs.text:
\[PET = 0.0023\,\frac{H_0}{\lambda}\,(\bar{T} + 17.8)\sqrt{T_{max} - T_{min}}\]

where \(H_0\) is extraterrestrial radiation (MJ/m²/day), taken as \(H_{max}\times 37.59/30\). PET is zero on days when \(T_{max}\) is not above \(T_{min}\). Hargreaves needs only temperature, which makes it a common choice where humidity, wind and radiation records are poor.

docs.title: PET read from file
docs.text:
With pet = 3 the HRU takes the daily PET of its weather station. SWAT+ 62.0.1 first loads the station's measured PET (filling missing days with Hargreaves), but later in the same day it recomputes the station PET with the Hargreaves equation for every station, for use in the climatic moisture index. The HRU therefore receives the Hargreaves value, and pet = 3 gives the same PET as pet = 2.

The same station PET (Hargreaves in every case) is the evaporative demand for channel and reservoir evaporation and for aquifer revap, whatever the pet setting.

docs.title: HRU adjustment
docs.text:
Whatever the method, PET is multiplied by pet_co from hydrology.hyd:

\[PET_{HRU} = \mathrm{pet\_co} \times PET\]

A blank or zero pet_co is taken as 1. A value below 0.01 is read as a Hargreaves coefficient and converted to a multiplier by dividing it by 0.0023.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A decision table is a set of rules of the form "if these conditions are met, do these actions". SWAT+ uses them wherever an operation depends on the state of the model instead of a fixed date: irrigation when plants are water stressed, planting when the soil is warm enough, fertilising only a share of the fields in a land use, releasing reservoir water by storage and season, or changing land use partway through a run.

There are four decision table files. They have the same format and are evaluated the same way.

File Used for Evaluated lum.dtl Conditional management of HRUs daily, for each HRU whose management schedule lists the table as an automatic operation res_rel.dtl Reservoir and wetland releases daily, for each reservoir or wetland that names the table as its release rule scen_lu.dtl Land use and management change scenarios daily, for every HRU, for each table listed in scen_dtl.upd flo_con.dtl Flow control (water allocation, saturated buffers) when the controlled object is processed

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Each table has conditions, alternatives and actions.

  • Conditions (rows) name a state variable, the object it is taken from, and a limit.
  • Alternatives (columns) are rules. For each condition, an alternative gives a comparison operator (<, >, <=, >=, =, /=) or - when that condition does not matter for the rule.
  • Actions (rows) say what to do. For each alternative, an action has an outcome y (do it if this rule is true) or n.

An example from refdata/Ames_sub1/lum.dtl irrigates with a sprinkler when the plant is water stressed, has accumulated more than 20 % of its heat units and has a leaf area index above 0.5, as long as less than 500 mm has been applied in the year:

name                     conds      alts      acts
irr_year_irr                4         1         1
var                        obj   obj_num           lim_var            lim_op  lim_const      alt1
irr_year                   hru         0              null                 -   500.00000         <
w_stress                   hru         0              null                 -   0.80000           <
phu_plant                  hru         0           phu_mat                 -     0.20000         >
leaf_area                  hru         0           null                    -     0.50000         >
act_typ                    obj   obj_num              name            option    const        const2                fp  outcome
irrigate                   hru        0           sprinkler     sprinkler_ilm    25.00000   20.00000  unlim  y

An object number of 0 means the object the table is being evaluated for (the current HRU, reservoir or wetland).

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Each time a table is evaluated:

  1. Every alternative starts as true.
  2. For each condition, the current value of the variable is compared with the limit. An alternative whose operator for that condition is not satisfied becomes false. A - leaves the alternative unchanged.
  3. Each action is taken if at least one alternative that is still true has y for that action.

Any number of alternatives can be true at once, and an action shared by several alternatives is taken once.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The limit a variable is compared with is built from three columns: lim_var, lim_op and lim_const. For variables measured against a property of the object, lim_var names the property and lim_op combines it with the constant. For example, for soil_water the property can be wp (taken as 0), fc (profile water at field capacity) or ul (profile water at saturation), and fc * 0.8 is written as lim_var = fc, lim_op = *, lim_const = 0.8. For reservoir volume, the property can be pvol or evol. For variables compared with a plain number, lim_var is null and only lim_const is used.

docs.title: Probabilistic conditions
docs.text:
Probability conditions make actions happen on a random day or on a random share of HRUs:

  • prob compares a uniform random number with lim_const, so the action happens on that fraction of evaluations.
  • prob_unif picks one random day in the window from day obj_num to day lim_const of the year, so the action happens once in the window.
  • prob_unif1 spreads the probability evenly over a window of lim_const days that starts on 1 January of the calendar year given in obj_num.
  • prob_unif_lu spreads an operation over the HRUs of a land use (named in a land_use condition) during the window from day obj_num to day lim_const, so that the share of HRUs treated grows evenly through the window. This is how an operation such as "fertilise 30 % of corn fields in May" is set up.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Erosion is the detachment, transport and deposition of soil particles by raindrop impact and flowing water. Raindrops detach particles on unprotected ground between rills, and the particles move to rills, then to larger channels and rivers, and can be deposited anywhere along the way. Erosion matters for reservoirs, which lose storage to deposited sediment, and for the soil, which loses the organic matter and nutrients in its surface layer.

SWAT+ computes soil loss from each HRU with the Modified Universal Soil Loss Equation (MUSLE) (Williams, 1975) on daily runs, or with a splash and overland flow erosion model on sub-daily runs. MUSLE replaces the rainfall energy factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) (Wischmeier and Smith, 1965, 1978) with a runoff factor, so it applies to single storms, reflects antecedent moisture through runoff, and needs no delivery ratio. Sediment is then lagged on its way to the channel together with surface runoff. Erosion and deposition in channels are covered on the Channels page.

Erosion is computed only on days with surface runoff and a positive peak runoff rate. HRUs with a ponded surface (wetlands and paddies) produce no surface runoff and no erosion.

docs.title: Peak runoff rate
docs.text:
The peak runoff rate is the largest flow rate during a runoff event. It sets the erosive power of the storm in MUSLE. The method is chosen with sed_det in codes.bsn.

NRCS peak rate equation (sed_det = 0):

\[q_{peak} = \frac{prf}{6578.6}\cdot\frac{A\,Q_{surf}}{t_{conc}}\cdot\frac{1}{35.3}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(q_{peak}\) Peak runoff rate m³/s \(prf\) Peak rate factor, adj_pkrt_sed in parameters.bsn - \(A\) HRU area ha \(Q_{surf}\) Surface runoff generated on the day mm H2O \(t_{conc}\) Time of concentration of the HRU (see Hydrology) hr

This is the NRCS triangular unit hydrograph peak, \(q = 484\,A\,Q/t_p\) in U.S. units, with the time of concentration used as the time to peak. The NRCS value of the peak rate factor is 484, which is also the built-in value. A zero in parameters.bsn is replaced by 1.0, and the SWAT+ reference data sets use 1.0, which gives peak rates 484 times smaller than the NRCS equation. Users of this method should check the value against their calibration.

Rational formula with half-hour rainfall (sed_det = 1):

\[q_{peak} = \frac{\alpha_{tc}\,Q_{surf}\,A_{km}}{3.6\,t_{conc}}, \qquad \alpha_{tc} = 1 - \exp\left[2\,t_{conc}\,\ln(1 - \alpha_{0.5})\right]\]

where \(\alpha_{tc}\) is the fraction of daily rain that falls in the time of concentration, \(\alpha_{0.5}\) the fraction that falls in the wettest half hour (generated daily, see Climate and weather) and \(A_{km}\) the HRU area in km².

docs.title: MUSLE
docs.text:
SWAT+ computes daily sediment yield as

\[sed = 11.8\left(V_{surf}\,q_{peak}\right)^{0.56} K_{USLE}\,C_{USLE}\,P_{USLE}\,LS_{USLE}\,CFRG\] Symbol Meaning Units \(sed\) Sediment yield on the day metric tons \(V_{surf}\) Surface runoff volume, \(10\,Q_{surf}\,A\) m³ \(K_{USLE}\) Soil erodibility factor, usle_k of the first layer in soils.sol 0.013 t m² hr/(m³ t cm) \(C_{USLE}\) Cover and management factor, computed daily - \(P_{USLE}\) Support practice factor, usle_p in cons_practice.lum - \(LS_{USLE}\) Topographic factor - \(CFRG\) Coarse fragment factor -

The runoff factor is the original MUSLE form of Williams (1975), with the runoff volume in m³. The SWAT 2009 documentation writes the same factor with runoff in mm and area in ha, without the factor 10, so SWAT+ sediment yields for the same inputs are larger by \(10^{0.56}\), about 3.6.

docs.title: Soil erodibility
docs.text: Some soils erode more easily than others even when all other factors are the same. \(K_{USLE}\) is the soil loss per unit of erosion index on a standard plot 22.1 m long on a 9% slope, kept in continuous fallow. Values are entered for each soil in soils.sol (see that page for estimation methods).

docs.title: Cover and management
docs.text:
The cover and management factor is the ratio of soil loss from land under given conditions to soil loss from clean-tilled, continuous fallow. Plant cover changes through the year, so SWAT+ computes \(C_{USLE}\) every day from the surface residue and the plant canopy:

\[C_{USLE} = \exp\left[-\mathrm{rsd\_cover}\,\frac{rsd + 1}{1000}\right]\left[1 - f_{gc}\,\exp(-0.328\,h_c)\right]\] \[f_{gc} = \frac{B}{B + \exp(1.175 - 1.748\,B)}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(\mathrm{rsd\_cover}\) Residue cover factor, rsd_cover in parameters.bsn (0.75 when zero) - \(rsd\) Surface residue kg/ha \(B\) Above-ground biomass of the plant community t/ha \(h_c\) Canopy height of the plant community m

The minimum C factor of each plant (usle_c_min in plants.plt) is not used by this daily calculation. It is used only by the sub-daily erosion model below. The daily C factor and its two parts are written to the erosion output.

docs.title: Support practice
docs.text: The support practice factor is the ratio of soil loss with a practice such as contouring, strip cropping or terracing to soil loss with up-and-down-slope culture. It comes from the row of cons_practice.lum named in the cons_prac column of landuse.lum.

docs.title: Topographic factor
docs.text:
\[LS_{USLE} = \left(\frac{L_{hill}}{22.1}\right)^m\left(65.41\,\sin^2\alpha_{hill} + 4.56\,\sin\alpha_{hill} + 0.065\right), \qquad m = 0.6\left[1 - \exp(-35.835\,slp)\right]\]

where \(L_{hill}\) is the slope length (slp_len in topography.hyd, m), \(slp\) the slope (slp, m/m) and \(\alpha_{hill} = \arctan(slp)\). cons_practice.lum also has a maximum slope length for each practice (slp_len_max); SWAT+ 62.0.1 reads it but the LS factor uses the full slope length.

docs.title: Coarse fragments
docs.text:
\[CFRG = \exp(-0.053\,rock)\]

where \(rock\) is the rock content of the first soil layer (rock in soils.sol, %).

docs.title: Snow cover
docs.text: The SWAT 2009 documentation reduces MUSLE sediment yield under a snowpack. In SWAT+ 62.0.1 that reduction is not reached for any snow depth, so snow cover does not change the sediment yield. Snowmelt runoff still produces erosion through \(Q_{surf}\) and \(q_{peak}\).

docs.title: USLE soil loss for output
docs.text:
Alongside MUSLE, SWAT+ computes the USLE soil loss from rainfall energy for output (usle in the HRU loss files):

\[A_{USLE} = 1.292\,EI_{USLE}\,K_{USLE}\,C_{USLE}\,P_{USLE}\,LS_{USLE}\,CFRG\] \[EI_{USLE} = R_{day}\left[12.1 + 8.9\left(\log_{10} I - 0.434\right)\right]\frac{I_{30}}{1000}\]

where \(I_{30} = 2\,\alpha_{0.5}\,R_{day}\) is the maximum 30-minute intensity (mm/hr) and \(I = -2\ln(1 - \alpha_{0.5})\,R_{day}\) the peak intensity. The USLE value is reported only. It does not add to the sediment yield.

docs.title: Sub-daily erosion
docs.text:
When the simulation uses a sub-daily time step with Green-Ampt infiltration, sediment for each time step comes from raindrop splash and overland flow erosion instead of MUSLE.

Splash erosion. Rain is split into direct throughfall and leaf drip by the canopy cover, \(\min(LAI, 1)\). Their kinetic energies are

\[KE_{direct} = 8.95 + 8.44\,\log_{10} I, \qquad KE_{leaf} = 15.8\sqrt{0.5\,h_c} - 5.87\]

in J/m²/mm, where \(I\) is the rainfall intensity of the step (mm/hr). Splash detachment is

\[sed_{spl} = k_d\,KE\,\exp\left(-\mathrm{splash}\,\frac{h_{flow}}{1000}\right)A_{km}\]

with \(k_d\) a soil detachability (g/J) set from the texture of the top layer (1.2 for silt up to 3.0 for loamy sand), \(KE\) the total kinetic energy of the step, \(h_{flow}\) the runoff depth of the step (mm) and splash in parameters.bsn. Splash stops when the runoff depth is at least three times the median raindrop diameter, or is negligible.

Overland flow erosion.

\[sed_{ov} = 11.02\,\mathrm{rill}\;K_{USLE}\;\mathrm{cov\_mgt}\;C\;\tau^{\,\mathrm{surq\_exp}}, \qquad \tau = 9807\,\frac{h_{flow}}{1000}\,slp\]

in kg/hr/m², converted to tons for the step and the HRU area. rill, cov_mgt and surq_exp are in parameters.bsn; \(C\) is the SWAT 2009 cover factor computed from usle_c_min and the soil cover. All three default to zero. The rate is proportional to rill and cov_mgt, so overland flow erosion is zero unless both are set; a zero surq_exp makes the shear stress term equal to 1.

On urban HRUs both terms apply only to the pervious fraction. The sediment of the day is the sum over the steps after the lag described below.

With a sub-daily time step and the curve number method, the splash and overland flow terms are not computed and MUSLE is not used either, so the HRU produces no lagged sediment from the surface.

docs.title: Sediment in lateral and tile flow
docs.text:
Lateral and tile flow transport a small sediment load:

\[sed_{lat} = \frac{\mathrm{lat\_sed}\,(Q_{lat} + Q_{tile})\,A}{100000}\]

in metric tons, with lat_sed from hydrology.hyd treated as a concentration in mg/L, and \(Q_{lat}\), \(Q_{tile}\) in mm. Sediment concentrations in subsurface flow are usually very low and matter only where return flow is large. Organic nitrogen and phosphorus in lateral flow are set by lat_orgn and lat_orgp in the same file.

docs.title: Particle size
docs.text:
The sediment from the surface is split into five classes (sand, silt, clay, small aggregates and large aggregates) using fractions set from the sand, silt and clay content of the top soil layer (Foster et al., 1980):

Class Fraction of detached sediment Sand \(f_{sa}(1 - f_{cl})^{2.49}\) Silt \(0.13\,f_{si}\) Clay \(0.20\,f_{cl}\) Small aggregates \(2.0\,f_{cl}\) for \(f_{cl} < 0.25\); \(0.28\,(f_{cl} - 0.25) + 0.5\) up to \(f_{cl} = 0.5\); 0.57 above Large aggregates the remainder

where \(f_{sa}\), \(f_{si}\) and \(f_{cl}\) are the sand, silt and clay fractions. If the first four add up to more than 1, they are rescaled and large aggregates are set to zero.

docs.title: Sediment lag
docs.text: Sediment, the particle size classes and the nutrients attached to sediment pass through the same surface lag store as runoff, and the same fraction, \(1 - \exp(-\mathrm{surq\_lag}/t_{conc})\), is released each day (see Hydrology).

docs.title: Urban areas
docs.text:
For an HRU with an urban land use (the urban and urb_ro columns of landuse.lum, parameters in urban.urb), the sediment and nutrient loads of the impervious fraction \(f_{imp}\) (frac_imp) are computed separately and mixed with the loads of the pervious part:

\[L = L_{urb}\,f_{imp} + L_{perv}\,(1 - f_{imp})\]

where \(L_{perv}\) is the load from MUSLE and the soil nutrient routines. Urban loads are computed before the surface lag store, and sediment from impervious surfaces is all silt. urb_ro selects one of two methods; any other value gives no urban loads.

USGS regression equations (usgs_reg). On days with more than 0.1 mm of precipitation and of surface runoff, the storm load of each constituent (kg) is

\[Y = \frac{\beta_0}{2.205}\left(\frac{R_{day}}{25.4}\right)^{\beta_1}\left(\frac{A\,f_{imp}}{2.589}\right)^{\beta_2}\left(100\,f_{imp} + 1\right)^{\beta_3}\beta_4\]

with \(R_{day}\) the precipitation (mm) and \(A\) the HRU area (km²). The coefficients (Driver and Tasker, 1988) depend on the mean annual precipitation of the HRU's weather generator station:

Constituent Below 508 mm 508 to 1016 mm 1016 mm and above Suspended solids 1778, 0.867, 0.728, 0.157, 2.367 812, 1.236, 0.436, 0.202, 1.938 97.7, 1.002, 1.009, 0.837, 2.818 Total N 20.2, 0.825, 1.070, 0.479, 1.258 4.04, 0.936, 0.937, 0.692, 1.373 1.66, 0.703, 0.465, 0.521, 1.845 Total P 1.725, 0.884, 0.826, 0.467, 2.130 0.697, 1.008, 0.628, 0.469, 1.790 1.618, 0.954, 0.789, 0.289, 2.247

Each cell lists \(\beta_0\) to \(\beta_4\). Total N is split into 70 % organic N and 30 % nitrate, and total P into 75 % sediment-bound and 25 % soluble P.

Build-up and wash-off (buildup_washoff). Solids build up on impervious surfaces between storms:

\[SED = \frac{SED_{mx}\,t}{t_{1/2} + t}\]

where \(SED_{mx}\) is dirt_max (kg per curb km), \(t_{1/2}\) is t_halfmax (days) and \(t\) the number of days since the surface was last washed. On a day with more than 0.1 mm of surface runoff the solids left after wash-off are

\[SED_{after} = SED\,\exp\!\left(-k_w\,q_{pk}\,t_{ro}\right)\]

with \(k_w\) = urb_wash (1/mm), \(q_{pk}\) the peak runoff rate (mm/h) and \(t_{ro}\) the storm duration from the half-hour rainfall fraction plus the time of concentration (h, at most 24). The washed-off solids are \((SED - SED_{after})\) times curb_den, in kg/ha; their N, P and nitrate contents are conc_totn, conc_totp and conc_no3n (mg/kg). Organic N is total N minus nitrate, and total P is split 75 % sediment-bound and 25 % soluble. After the storm, \(t\) is reset to the time that would build up \(SED_{after}\). Sub-daily runs apply the same method for each time step. Street sweeping has no effect in 62.0.1 (see sweep.ops).

docs.title: Filter strips, grassed waterways and user BMPs
docs.text: These practices are attached to a land use through the vfs, grww and bmp columns of landuse.lum (parameters in the structural practice files). They act on the loads released from the surface lag store each day. None of them changes the runoff volume, so the water balance is unchanged.

docs.title: Filter strips
docs.text:
A vegetative filter strip at the field edge (White and Arnold, 2009) is split into two sections. Section 1, 90 % of the strip area, receives the fraction \(1 - c\) of the field runoff; section 2, 10 % of the strip area, receives the fraction \(c\,(1 - h)\). The rest, \(c\,h\), is channelized and passes the strip unchanged. Here \(c\) is con_vfs and \(h\) is cha_q, and the strip area is the HRU area divided by fld_vfs.

For each section \(i\), the runoff depth over the strip \(q_i\) (mm) and the sediment load per strip area \(s_i\) (kg/m²) give the percent reductions

\[RR_i = 75.8 - 10.8\,\ln q_i + 25.9\,\ln K_{sat}, \qquad SR_i = 79.0 - 1.04\,s_i + 0.213\,RR_i\]

with \(K_{sat}\) the saturated conductivity of the top soil layer (mm/h). The runoff reduction \(RR_i\) is used only to estimate nutrient removal. The other reductions follow from these:

Load Reduction (%) Sediment \(SR_i\) Organic N \(0.036\,SR_i^{1.69}\) Nitrate in surface runoff \(39.4 + 0.584\,RR_i\) Sediment-bound P \(0.903\,SR_i\) Soluble P \(29.3 + 0.51\,RR_i\) Pesticide in runoff and on sediment \(RR\) and \(SR\)

Each reduction is limited to 0 to 100 % and weighted by the share of the HRU runoff each section receives. Pesticide removed by the strip is returned to the top soil layer. In 62.0.1 the soluble P reduction of section 2 uses the value computed for sediment-bound P, and pesticide loads are reduced a second time after the removed amount is returned.

docs.title: Grassed waterways
docs.text:
A grassed waterway is a vegetated trapezoidal channel with 8:1 side slopes through the field. The peak flow is computed from the day's runoff with a triangular hydrograph, and the flow depth in the waterway from Manning's equation. Part of the runoff enters the waterway as sheet flow over its side slopes; 20 % of the wetted side slope area above the flow, at most 10 % of the HRU, acts as a filter, with reductions computed as for filter strips:

\[RR = 95.6 - 10.79\,\ln q_{sf}, \qquad SR = 79.0 - 1.04\,s_{sf} + 0.213\,RR\]

both limited to 95 %. The sediment left after this filtering is then routed through the waterway: where its concentration exceeds the transport capacity \(C_{ch} = \mathrm{sed\_co}\;v^{1.5}\) (with \(v\) the flow velocity), the excess is deposited. Sediment, organic N and sediment-bound P are reduced by the fraction of sediment that leaves the waterway, and nitrate and soluble P in surface runoff by \(RR\).

docs.title: User BMPs
docs.text: A user BMP multiplies the HRU loads by \(1 - e\) for each removal efficiency \(e\) in bmpuser.str: sediment, sediment-bound P, soluble P, organic N, and nitrate in surface runoff and lateral flow.

docs.title: Riparian buffers and saturated buffers
docs.text: A riparian buffer reduction of nitrate in lateral flow is coded but depends on a buffer width that no input sets, so it has no effect in 62.0.1. A saturated buffer diverts part of the tile flow of one HRU into the soil of another HRU under a decision table (see satbuffer.str).

docs.title: Channel erosion and deposition
docs.text: Sediment that reaches a channel can be deposited on the floodplain, deposited in the channel, or joined by sediment eroded from the channel banks and bed. These processes use the channel properties in hyd-sed-lte.cha and are described on the Channels page.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Precipitation reaching an HRU may be caught by the plant canopy or fall on the soil surface. Water on the surface infiltrates into the soil profile or runs off. Runoff moves quickly towards a channel and gives the short-term response of a stream. Infiltrated water is stored in the soil and later evaporated or transpired, or it moves slowly through the profile: laterally towards the channel, into tile drains, or down past the bottom of the profile to recharge groundwater.

Evaporation from the soil is described in Soil water and temperature. What happens to the water once it reaches a channel is on the Channels page.

docs.title: Canopy interception
docs.text:
The plant canopy intercepts part of the rain, and the amount stored depends on how much canopy there is. The storage capacity on a day is

\[can_{day} = can_{mx}\,\frac{LAI}{LAI_{mx}}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(can_{day}\) Maximum canopy storage on the day mm H2O \(can_{mx}\) Maximum canopy storage when the canopy is fully developed, can_max in hydrology.hyd mm H2O \(LAI\) Leaf area index of the plant community on the day m²/m² \(LAI_{mx}\) Maximum leaf area index of the plant community m²/m²

Precipitation first fills the empty part of the canopy store, and only the rest reaches the ground. In sub-daily runs the store is filled from the first time steps of the day. Water stored in the canopy is the first water evaporated (see Soil water and temperature). Interception applies with both the curve number and the Green-Ampt method. HRUs with no leaf area have no interception.

docs.title: Surface runoff
docs.text: Surface runoff, or overland flow, occurs when water reaches the ground faster than it can infiltrate. SWAT+ has two methods, chosen with gampt in codes.bsn: the SCS curve number method (0) and the Green and Ampt infiltration method (1). Runoff is computed only on days when more than 0.1 mm of water reaches the surface. Runoff from irrigation is added to it afterwards.

docs.title: SCS curve number
docs.text:
The SCS runoff equation (SCS, 1972) is an empirical model that came into common use in the 1950s, built from more than 20 years of rainfall and runoff studies on small rural watersheds across the U.S.:

\[Q_{surf} = \frac{(R_{day} - I_a)^2}{R_{day} - I_a + S} \quad\text{for } R_{day} > I_a, \qquad Q_{surf} = 0 \text{ otherwise}\]

with the initial abstraction \(I_a = 0.2\,S\), so that

\[Q_{surf} = \frac{(R_{day} - 0.2\,S)^2}{R_{day} + 0.8\,S}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(Q_{surf}\) Accumulated runoff or rainfall excess mm H2O \(R_{day}\) Rain and snowmelt reaching the surface on the day, after interception mm H2O \(I_a\) Initial abstraction: surface storage, interception and infiltration before runoff mm H2O \(S\) Retention parameter for the day mm H2O

The retention parameter is linked to the curve number for the day, \(CN\):

\[S = 25.4\left(\frac{1000}{CN} - 10\right)\]

Curve number for average conditions. Each HRU takes its moisture condition II curve number, \(CN_2\), from the row of cntable.lum named in the cn2 column of its landuse.lum row, using the column for the soil's hydrologic group (cn_a to cn_d, from hyd_grp in soils.sol). SWAT+ 62.0.1 does not adjust \(CN_2\) for slope. The curve number for dry conditions (wilting point) and for wet conditions are

\[CN_1 = CN_2 - \frac{20\,(100 - CN_2)}{100 - CN_2 + \exp\left[2.533 - 0.0636\,(100 - CN_2)\right]}, \qquad CN_1 \ge 0.4\,CN_2\] \[CN_3 = CN_2\,\exp\left[0.006729\,(100 - CN_2)\right]\]

Daily curve number from soil water. The retention parameter varies with the water content of the soil profile:

\[S = S_{max}\left(1 - \frac{SW}{SW + \exp(w_1 - w_2\,SW)}\right), \qquad S \ge 3 \text{ mm}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(S_{max}\) Retention parameter for \(CN_1\) mm H2O \(SW\) Soil water content of the whole profile, excluding water below wilting point mm H2O \(w_1\), \(w_2\) Shape coefficients -

The shape coefficients are fixed at the start of the run so that \(S\) equals \(S_{max}\) for a dry profile, equals the \(CN_3\) retention parameter when the profile water content is \(SW_3\), and equals 2.54 mm (a curve number of 99) when the profile is saturated:

\[SW_3 = FC + \mathrm{cn3\_swf}\,(SAT - FC)\]

where \(FC\) and \(SAT\) are the profile water contents at field capacity and saturation, and cn3_swf is the column in hydrology.hyd. With cn3_swf = 0 the wet condition is reached at field capacity; values towards 1 move it towards saturation and reduce runoff from wet soils. For HRUs with a tile drain SWAT+ sets cn3_swf to 0.95.

SWAT 2009 offered a second method that ties the curve number to accumulated plant evapotranspiration. SWAT+ 62.0.1 has only the soil water method.

Frozen soil. When the second soil layer is at or below 0 °C, infiltration is reduced:

\[S_{frz} = S_{max}\left[1 - \exp(-\mathrm{cn\_froz}\;S)\right]\]

where cn_froz is the frozen soil parameter in parameters.bsn.

Urban areas. For an HRU with an urban land use, runoff from the directly connected impervious fraction (frac_dc_imp in urban.urb) is computed with a curve number of 98 and mixed with the runoff from the rest of the HRU by area. The urb_cn column of urban.urb is read but not used.

docs.title: Green and Ampt infiltration
docs.text:
The Green and Ampt method (Green and Ampt, 1911) needs precipitation at a sub-daily time step, set in time.sim and supplied in the precipitation files. It assumes a sharp wetting front that separates saturated soil above from soil at its initial water content below. SWAT+ uses the Mein and Larson (1973) form with the modification of Kim et al., where the infiltration rate at the end of a time step is

\[f_{inf} = K_e\left(1 + \frac{\Psi_{wf}\,\Delta\theta_v}{F_{inf}}\right)\] Symbol Meaning Units \(f_{inf}\) Infiltration rate mm/hr \(K_e\) Effective hydraulic conductivity mm/hr \(\Psi_{wf}\) Wetting front matric potential mm \(\Delta\theta_v\) Change in volumetric water content across the wetting front mm/mm \(F_{inf}\) Cumulative infiltration since the start of the day mm H2O

Within each time step, while the rainfall intensity is below the infiltration rate all rain infiltrates. Otherwise the cumulative infiltration at the end of the step is solved by iteration from

\[F_{inf,t} = F_{inf,t-1} + K_e\,\Delta t + \Psi_{wf}\,\Delta\theta_v\,\ln\!\left(\frac{F_{inf,t} + \Psi_{wf}\,\Delta\theta_v}{F_{inf,t-1} + \Psi_{wf}\,\Delta\theta_v}\right)\]

and the rain that does not infiltrate becomes runoff for that step.

The effective conductivity is estimated from the saturated conductivity of the top soil layer, \(K_{sat}\), and the curve number (Nearing et al., 1996):

\[K_e = \frac{56.82\,K_{sat}^{0.286}}{1 + 0.051\,\exp(0.062\,CN)} - 2, \qquad K_e \ge 0.001\]

The curve number used here is updated every time step from the soil water plus the water infiltrated so far, with the same relationship as the curve number method. The moisture deficit is

\[\Delta\theta_v = 0.95\,\phi_{soil}\left(1 - \frac{SW}{FC}\right)\]

where \(\phi_{soil}\) is the porosity of the top layer and \(SW/FC\) is limited to 0.999. If more than 12 mm of rain fell on the previous day, the soil is assumed to be nearly saturated at the start of the day and the previous day's final infiltration rate is used as the starting rate. \(\Psi_{wf}\) is estimated once for each HRU from the porosity and the sand and clay content of the top layer (Rawls and Brakensiek, 1985).

On urban HRUs the directly connected impervious fraction produces runoff from the rain left after an initial abstraction store. The store is depleted by rain and recovers on dry time steps up to urb_init_abst in parameters.bsn.

docs.title: Crack flow
docs.text: When crack is 1 in codes.bsn, SWAT+ computes a crack volume for each layer from the soil's perc_crk value in soils.sol and its current water deficit. Cracks develop slowly as the soil dries and close as it wets. Runoff up to the total crack volume is moved into the cracks, where it fills layers below field capacity from the bottom of the profile upward, and any remainder percolates from the bottom of the profile.

docs.title: Surface runoff lag
docs.text:
In large HRUs, or HRUs with a long time of concentration, only part of the runoff generated on a day reaches the channel that day. SWAT+ keeps a surface runoff store and releases a fixed fraction of it each day:

\[Q_{surf,lag} = \left(Q'_{surf} + Q_{stor,i-1}\right)\left[1 - \exp\left(\frac{-\mathrm{surq\_lag}}{t_{conc}}\right)\right]\] Symbol Meaning Units \(Q_{surf,lag}\) Surface runoff released to the channel on the day mm H2O \(Q'_{surf}\) Surface runoff generated on the day mm H2O \(Q_{stor,i-1}\) Runoff stored or lagged from the previous day mm H2O \(\mathrm{surq\_lag}\) Surface runoff lag coefficient, surq_lag in parameters.bsn - \(t_{conc}\) Time of concentration of the HRU hr

For a given time of concentration, a smaller surq_lag keeps more water in storage. In sub-daily runs the time of concentration is expressed in time steps, and the same fraction is released every step. Sediment, nutrients and other constituents in surface runoff are lagged in the same way.

The time of concentration is the sum of the overland flow time and a channel flow time within the HRU:

\[t_{ov} = \frac{0.0556\,(L_{slp}\,n)^{0.6}}{slp^{0.3}}, \qquad t_{ch} = \frac{0.31\,L\,n^{0.75}}{A^{0.125}\,(0.5\,slp + 0.001)^{0.375}}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(L_{slp}\) Slope length, slp_len in topography.hyd m \(slp\) Average slope, slp in topography.hyd m/m \(n\) Manning's n for overland flow, from the ov_mann column of landuse.lum - \(L\) Flow length, taken as \(0.5\sqrt{\text{HRU area in ha}/2}\) km \(A\) HRU area km²

docs.title: Soil water routing
docs.text: Water that infiltrates enters the top soil layer and is routed down the profile layer by layer. A layer can lose water by percolation to the layer below and by lateral flow, but only the water stored above field capacity can move.

docs.title: Percolation
docs.text:
Percolation from a layer is computed with a storage routing method:

\[w_{perc} = SW_{ex}\left[1 - \exp\left(\frac{-24}{TT_{perc}}\right)\right], \qquad TT_{perc} = \frac{SAT - FC}{K_{sat}}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(w_{perc}\) Water percolating to the next layer on the day mm H2O \(SW_{ex}\) Water in the layer above field capacity mm H2O \(TT_{perc}\) Travel time for percolation, at least 2 hours hr \(SAT\), \(FC\) Water content of the layer at saturation and at field capacity mm H2O \(K_{sat}\) Saturated hydraulic conductivity of the layer, soil_k in soils.sol mm/hr

No water percolates or flows laterally from a layer whose temperature is at or below 0 °C. Percolation from the bottom layer leaves the soil profile as recharge, and is multiplied by a factor derived from perco in hydrology.hyd:

\[f_{perco} = \min\left(1,\; \exp\left[-\left(1.0052\,\ln(-\ln \mathrm{perco}) + 5.6862\right)\right]\right)\]

perco close to 1 gives a factor of 1, so the bottom layer drains freely. Smaller values keep water in the profile, and perco = 0 stops deep percolation. For HRUs with a tile drain, SWAT+ sets perco to 0.1. Above the bottom layer, percolation is not restricted.

docs.title: Lateral flow
docs.text:
Lateral subsurface flow is computed with a kinematic storage model (Sloan et al., 1983), applied to every layer below the top one:

\[Q_{lat} = \mathrm{latq\_co}\times 0.024\,\frac{2\,SW_{ex}\,K_{sat}\,slp}{\phi_d\,L_{hill}}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(Q_{lat}\) Lateral flow from the layer mm H2O/day \(\mathrm{latq\_co}\) Lateral flow coefficient, latq_co in hydrology.hyd - \(\phi_d\) Drainable porosity of the layer, \((SAT - FC)\) divided by layer thickness mm/mm \(slp\) Average slope of the HRU m/m \(L_{hill}\) Slope length for lateral flow, lat_len in topography.hyd; 50 m when blank or zero m

If percolation and lateral flow together exceed the water above field capacity, both are reduced in proportion. The top soil layer, which is the 10 mm surface layer for most soils (see Soil water and temperature), produces no lateral flow in SWAT+.

docs.title: Saturation excess
docs.text: After percolation, any layer with more water than it can at saturation passes the excess to the layer above. Excess in the top layer is pushed down to the next layer with room, and what cannot be stored becomes surface runoff (or, on HRUs with a ponded surface, flows into the wetland or over its weir).

docs.title: Tile drainage
docs.text:
Tile drains take water from the soil when a perched water table rises above the drain. Tile flow is computed for HRUs with a tile drain (tile in landuse.lum, pointing to a row of tiledrain.str) when the second soil layer is above freezing. The method is set by tiledrain in codes.bsn: 0 uses the drawdown equation below, 1 the DRAINMOD equations.

With wtable = 0 in codes.bsn, the height of the water table above the bottom of the profile is estimated from the water stored above field capacity:

\[h_{wtbl} = \frac{SW - FC}{SAT_{90} - FC}\,depth_{prof}, \qquad SAT_{90} = \max(0.9\,SAT,\; 1.1\,FC)\]

where \(SW\), \(FC\) and \(SAT\) are profile totals and \(depth_{prof}\) is the profile depth. When the water table is above the drain, the drawdown method gives

\[Q_{tile} = \frac{h_{wtbl} - h_{drain}}{h_{wtbl}}\,(SW - FC)\left[1 - \exp\left(\frac{-24}{t_{drain}}\right)\right]\] Symbol Meaning Units \(Q_{tile}\) Tile flow on the day, at most drain in tiledrain.str mm H2O \(h_{drain}\) Height of the drain above the bottom of the profile, profile depth minus dp mm \(t_{drain}\) Time to drain the soil to field capacity, t_fc in tiledrain.str; all excess drains in one day when it is under 1 hour hr

Tile flow is taken from the layers with water above field capacity, starting at the top.

docs.title: Lag of lateral and tile flow
docs.text:
In large HRUs with a mild slope, lateral and tile flow can take more than a day to reach the channel. Both pass through a store, and the part released on a day is

\[Q_{lat,lag} = \left(Q'_{lat} + Q_{latstor,i-1}\right)\left[1 - \exp\left(\frac{-1}{TT_{lag}}\right)\right]\]

\(TT_{lag}\) is lat_ttime in hydrology.hyd, in days. When lat_ttime is zero, SWAT+ estimates it from the slope length for lateral flow and the highest conductivity in the profile, \(TT_{lag} = 10.4\,L_{hill}/K_{sat,mx}\) (at least one day). Tile flow uses \(1 - \exp(-24/lag)\), with lag in hours from tiledrain.str. Nitrate in lateral and tile flow is lagged with the water.

docs.title: Channel routing
docs.text: Water yield from the HRUs enters channels, where it is routed downstream by the variable storage method or the Muskingum method, chosen with rte_cha in codes.bsn. See Channels.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SWAT+ follows nitrogen and phosphorus through mineral, organic and plant pools in every soil layer. Fertiliser, manure, residue and atmospheric deposition add nutrients; plants take them up; and runoff, sediment, lateral flow, tile flow, percolation, denitrification and volatilisation remove them. The nutrients that leave the HRU are routed through channels, where in-stream processes are described on the Channels page.

The soil processes below are those of the static carbon option (carbon = 0 in codes.bsn). With carbon = 2 the residue and humus pools and their decomposition follow the CENTURY-based model on the Carbon page, while nitrification, volatilisation, mineral phosphorus, deposition and all the transport processes below stay the same. carbon = 1 is reserved for C-FARM, which is not implemented; with it SWAT+ 62.0.1 skips residue decomposition and mineralisation altogether.

Plant uptake and nitrogen fixation are described in Plant growth and land use management.

docs.title: Soil pools
docs.text:
Element Pool Contents N Nitrate NO3-N in solution, mobile with water N Ammonium NH4-N, adsorbed on the soil N Active humus N The part of humus organic N that mineralises N Stable humus N The rest of humus organic N N Residue N Organic N in fresh residue, kept separately for each plant in each layer and on the surface P Labile (solution) P Soluble mineral P available to plants and mobile with water P Active mineral P Mineral P in rapid equilibrium with labile P P Stable mineral P Mineral P in slow equilibrium with active P P Humus organic P Organic P in humus P Residue P Organic P in fresh residue

Manure applied to the soil has separate organic pools, which are also lost with sediment.

docs.title: Initial values
docs.text:
The initial nutrient contents come from the row of nutrients.sol named for the HRU in soil_plant.ini, with built-in values when there is none:

Pool Initial value Nitrate nitrate (7 mg/kg) at the surface, decreasing with depth as \(\exp(-\mathrm{exp\_co}\,z)\), with \(z\) the depth to the bottom of the layer in mm Labile P lab_p (5 mg/kg) at the surface, decreasing with depth the same way Active mineral P Labile P × (1 − PSP)/PSP Stable mineral P 4 × active P; with the Vadas and White P model, from the White et al. (2009) ratio of 1 to 7 times active plus labile P Humus C, N and P Humus C from the organic carbon of the layer (carbon in soils.sol); N and P from the humus C:N and C:P ratios hum_c_n (10) and hum_c_p (80) Active and stable humus fr_hum_act (0.02) of humus in the active pool

Concentrations in mg/kg are converted to kg/ha with the bulk density and thickness of each layer. The other soil test columns of nutrients.sol (inorgp, watersol_p, h3a_p, mehlich_p, bray_strong_p) are not used.

docs.title: Temperature and water factors
docs.text:
Mineralisation, decomposition and denitrification depend on soil temperature and water through two factors:

\[\gamma_{tmp} = \max\left(0.1,\; 0.9\,\frac{T_{soil}}{T_{soil} + \exp(9.93 - 0.312\,T_{soil})} + 0.1\right), \qquad \gamma_{sw} = \max\left(0.05,\; 0.1 + 0.9\sqrt{\frac{SW_{ly}}{FC_{ly}}}\right)\]

where \(T_{soil}\) is the layer temperature (°C), \(SW_{ly}\) the layer water and \(FC_{ly}\) its field capacity water. They combine as \(\gamma = \sqrt{\gamma_{tmp}\,\gamma_{sw}}\). None of these processes runs in a layer at or below 0 °C. For the 10 mm surface layer, SWAT+ uses the temperature and water content of the second layer.

docs.title: Humus mineralisation
docs.text:
Nitrogen moves between the active and stable humus pools towards a fixed active fraction:

\[N_{trns} = 10^{-5}\left[orgN_{act}\left(\frac{1}{fr_{actN}} - 1\right) - orgN_{sta}\right]\]

where \(fr_{actN}\) is n_act_frac in carbon.bsn (0.02). A positive value moves N from active to stable humus.

Active humus N mineralises to nitrate:

\[N_{mina} = \beta_{min}\,\gamma\,orgN_{act}\]

with \(\beta_{min}\) the rate coefficient for humus mineralisation, orgn_min in parameters.bsn. Phosphorus is mineralised from humus in proportion:

\[P_{mina} = 1.4\,N_{mina}\,\frac{orgP_{hum}}{orgN_{act} + orgN_{sta}}\]

and added to the labile pool.

docs.title: Residue decomposition
docs.text:
Fresh residue decomposes at a rate limited by its C:N and C:P ratios. For each plant's residue in each layer,

\[\gamma_{ntr} = \min\left(\exp\left[-0.693\,\frac{\varepsilon_{C:N} - 25}{25}\right],\; \exp\left[-0.693\,\frac{\varepsilon_{C:P} - 200}{200}\right],\; 1\right)\]

with \(\varepsilon_{C:N}\) capped at 500 and \(\varepsilon_{C:P}\) at 5000. The fraction decomposed on the day is

\[\delta_{ntr} = \min\left[1,\; \max\left(\mathrm{rsd\_decay},\; \beta_{rsd}\,\gamma_{ntr}\,\gamma\right)\right]\]

where \(\beta_{rsd}\) is the residue decomposition coefficient of the plant (plnt_decomp in plants.plt) and rsd_decay in parameters.bsn is a minimum daily rate. Of the N and P released, 80% goes to nitrate and labile P, and 20% to humus (active humus N; stable humus P for soil residue, active humus P for surface residue).

Surface residue decomposes the same way, using the temperature and water of the top layer.

docs.title: Nitrification and ammonia volatilisation
docs.text:
Ammonium is nitrified and volatilised together in each layer (Reddy et al., 1979; Godwin et al., 1984). The temperature factor is

\[\eta_{tmp} = 0.41\,\frac{T_{soil} - 5}{10}\]

and both processes need \(\eta_{tmp} \ge 0.001\). The water factor for nitrification rises linearly from 0 at wilting point to 1 at wilting point plus 25% of the field capacity water. Volatilisation decreases with depth through

\[\eta_{midz} = 1 - \frac{z_{mid}}{z_{mid} + \exp(4.706 - 0.0305\,z_{mid})}\]

with \(z_{mid}\) the depth to the middle of the layer (mm), and uses a cation exchange factor of 0.15. With \(\eta_{nit} = \eta_{tmp}\,\eta_{sw}\) and \(\eta_{vol} = 0.15\,\eta_{tmp}\,\eta_{midz}\), the ammonium lost to both is

\[N_{nit|vol} = NH_4\left[1 - \exp(-\eta_{nit} - \eta_{vol})\right]\]

and is split between nitrification and volatilisation in proportion to \(1 - \exp(-\eta_{nit})\) and \(1 - \exp(-\eta_{vol})\).

docs.title: Denitrification
docs.text:
When the water factor reaches a threshold, nitrate in the layer is denitrified:

\[N_{denit} = NO_3\left[1 - \exp\left(-\beta_{denit}\,\gamma_{tmp}\,\frac{orgC}{100}\right)\right] \quad\text{for } \gamma_{sw} \ge \gamma_{sw,thr}\] Symbol Meaning Input \(\beta_{denit}\) Denitrification rate coefficient denit_exp in parameters.bsn \(\gamma_{sw,thr}\) Threshold of the water factor denit_frac in parameters.bsn \(orgC\) Organic carbon of the layer carbon in soils.sol, %

The septic biozone layer of an active septic system is excluded.

docs.title: Atmospheric deposition
docs.text: Nitrate and ammonium in rain and dry deposition are added to the surface layer every day from the station named in the atmo_dep column of weather-sta.cli. Rain deposition is the concentration in rain (mg/L) times the day's precipitation; dry deposition is spread evenly over the days of the month or year, depending on whether atmodep.cli gives monthly, yearly or average annual values.

docs.title: Nitrate movement
docs.text:
Nitrate is mobile and moves with water. In each layer the water that moves is the percolation, lateral flow, surface runoff (top layer only) and tile flow (tile layer only), \(w_{mobile}\). The nitrate concentration in the mobile water is

\[conc_{NO_3} = \frac{NO_3\left[1 - \exp\left(\dfrac{-w_{mobile}}{(1 - \theta_e)\,SAT_{ly}}\right)\right]}{w_{mobile}}\]

where \(\theta_e\) is the fraction of porosity from which anions are excluded (anion_excl in soils.sol) and \(SAT_{ly}\) the saturation water of the layer. Then:

Path Nitrate removed Surface runoff \(\beta_{NO_3}\,conc_{NO_3}\,Q_{surf}\), top layer, with \(\beta_{NO_3}\) = n_perc in parameters.bsn Lateral flow \(conc_{NO_3}\,Q_{lat,ly}\) for each layer Tile flow nperco_lchtile × concentration in the tile flow × \(Q_{tile}\), with the concentration taken over the tile layer and all layers below Percolation \(conc_{NO_3}\,w_{perc,ly}\), added to the next layer; from the bottom layer it leaves the profile

n_perc close to 0 gives little nitrate in surface runoff; close to 1 gives runoff the same concentration as percolate. As water evaporates from the second layer, a small amount of nitrate moves up with it into the surface layer.

Nitrate in lateral and tile flow passes through the same lag stores as the water (see Hydrology). When the gwflow module passes groundwater into the soil profile, it also adds the nitrate and phosphorus that the groundwater contains.

docs.title: Organic N and P with sediment
docs.text:
Organic nitrogen leaving with sediment is

\[orgN_{surf} = 1000\,\frac{orgN_{ly1}}{M_{ly1}}\,\varepsilon_N\,\frac{sed}{A}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(orgN_{surf}\) Organic N removed in sediment kg N/ha \(orgN_{ly1}\) Active plus stable humus N in the surface layer kg N/ha \(M_{ly1}\) Mass of the surface layer, \(10000\,\rho_b\,depth\) kg/ha \(\varepsilon_N\) Nitrogen enrichment ratio - \(sed\) Sediment yield metric tons \(A\) HRU area ha

Sediment-attached phosphorus is computed the same way from the humus, manure and active and stable mineral P of the surface layer, using \(\varepsilon_P\), and is reported as organic P and mineral P.

The enrichment ratio accounts for the finer, nutrient-rich particles that erosion removes. It is orgn_enrich (N) or orgp_enrich (P) in hydrology.hyd when that is above 0.001. Otherwise it is computed from the sediment concentration in runoff (Menzel, 1980):

\[\varepsilon = 0.78\,(conc_{sed})^{-0.2468}, \qquad conc_{sed} = \frac{sed}{10\,A\,Q_{surf}}, \qquad \varepsilon \le 3\]

docs.title: Soluble phosphorus
docs.text:
Labile phosphorus is strongly bound by the soil, so little of it moves with water. The amount removed in surface runoff is

\[P_{surf} = \frac{P_{lab,1}\,Q_{surf}}{\rho_b\,depth_1\,k_{d,surf} + 1}\]

where \(P_{lab,1}\) is the labile P of the surface layer (kg/ha), \(\rho_b\) and \(depth_1\) its bulk density and thickness (mm), and \(k_{d,surf}\) the phosphorus soil partitioning coefficient, p_soil in parameters.bsn (m³/Mg).

Leaching of labile P from each layer to the next is

\[P_{perc} = 0.001\,P_{lab}\left[1 - \exp\left(\frac{-w_{perc}}{0.01\,SW_{ly} + 0.1\,k_{d,perc}\,\rho_b}\right)\right]\]

with \(k_{d,perc}\) the phosphorus percolation coefficient p_perc in parameters.bsn. The same expression with tile flow in place of percolation gives the P in tile flow from the tile layer. This form differs from the SWAT 2009 leaching equation.

docs.title: Original model
docs.text:
With soil_p = 0 in codes.bsn, labile and active mineral P move towards the ratio set by the phosphorus availability index \(pai\) (p_avail in parameters.bsn):

\[P_{sol|act} = P_{lab} - P_{act}\,\frac{pai}{1 - pai}\]

Movement from labile to active P takes 10% of the imbalance per day; movement back takes 60%. Active and stable P move towards a stable pool four times the active pool:

\[P_{act|sta} = 0.01\,(4\,P_{act} - P_{sta})\]

with a tenth of that rate when stable P returns to the active pool.

docs.title: Vadas and White model
docs.text: With soil_p = 1, SWAT+ uses the phosphorus model of Vadas and White (2010). The availability index is computed for each layer from clay content, labile P and organic carbon, and averaged over 30 days. The rate of movement between labile and active P depends on how many days the imbalance has lasted. The active to stable equilibrium ratio follows the White et al. (2009) relationship, and the active to stable rate depends on the calcium carbonate content (caco3 in soils.sol). Both rates are scaled by the water content of the layer relative to field capacity, with a lower limit of 0.25.

docs.title: Lag of nutrients in surface runoff
docs.text: Nitrate and labile P in surface runoff, organic N and P, and mineral P attached to sediment pass through the surface lag store with the runoff and sediment, and the same daily fraction is released (see Hydrology).

docs.title: Algae, CBOD and dissolved oxygen in runoff
docs.text:
Each day SWAT+ also gives the water leaving an HRU a chlorophyll-a, carbonaceous BOD and dissolved oxygen load, which the channels then use as inflow concentrations. On days without water yield all three are zero. With water yield \(Q\) (surface runoff, lateral flow and tile flow, mm):

  • Chlorophyll-a is 0.1 times the concentration of organic N in sediment plus nitrate in surface runoff, \(100\,(N_{org,sed} + NO_{3,surq})/Q\).
  • CBOD is 2.7 times the organic carbon in the day's sediment yield, divided by the water yield. The carbon is the soil carbon content of the top layer times the sediment yield and the enrichment ratio, or, with carbon = 2 in codes.bsn, the carbon the carbon model reports in the sediment.
  • Dissolved oxygen is \(O_{sat}\,e^{-0.1\,CBOD}\), limited to between 0 and \(O_{sat}\), with \(O_{sat}\) the saturation concentration at a water temperature of \(5 + 0.75\,\bar{T}_{air}\) (see Channels for the formula).

docs.title: Septic systems
docs.text: A land use with a septic system (the sep column of landuse.lum) adds a biozone layer to the soil, and the biozone routine runs on days when that layer is above freezing. In 62.0.1 the effluent volume is never computed, so septic systems add no water, nitrogen, phosphorus or BOD to the soil. See septic.str for the inputs.

docs.title: In-stream processes
docs.text: Nutrients entering channels are transformed by the QUAL2E water quality routines. With i_fpwet = 1 in codes.bsn (the column read as the QUAL2E switch), a simplified exchange between dissolved and particulate N and P is added. See Channels.

docs.text:
Input File Effect carbon codes.bsn 0 static pools, 2 CENTURY-based carbon, 1 reserved soil_p codes.bsn 0 original mineral P model, 1 Vadas and White (2010) orgn_min parameters.bsn Humus mineralisation rate coefficient rsd_decay parameters.bsn Minimum daily residue decomposition denit_exp, denit_frac parameters.bsn Denitrification rate and water threshold n_perc parameters.bsn Nitrate in surface runoff relative to percolate nperco_lchtile parameters.bsn Nitrate concentration coefficient for tile flow p_soil, p_perc parameters.bsn Phosphorus partitioning in runoff and percolation p_avail parameters.bsn Phosphorus availability index (original model) n_act_frac carbon.bsn Active fraction of humus N orgn_enrich, orgp_enrich hydrology.hyd Fixed enrichment ratios plnt_decomp plants.plt Residue decomposition coefficient of each plant nitrate, lab_p, exp_co, fr_hum_act, hum_c_n, hum_c_p nutrients.sol Initial nutrient contents carbon, anion_excl, caco3 soils.sol Organic carbon, anion exclusion, CaCO3
