docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The water balance drives everything else SWAT+ simulates: to predict the movement of sediment, nutrients, pesticides or salts, the model first has to reproduce the movement of water. SWAT+ splits the hydrology of a watershed into two parts. The land phase, covered here and in the pages that follow, controls how much water, sediment and chemical load each hydrologic response unit (HRU) delivers. The routing phase moves those loads through channels, aquifers, reservoirs and wetlands to the outlet.

Each HRU is computed once per day (or per sub-daily time step for runoff when Green-Ampt infiltration is used). The HRU keeps track of four water stores: the plant canopy, the snowpack, the soil profile and, where one is defined, a ponded surface such as a wetland or rice paddy. Water that leaves the soil profile at the bottom becomes recharge to an aquifer object or to the gwflow module.

docs.title: Soil water balance
docs.text:
The land-phase balance for the soil profile of an HRU over a period of \(t\) days is

\[SW_t = SW_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(R_{day} + I - Q_{surf} - E_a - w_{perc} - Q_{lat} - Q_{tile}\right)\] Symbol Meaning Units \(SW_t\) Soil water content at the end of day \(t\) mm H2O \(SW_0\) Soil water content at the start of the period mm H2O \(R_{day}\) Rain and snowmelt reaching the soil surface, after canopy interception and snowfall mm H2O \(I\) Irrigation and run-on from upslope objects mm H2O \(Q_{surf}\) Surface runoff generated on the day mm H2O \(E_a\) Evaporation from the soil and transpiration by plants mm H2O \(w_{perc}\) Percolation from the bottom of the soil profile mm H2O \(Q_{lat}\) Lateral subsurface flow leaving the soil layers mm H2O \(Q_{tile}\) Tile drain flow mm H2O

All terms are depths over the HRU area. Water in the canopy and in the snowpack is stored outside the soil profile: precipitation first fills canopy storage, then falls as snow on cold days, and only the remainder (plus snowmelt) is available for runoff and infiltration. Total evapotranspiration reported for the HRU is the sum of canopy evaporation, plant transpiration and soil evaporation, with snow sublimation and evaporation from ponded water counted in soil evaporation.

Surface runoff, lateral flow and tile flow do not all reach the channel on the day they are generated. Each passes through a lag store (see Hydrology), so the HRU water yield on a day is

\[Q_{yld} = Q_{surf,lag} + Q_{lat,lag} + Q_{tile,lag}\]

where the subscript \(lag\) marks the part of each store released that day.

docs.title: Daily order of calculations
docs.text:
The order matters because each process sees the state left by the processes before it. For each HRU on each day SWAT+ 62.0.1 runs:

  1. Elevation lapse corrections to precipitation and temperature, when lapse is on in codes.bsn.
  2. Decision table operations and water allocation demands for the HRU.
  3. Base-zero heat unit accumulation, albedo, salt and constituent soil chemistry.
  4. Soil temperature for every layer.
  5. Canopy interception.
  6. Snowfall, snowpack temperature and snowmelt.
  7. Run-on from upslope objects: surface runoff, lateral flow, tile flow and aquifer flow routed onto the HRU.
  8. Soil crack volume, when crack is on in codes.bsn.
  9. Potential evapotranspiration, canopy evaporation and soil evaporation.
  10. Scheduled management operations from the HRU's management schedule.
  11. Surface runoff, peak runoff rate and erosion. HRUs with a ponded surface (wetland or paddy) produce no surface runoff or erosion here; their water is handled in the next step.
  12. Wetland and paddy water balance.
  13. Infiltration and soil water routing: percolation, lateral flow, tile flow and saturation excess.
  14. Grazing, residue decomposition, mineralisation, nitrification and volatilisation, and mineral phosphorus transformations.
  15. Plant growth, including plant water and nutrient uptake (transpiration).
  16. Pesticide wash-off, uptake, decay and leaching; nutrient and pesticide losses with runoff and sediment; atmospheric deposition; nitrate and soluble phosphorus movement.
  17. Urban build-up and wash-off, sediment in lateral flow, and the surface lag store for sediment and chemicals.
  18. Lag of lateral and tile flow, filter strips, grassed waterways and user-defined BMPs.
  19. Lag of surface runoff.
  20. Water yield and routing of the HRU's outflow to the objects it is connected to.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SWAT+ simulates any number of pesticides, listed in the constituent setup and described in pesticide.pes. Each pesticide has a sorption coefficient, a solubility, half-lives on foliage, in soil, in water and in benthic sediment, and optional degradation products (metabolites). On land, a pesticide is applied by a management operation, split between plant foliage and the soil, washed from foliage by rain, decayed, taken up by plants, and moved by surface runoff, lateral flow, tile flow, percolation and eroded sediment. Pesticide that reaches channels, reservoirs and aquifers continues to react and move there.

The daily order in an HRU is washoff (on days with at least 2.54 mm of rain), plant uptake, decay, transport in water, then transport with sediment (on days with erosion).

docs.title: Application
docs.text:
A pesticide application operation names the pesticide, the amount and an application method from chem_app.ops. The amount reaching the field is the applied amount multiplied by the application efficiency of the method:

\[ P_{app} = P_{op}\,\varepsilon_{app} \]

The fraction intercepted by the canopy depends on the leaf area index of all plants in the HRU:

\[ f_{gc} = \frac{1.99532 - \operatorname{erfc}(1.333\,LAI - 2)}{2.1}, \qquad f_{gc} \ge 0 \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(P_{app}\) pesticide reaching the field kg/ha \(P_{op}\) amount in the operation kg/ha application operation \(\varepsilon_{app}\) application efficiency fraction app_eff in chem_app.ops \(f_{gc}\) fraction intercepted by foliage fraction \(LAI\) sum of leaf area index of all plants m²/m²

The intercepted part, \(f_{gc}P_{app}\), is divided among the plants in proportion to their leaf area. The rest reaches the soil: the surface fraction surf_frac of the application method goes to the top soil layer (10 mm) and the remainder to the second layer.

docs.title: Washoff
docs.text:
On days with at least 2.54 mm of precipitation, a fixed fraction of the pesticide on each plant's foliage is washed to the top soil layer:

\[ P_{wash} = f_{wash}\,P_{fol} \]

where \(f_{wash}\) is the washoff fraction frac_wash of the pesticide and \(P_{fol}\) the pesticide on the foliage (kg/ha).

docs.title: Decay
docs.text:
Pesticide on foliage and in each soil layer decays by first-order kinetics. The daily survival factor is computed from the half-life:

\[ P_{i} = P_{i-1}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{-0.693}{t_{1/2}}\right) \]

with \(t_{1/2}\) the foliar half-life hl_foliage for foliage and the soil half-life hl_soil for soil (days). A half-life of 0 removes all of the pesticide in one day.

docs.title: Temperature adjustment
docs.text:
When the temperature switch for pesticide decay in parameters.bsn is 1, the half-lives are treated as values at 25 °C and adjusted each day with a Q10 relation:

\[ t_{1/2}(T) = t_{1/2,25}\;Q_{10}^{\,(25 - T)/10}, \qquad Q_{10} = 2.58 \] Pool Half-life used Temperature \(T\) Soil layer hl_soil temperature of that layer Foliage hl_foliage temperature of the top soil layer Channel water aq_hlife channel water temperature (at least 0.1 °C) Channel benthic sediment ben_hlife channel water temperature Aquifer aq_hlife 0 °C; the aquifer temperature is not set in 62.0.1

Each 10 °C below 25 °C multiplies the half-life by 2.58, and each 10 °C above 25 °C divides it by 2.58. Reservoirs always use the unadjusted half-lives.

The temperature switch and the pesticide groundwater mixing factor are read as the 6th and 7th values of parameters.bsn. Files written by the SWAT+ Editor label these columns lin_sed and exp_sed, which older revisions did not use. A file with exp_sed = 1 therefore turns temperature-adjusted decay on, and the lin_sed value becomes the groundwater mixing factor. Check both columns before running pesticides with an older parameters.bsn.

docs.title: Metabolites
docs.text:
When a pesticide has degradation products, a share of the mass that decays is added to each daughter pesticide:

\[ \Delta P_{d} = \Delta P_{parent}\;f_{d}\;\frac{M_{d}}{M_{parent}} \] Symbol Meaning Units \(\Delta P_{d}\) mass added to the daughter kg/ha \(\Delta P_{parent}\) parent mass decayed on the day kg/ha \(f_{d}\) fraction of the parent that degrades to this daughter, set separately for foliage, soil, water and benthic sediment fraction \(M\) molecular weight mol_wt g/mol

Metabolites form on foliage, in soil, in channel water and benthic sediment, and in aquifers.

docs.title: Plant uptake
docs.text:
Growing plants take up dissolved pesticide with the water they extract from each soil layer. Uptake from a layer is

\[ P_{up} = f_{TSCF}\;\frac{w_{up}}{SW_{eff} + w_{up} + K_d\,\rho_b\,z}\;P_{ly} \] \[ SW_{eff} = SW + n\,\max(0,\;FC - SW) \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(P_{up}\) pesticide taken up from the layer kg/ha \(f_{TSCF}\) transpiration stream concentration factor - pl_uptake \(w_{up}\) plant water uptake from the layer mm \(SW\), \(FC\) layer soil water and field capacity mm \(n\) resistance blending factor, 0 uses actual soil water and 1 uses field capacity 0 to 1 resistance_n (default 1) \(K_d\) soil partition coefficient, \(K_{oc}\cdot OC/100\) mL/g soil_ads \(\rho_b\), \(z\) bulk density and layer thickness Mg/m³, mm \(P_{ly}\) pesticide in the layer kg/ha

When harvest_sink is 1 (default), pesticide taken up is lost from the system. When it is 0, it is stored in the plant, removed with the harvested yield, and returned to the soil surface when the plant is killed.

docs.title: Transport in water
docs.text:
In each soil layer, pesticide is shared between the soil water and sorbed phases with a linear partition coefficient based on the organic carbon content of the layer:

\[ K_d = \frac{K_{oc}\;OC}{100} \]

where \(K_{oc}\) is soil_ads (mL/g) and \(OC\) the organic carbon content of the layer (%). The concentration of pesticide in water leaving the layer is

\[ C = \min\!\left(\frac{P_{ly}\left[1 - \exp\!\left(\dfrac{-w}{SAT + K_d\,\rho_b\,z}\right)\right]}{w},\;\frac{S_w}{100}\right) \] Symbol Meaning Units \(C\) pesticide concentration in mobile water kg/ha per mm \(w\) water leaving the layer: percolation and lateral flow, plus surface runoff for the top layer and tile flow for the drained layer mm \(SAT\) water content of the layer at saturation mm \(S_w\) solubility solub mg/L

Mass moved by each flow path is the concentration times the flow:

  • surface runoff removes \(\beta_{perc}\,C\) times the runoff depth, where \(\beta_{perc}\) is the pesticide percolation coefficient pest_perc in parameters.bsn;
  • lateral flow from the top layer also uses \(\beta_{perc}\,C\); lateral flow from deeper layers uses \(C\);
  • tile flow and percolation use \(C\). Percolation moves pesticide to the next layer, and out of the bottom layer to the aquifer.

docs.title: Transport with sediment
docs.text:
On days with erosion, pesticide sorbed to the top soil layer leaves with the sediment yield:

\[ P_{sed} = 0.001\;\frac{C_{sorb}\;sed\;\varepsilon_{er}}{A} \] Symbol Meaning Units \(P_{sed}\) pesticide removed with sediment kg/ha \(C_{sorb}\) sorbed concentration in the top layer g/t \(sed\) sediment yield t \(\varepsilon_{er}\) enrichment ratio, erorgn in hydrology.hyd if above 0.001, otherwise computed from the sediment concentration - \(A\) HRU area ha

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Pesticide entering a channel is split into dissolved and sorbed phases using the channel carbon content and the sediment concentration of the inflow. Over the travel time through the reach (as a fraction of a day, at most 1) the dissolved and sorbed mass in water decays with the aquatic half-life aq_hlife. Dissolved pesticide volatilises at rate aq_volat and sorbed pesticide settles to the bed at rate aq_settle (m/day, divided by flow depth). Bed pesticide is resuspended at rate aq_resus, exchanges with the water by diffusion (a mixing velocity derived from the molecular weight and bed porosity), is buried at rate ben_bury over the active bed depth ben_act_dep, and decays with the benthic half-life ben_hlife. Dissolved pesticide above the solubility limit is moved to the bed. The pesticide left in the water leaves the reach in proportion to outflow over outflow plus storage.

Reservoirs follow the same set of processes (decay, volatilisation, settling, resuspension, diffusion and burial) without temperature adjustment. Pesticide reactions in wetlands are not simulated in this revision.

docs.title: Aquifers
docs.text: Pesticide reaching an aquifer decays with the aquatic half-life and leaves in baseflow and deep seepage. Its concentration is the aquifer pesticide mass divided by a mixing volume made of baseflow, seepage, revap and a fraction of aquifer storage. That fraction is the pesticide groundwater mixing factor in parameters.bsn (default 0, so only the day's outflows dilute the pesticide). See Aquifers.

docs.title: Plant Growth and Land Use Management
Overview
docs.text:
Each HRU has a plant community: one or more plants listed in plant.ini and described in plants.plt. SWAT+ grows every living plant of the community each day with a simplified version of the EPIC plant growth model. Phenological development follows accumulated heat units. Potential growth comes from intercepted light and the radiation use efficiency of the plant, and is reduced by water, temperature, nitrogen, phosphorus, aeration and (when salts are simulated) salinity stress. Growth removes water and nutrients from the soil, and harvest, kill and senescence return plant material to the residue and soil pools.

Plants are planted, harvested and killed by the management schedule of the HRU and by decision tables (see Land use management).

docs.title: Plant types
docs.text:
The plnt_typ column of plants.plt sets how a plant develops:

plnt_typ Behaviour warm_annual, warm_annual_tuber Annual; leaf area declines towards the end of the season cold_annual, cold_annual_tuber Annual; goes dormant in winter if planted late enough perennial Grows over several years towards maturity (yrs_mat); goes dormant each year

The gro_trig column sets what restarts growth: temp_gro for plants driven by temperature and day length, moisture_gro for plants in climates with a wet and dry season, where growth follows the ratio of precipitation to PET.

docs.title: Heat units
docs.text:
Plants develop at a rate set by temperature. Each day a plant above its base temperature accumulates heat units:

\[HU = \bar{T} - T_{base} \quad\text{when } \bar{T} > T_{base}\]

and the fraction of potential heat units reached is

\[fr_{PHU} = \sum_{i=1}^{d}\frac{HU_i}{PHU}\] Symbol Meaning Input \(\bar{T}\) Mean air temperature of the day °C \(T_{base}\) Minimum (base) temperature for growth tmp_base in plants.plt, °C \(PHU\) Potential heat units needed to bring the plant to maturity see below

\(fr_{PHU}\) starts at 0 at planting and reaches 1 at maturity. SWAT+ sets PHU for each plant at the start of the run from the long-term monthly temperatures of the weather generator station and days_mat in plants.plt:

  • days_mat > 0: the heat units accumulated over days_mat days, starting from an estimated planting date. For annuals the planting date is taken where base-zero heat units reach 15% of their annual total.
  • days_mat = 0: 95% of the heat units above \(T_{base}\) in a whole year, so the plant can stay active through the entire growing season.

For perennials a second counter runs over the years to maturity, with \(PHU \times\) yrs_mat as its target. It sets canopy height and root depth.

Base-zero heat units (\(T_{base} = 0\), divided by the annual total) are also accumulated each year from 1 January. They schedule operations that happen when no plant is growing.

docs.title: Dormancy
docs.text: Perennials and cold-season annuals go dormant when the day length falls below the minimum day length of the station plus a threshold. While dormant a plant does not grow. When a perennial goes dormant its seed mass is moved to residue and its heat unit counter is reset; it starts accumulating heat units again when the day length rises above the threshold. Cold-season annuals go dormant only if they have reached less than 75% of their heat units.

docs.title: Light interception and biomass
docs.text:
Each growing plant intercepts photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), taken as half of incoming solar radiation, according to Beer's law:

\[H_{phosyn} = 0.5\,H_{day}\left[1 - \exp\left(-k_\ell\,(LAI + 0.05)\right)\right]\]

where \(H_{day}\) is the solar radiation (MJ/m²), \(k_\ell\) the light extinction coefficient (ext_co in plants.plt) and \(LAI\) the leaf area index of the plant. Each plant intercepts light as though it were alone: SWAT+ 62.0.1 has a routine for competition for light between taller and shorter plants, but it is switched off.

docs.title: Radiation use efficiency
docs.text:
The radiation use efficiency (RUE) is the biomass produced per unit of intercepted light. It responds to CO2 (Stockle et al., 1992). When co2 in parameters.bsn is above 350 ppm,

\[RUE = \frac{100\,CO_2}{CO_2 + \exp(r_1 - r_2\,CO_2)}\]

where \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are fitted so that RUE equals bm_e at 330 ppm and bm_e_hi at co2_hi. Otherwise RUE is bm_e. \(CO_2\) is the concentration for the year (see Climate and weather).

When the vapour pressure deficit \(vpd\) is above 1 kPa, RUE declines:

\[RUE = RUE - \Delta ruedcl_{vpd}\,(vpd - 1), \qquad RUE \ge 0.27\,\mathrm{bm\_e}\]

where \(\Delta ruedcl_{vpd}\) is ru_vpd in plants.plt.

docs.title: Biomass growth
docs.text:
Potential daily biomass growth is \(\Delta bio = RUE \times H_{phosyn}\) (kg/ha). The actual growth is

\[\Delta bio_{act} = \Delta bio\;\gamma_{reg}, \qquad \gamma_{reg} = \min\left(\gamma_w,\;\gamma_t,\;\gamma_n,\;\gamma_p,\;\gamma_a,\;\gamma_s\right)\]

where each \(\gamma\) is a growth factor between 0 (no growth) and 1 (no stress) for water, temperature, nitrogen, phosphorus, aeration and salinity. When salinity is simulated with the salt tolerance option, the salinity factor multiplies the minimum of the others instead. Plant carbon is taken as 42% of biomass. nostress in codes.bsn turns stresses off: 1 sets all factors to 1 and 2 sets only the nitrogen and phosphorus factors to 1.

The new biomass is split into roots, leaves, stems and seed. The root fraction falls from rt_st_beg at the start of the season to rt_st_end at maturity (for perennials, over the first 20% of the years to maturity).

docs.title: Leaf area development
docs.text:
Leaf area follows an optimal curve defined by two points from plants.plt: at frac_hu1 of the heat units the plant reaches lai_max1 of its maximum LAI, and at frac_hu2 it reaches lai_max2. The fraction of maximum LAI for a given \(fr_{PHU}\) is

\[fr_{LAImx} = \frac{fr_{PHU}}{fr_{PHU} + \exp(\ell_1 - \ell_2\,fr_{PHU})}\]

with the shape coefficients \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) fitted to the two points. Until \(fr_{PHU}\) reaches hu_lai_decl, the leaf area added on a day is

\[\Delta LAI = \left(fr_{LAImx,i} - fr_{LAImx,i-1}\right)LAI_{mx}\left[1 - \exp\left(5\,(LAI_{i-1} - LAI_{mx})\right)\right]\sqrt{\gamma_w}\]

and is shared among plants in proportion to their LAI times canopy height. \(LAI_{mx}\) is lai_pot. For perennials it grows with age:

\[LAI_{mx} = \mathrm{lai\_pot}\left(\frac{yr_{cur}}{\mathrm{yrs\_mat}}\right)^{\mathrm{bm\_tree\_acc}}\]

docs.title: Leaf senescence
docs.text:
After hu_lai_decl, annuals lose leaf area until maturity:

\[LAI = LAI_{mx}\left(\frac{1 - fr_{PHU}}{1 - fr_{PHU,sen}}\right)^{\mathrm{dlai\_rate}}\]

where \(fr_{PHU,sen}\) is the heat unit fraction at which decline started. Temperature-driven perennials drop to lai_min over 15 days once hu_lai_decl is passed. Moisture-driven perennials shed leaves continuously at a turnover rate between leaf_tov_mn and leaf_tov_mx months, faster when the 30-day precipitation to PET ratio is below 0.5. Leaves that fall are added to the surface residue.

docs.title: Canopy height and roots
docs.text:
\[h_c = h_{c,mx}\sqrt{fr_{LAImx}}\]

with \(h_{c,mx}\) = can_ht_max. Root depth grows with heat units:

\[z_{root} = 2.5\,fr_{PHU}\,z_{root,mx}, \qquad 25.4\text{ mm} \le z_{root} \le \text{profile depth}\]

with \(z_{root,mx}\) = rt_dp_max (converted to mm). Perennials use the multi-year heat unit fraction, so their roots keep deepening until maturity.

docs.title: Water uptake
docs.text:
The potential transpiration of the HRU (see Soil water and temperature) is shared among growing plants in proportion to their LAI. Each plant takes up water from the layers within its root zone. The potential uptake down to depth \(z\) is

\[w_{up,z} = \frac{E_t}{1 - \exp(-\beta_w)}\left[1 - \exp\left(-\beta_w\,\frac{z}{z_{root}}\right)\right]\]

with the water use distribution parameter \(\beta_w\) fixed at 10, so about half of the demand comes from the top 7% of the root zone. The uptake from a layer is the potential uptake to its bottom minus that to its top, with the shortfall of the layers above added back in part:

\[w'_{up,ly} = w_{up,z_l} - w_{up,z_u}\,(1 - \mathrm{epco})\]

where epco is the plant uptake compensation factor in hydrology.hyd. With epco near 1 deeper layers can make up for dry layers above; near 0 they cannot. The second soil layer always compensates fully. Uptake is limited by the water in the layer, and SWAT+ does not reduce uptake as the soil dries below 25% of available water as SWAT 2009 did.

The water stress factor is the ratio of actual to potential transpiration:

\[\gamma_w = \frac{\sum w_{actualup}}{E_t}\]

docs.title: Aeration stress
docs.text:
When the profile contains more water than field capacity, roots lack oxygen. With \(sat_{co} = (SW - FC)/(SAT - FC)\) for the whole profile and \(a\) = aeration in plants.plt,

\[\gamma_a = 1 - \frac{s}{s + \exp(2.9014 - 0.03867\,s)}, \qquad s = 100\,\frac{sat_{co} - a}{1.0001 - a}\]

for \(s > 0\); otherwise \(\gamma_a = 1\).

docs.title: Temperature stress
docs.text:
In SWAT+ 62.0.1 temperature stress is

\[\gamma_t = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\frac{\bar{T} - T_{base}}{T_{opt} - T_{base}}\right), \qquad 0 \le \gamma_t \le 1\]

where \(T_{opt}\) is tmp_opt. The factor is 0 at or below the base temperature, 1 at the optimum, falls again above it, and reaches 0 at \(2\,T_{opt} - T_{base}\). The SWAT 2009 exponential temperature stress and the cold-night rule (no growth when the minimum temperature is 15 °C below the annual mean) are computed first but replaced by this sine function.

docs.title: Demand
docs.text:
The optimal nitrogen fraction of the plant falls as it develops:

\[fr_N = (fr_{N,1} - fr_{N,3})\left[1 - \frac{x}{x + \exp(n_1 - n_2\,x)}\right] + fr_{N,3}\]

where \(fr_{N,1}\), \(fr_{N,2}\) and \(fr_{N,3}\) are frac_n_em, frac_n_50 and frac_n_mat (at emergence, at 50% of maturity and at maturity), \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are fitted to them, and \(x\) is \(fr_{PHU}\) for annuals or the fraction of yrs_mat reached for perennials. The demand is the optimal nitrogen mass, \(fr_N \times\) biomass, minus the nitrogen in the plant, and is limited to four times frac_n_mat times the day's potential growth. Phosphorus follows the same form with frac_p_em, frac_p_50 and frac_p_mat.

docs.title: Uptake
docs.text: Nitrate is taken from the root zone with a depth distribution like water uptake, using n_uptake in parameters.bsn as the distribution parameter; labile phosphorus uses p_uptake. When several plants compete and the soil cannot meet the total demand, each plant gets a share in proportion to its demand.

docs.title: Nitrogen fixation
docs.text:
Legumes (nfix_co > 0 in plants.plt) fix nitrogen when the soil cannot supply their demand. Fixation depends on growth stage, soil water and soil nitrate:

\[N_{fix} = \min\left(6,\; f_{gr}\,\min(1, f_{sw}, f_{no3})\,(N_{dem} - N_{up})\right)\] Factor Value \(f_{gr}\) 0 before 15% of heat units; rises to 1 at 30%; 1 to 55%; falls to 0 at 75% \(f_{sw}\) \(SW/(0.85\,FC)\) for the profile \(f_{no3}\) 1 for profile nitrate up to 100 kg N/ha, falling linearly to 0 at 300 kg N/ha

The result is blended with the unmet demand by the legume coefficient, \(N'_{fix} = \mathrm{nfix\_co}\,N_{fix} + (1 - \mathrm{nfix\_co})(N_{dem} - N_{up})\), and limited to the unmet demand and to n_fix_max in parameters.bsn (kg N/ha/day).

docs.title: Nutrient stress
docs.text:
For non-legumes the nitrogen stress factor is

\[\gamma_n = \frac{\varphi}{\varphi + \exp(3.535 - 0.02597\,\varphi)}, \qquad \varphi = 200\left(\frac{N_{plant}}{N_{opt}} - 0.5\right)\]

which is 0 when the plant contains half its optimal nitrogen and close to 1 at the optimum. It is raised to the ratio of the day's uptake to demand when that is larger. Legumes have no nitrogen stress. Phosphorus stress uses the same form.

docs.title: Harvest index and yield
docs.text:
The harvest index is the fraction of above-ground biomass removed as yield. It grows through the season towards the optimal value harv_idx in plants.plt:

\[HI = \mathrm{harv\_idx}\,\frac{100\,fr_{PHU}}{100\,fr_{PHU} + \exp(11.1 - 10\,fr_{PHU})}\]

After half the heat units are reached, water deficit lowers it. With \(wu = 100\,\sum E_t/\sum PET\) accumulated from that point,

\[HI_{act} = (HI - HI_{min})\frac{wu}{wu + \exp(6.13 - 0.0883\,wu)} + HI_{min}\]

with \(HI_{min}\) = HI/2. The seed (yield) pool of the plant is kept at this fraction of the above-ground biomass as the plant grows. A grain harvest raises the plant's harvest index target to at least harv_idx_ws, but only after the seed pool has been built, so harv_idx_ws does not change the yield of that harvest.

Harvest operations are defined in harv.ops by harv_typ, harv_idx, harv_eff and harv_bm_min. A harvest takes place only when the plant biomass is above harv_bm_min (kg/ha).

harv_typ Yield removed grain, picker harv_eff × seed mass; the rest of the seed goes to the soil's active humus biomass, tree, stripper harv_idx × harv_eff × (seed + leaf + stem) tuber, peanuts Below-ground yield residue A fraction of surface residue, given in the operation

Yield is reduced by any pesticide stress on the plant, and pesticide in the plant is removed with the yield.

docs.title: landuse.lum
docs.text: Each HRU points to a row of landuse.lum, which names the plant community (plnt_com), the management schedule (mgt), the curve number row (cn2), the conservation practice (cons_prac), the urban land type, the overland Manning's n row (ov_mann), and any tile drain, septic system, filter strip, grassed waterway or user BMP.

docs.title: Management schedules
docs.text:
A schedule in management.sch lists operations by date or by heat units, followed by the names of any decision tables that apply to the HRU. Each operation has a type, a month and day, a heat unit value and up to three data columns:

Operation Action plnt Plant one plant or the whole community harv Harvest (see above) kill Kill the plant; biomass goes to residue hvkl Harvest and kill till Tillage, mixing residue and nutrients into the soil (tillage.til) irrm Irrigation by date (irr.ops) fert Fertiliser (fertilizer.frt) manu Manure application pest Pesticide application (chem_app.ops) graz Start grazing (graze.ops) cnup Change the curve number burn Prescribed burn (fire.ops) swep Street sweeping dwm Set drain depth for drainage water management weir Set or change a paddy or wetland weir height irrp, irpm, pudl Rice paddy irrigation and puddling mons Start or end of a monsoon planting window skip Skip to the end of the year

What each operation does to plants and soil, with its equations, is described with its parameters: harvest types and harvest efficiency, grazing, irrigation, burning and street sweeping in *.ops; fertilizer and manure placement in fertilizer.frt; tillage and biological mixing in tillage.til; and automatic irrigation and fertilization by decision table in *.dtl.

An operation with a heat unit value runs when the heat unit fraction passes it: \(fr_{PHU}\) of the plant named in the operation if that plant is growing, or the base-zero heat units otherwise. An operation without a heat unit value runs on its month and day. When all remaining operations of a year share one date, the scheduler moves on after one full pass.

docs.title: Decision tables
docs.text: Decision tables in lum.dtl are conditional rule sets: each table has conditions, alternatives that combine them, and actions that fire when an alternative is true. The tables named in an HRU's schedule are evaluated every day before the other landscape processes, so they can plant, harvest, irrigate, fertilise or change land use in response to weather, soil water or plant growth. See Decision tables.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Three object types put water and loads into the routing network without simulating the land surface that produced them, or change how much of a load reaches the next object:

  • Recall objects release a time series of flow and loads read from a file: measured inflow at a gauge, a wastewater treatment plant, an industrial discharge, or the output of another model. A negative flow represents a diversion.
  • Export coefficient objects release the same daily flow and loads every day of the run.
  • Delivery ratios scale the loads leaving the elements of a routing unit, or the loads passing through a delivery ratio object.

Recall, export coefficient and delivery ratio objects are connected to the network through recall.con, exco.con and delratio.con, like any other spatial object.

docs.title: Input structure
docs.text:
recall.rec (the file named in the recall line of file.cio) lists the recall objects. Each row has an id, a name, a time step code and the name of the data file:

Code Data file content Value used each day 0 sub-daily values the values of the day's time steps 1 daily values the value of the day 2 monthly values the value of the month, on every day of that month 3 annual values the value of the year, on every day of that year 4 none; the file name is the name of an export coefficient record the export coefficient record

Each data file has a title line, a line with the number of years, a column header, and one row per day, month or year: day of year, month, day of month, year, object type, object name, and then the hydrograph values

flo sed orgn sedp no3 solp chla nh3 no2 cbod dox sand silt clay sag lag gravel temp

in m³ for flow, metric tons for sediment and its classes, kg for nutrients, chlorophyll-a, CBOD and oxygen, and °C for temperature. The values are daily amounts, also in monthly and annual files: a monthly value is released on every day of the month, so it must be the daily amount for that month.

Rows before the simulation start year are skipped, and reading stops after the simulation end year.

docs.title: Daily release
docs.text:
On each day inside the period covered by its file, a recall object sends the stored values for that day, month or year to the objects listed in recall.con. Outside that period a daily or monthly recall object releases nothing.

When a daily value has negative flow, the object takes water out of the network (a diversion). Nutrients are then removed in proportion to the diverted volume at the concentration of the source, as are salts and constituents when they are simulated.

docs.title: Salts, constituents and pesticides
docs.text: Salt and constituent loads for recall objects are read from separate salt and constituent recall files (see Salts and constituents). Pesticide loads for recall objects are read from pest.com when that file is present.

docs.title: Recall database
docs.text: recall_db.rec is a separate index that names, for each source, the organic-mineral, pesticide, pathogen, heavy metal, salt and constituent data. Water allocation uses it to set the quality of water from outside sources, treatment plants and water uses, and reservoir release tables use it to find measured releases.

docs.title: Export coefficient objects
docs.text:
exco.exc lists the export coefficient objects. Each row has a name followed by the names of its records in the organic-mineral (exco_om.exc), pesticide, pathogen, heavy metal and salt files. Each row of exco_om.exc has a name followed by the same hydrograph values as a recall file.

The hydrograph of an export coefficient object is set once at the start of the run and released unchanged every day, so the values in exco_om.exc are daily amounts. An export coefficient can also be an element of a routing unit, in which case the routing unit's delivery ratio is applied to it.

docs.title: Routing unit elements
docs.text:
Each element of a routing unit (an HRU, an HRU-lte, a channel or another routing unit) has a delivery ratio named in the dlr column of rout_unit.ele. The ratio multiplies the flow and loads the element contributes to the routing unit outflow.

dlr value Ratio calc or 0 Flow is delivered in full. Sediment and nutrients are multiplied by \(\min\left(1,\;\sqrt{t_{c,elem}/t_{c,ru}}\right)\), the square root of the ratio of the element's time of concentration to the routing unit's, for HRU and HRU-lte elements. For sdc channel and routing unit elements the ratio is 1. Other element types, including legacy channels, take the ratio last calculated for an earlier element (0 if there is none). full or 1 Everything is delivered in full. any other value 0 for every variable, so the element delivers only its recharge. This includes the name of a delratio.del record: the names are looked up before delratio.del is read, so none is found.

The details are on Routing and landscape units.

Pesticide loads from routing unit elements are not scaled by the delivery ratio.

docs.title: Delivery ratio objects
docs.text: A delivery ratio object placed in the routing network multiplies all of its incoming hydrograph by the ratios of its delratio.del record and passes the result on.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SWAT+ has two kinds of water body:

  • Reservoirs are spatial objects in the routing network. They receive water from channels, HRUs, routing units, aquifers or recall objects, store it, and release it by rules written in a decision table. They are defined in reservoir.res, which points to records in hydrology.res, sediment.res, nutrients.res, initial.res and a release table in res_rel.dtl.
  • Wetlands belong to an HRU. They store water on the HRU surface (including rice paddies and other impoundments), receive rain, irrigation and the HRU's runoff, and release water by the same kind of decision table. They are defined in wetland.wet and hydrology.wet and assigned to HRUs through the surf_stor column of hru-data.hru.

Both use the same release, sediment and nutrient calculations.

docs.title: Reservoir water balance
docs.text:
A reservoir starts to operate in the year and month given by yr_op and mon_op in hydrology.res. Before that date, inflow passes through unchanged.

Each day:

  1. Inflow is added to storage. If the reservoir is a point of diversion in the water allocation inputs, withdrawals are taken.
  2. The release table is evaluated and the release computed (see below). The release is smoothed with lag factors.
  3. Rain on the water surface is added, then release, evaporation and seepage are removed, each limited to the water available.
  4. The surface area is updated from the new storage.
\[ V_i = V_{i-1} + V_{in} + V_{pcp} - V_{out} - V_{evap} - V_{seep} \] \[ V_{pcp} = 10\,R\,A, \qquad V_{evap} = 10\,\eta\,E_o\,A, \qquad V_{seep} = 240\,K_{sat}\,A \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(V\) water stored m³ \(R\) precipitation mm \(E_o\) potential evapotranspiration mm \(\eta\) evaporation coefficient - evap_co \(K_{sat}\) hydraulic conductivity of the reservoir bottom mm/h k \(A\) water surface area on the previous day ha

When gwflow is active, seepage is computed by gwflow as exchange with the groundwater cells under the reservoir.

docs.title: Surface area
docs.text:
Surface area is a power function of storage, \(A = \beta_1 V^{\beta_2}\). The coefficients are computed from the areas and volumes at the principal and emergency spillways (area_ps, vol_ps, area_es, vol_es):

\[ \beta_2 = \frac{\log_{10} A_{es} - \log_{10} A_{ps}}{\log_{10} V_{es} - \log_{10} V_{ps}} \;(\le 0.9), \qquad \beta_1 = \left(\frac{A_{es}}{V_{es}}\right)^{\beta_2} \]

If \(\beta_2\) would exceed 0.9, it is set to 0.9 and \(\beta_1 = (A_{ps}/V_{ps})^{0.9}\).

docs.title: Release smoothing
docs.text:
The release from the decision table is blended with the previous day's release so that outflow does not jump:

\[ Q_i = \alpha\,Q^{*} + (1 - \alpha)\,Q_{i-1}, \qquad \alpha = e^{-\lambda} \]

where \(Q^{*}\) is the release from the table and \(\lambda\) is the lag for rising releases or the lag for falling releases. The two lags are read from the last two columns of hydrology.res, which the SWAT+ Editor labels shp_co1 and shp_co2 (formerly area-volume shape coefficients). A lag of 0 gives no smoothing.

docs.title: Release rules
docs.text:
Each reservoir names a release table. Names that begin with ctbl_ refer to a conditions table; all others refer to a decision table in res_rel.dtl. The decision table conditions are evaluated as described in Decision tables, and every action that fires adds a release. Release options (the option of a release action):

Option Release for the day rate constant × 86400 (constant in m³/s) rate_pct constant % of the principal volume inflo_rate larger of (inflow + second constant × 86400) and constant × 86400 inflo_frac constant × inflow ab_emer all storage above the emergency volume days (storage − lower bound) / constant days, where the lower bound is 0, or a fraction (second constant) of the principal or emergency volume dyrt (storage − lower bound) / constant days + second constant % of the principal volume, with the lower bound 0, the principal or the emergency volume dyrt1 as dyrt, with the lower bound taken from a condition of the table inflo_targ inflow + (storage − target), with the target a fraction of the principal volume taken from a condition weir discharge over a weir from weir.res meas measured release from a recall file natlake natural lake outflow, \(k_r\,S_{eff}\,(S_{eff}/(S_{max} - S_0))^{1.5}\) with \(S_0\) a fraction of the principal volume and \(S_{max}\) the principal volume nonirr-h06, irr-h06 Hanasaki et al. (2006) release for non-irrigation and irrigation reservoirs, from the long-term mean monthly inflow and demand hydrop hydropower release: mean inflow scaled by a storage factor and a seasonal factor

docs.title: Reservoir sediment
docs.text:
When the suspended sediment concentration is above the equilibrium concentration nsed, the excess settles:

\[ C_{sed,i} = (C_{sed} - C_{eq})\,e^{-0.184\,d_{50}} + C_{eq} \]

where \(d_{50}\) is the median particle size in sediment.res (µm). Sediment leaves with the release at the settled concentration. When the concentration is at or below nsed, no sediment is released.

docs.title: Reservoir nutrients
docs.text:
Organic N, particulate P, soluble N (nitrate, ammonium, nitrite) and soluble P are removed by settling. The fraction removed each day is

\[ f = \min\left(1,\;(C - C_{min})\,r\,\theta^{\,T - 20}\right) \] Symbol Meaning Input \(C\) concentration of the pool mg/L \(C_{min}\) minimum concentration for settling n_min_stl, p_min_stl \(r\) settling rate; for organic N and particulate P it differs between the mid-year period (mid_start to mid_end months) and the rest of the year; soluble N and P have one rate each mid_n_stl, n_stl, mid_p_stl, p_stl; positions 8 and 9 for soluble N and P \(\theta\) temperature factor theta_n, theta_p \(T\) air temperature °C

For soluble N and P the fraction is multiplied by 0.2. After settling, the release takes nutrients in proportion to its share of the water.

Pesticides, salts and constituents in reservoirs are described on the Pesticides and Salts and constituents pages.

docs.title: Wetlands and paddies
docs.text:
A wetland covers part of its HRU and stores water on the surface. Its principal and emergency volumes are the HRU area times the depths dp_ps and dp_es in hydrology.wet. When a weir is assigned in weir.res, the principal volume is the HRU area times the weir height, and the emergency volume is at least 1.2 times that.

Each day:

  1. Rain and irrigation are added to the wetland.
  2. The wetted area is updated from storage with the volume-depth coefficients of hydrology.wet. Rice paddies are treated as flat and cover the whole HRU.
  3. Seepage into the soil is \(24\,K_{sat}\,A\), with \(K_{sat}\) the k of hydrology.wet (or the conductivity set by a puddling operation). Seepage that the soil cannot take because it is saturated stays in the wetland. Nutrients move into the top soil layer with the seepage.
  4. Release follows the decision table, or the weir equation for paddies, and becomes surface runoff of the HRU.
  5. Sediment, nutrients, salts and constituents are updated as for reservoirs.

Evaporation from standing water is taken from the wetland first, as part of the HRU soil evaporation, before any water is taken from the soil.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SWAT+ can simulate two optional groups of dissolved substances, both listed in constituents.cs:

  • Salt ions: the eight major ions sulfate (SO₄), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg), sodium (Na), potassium (K), chloride (Cl), carbonate (CO₃) and bicarbonate (HCO₃). In soil and aquifers they take part in mineral precipitation and dissolution and in cation exchange, and soil salinity can reduce plant growth.
  • Constituents: selenate (SeO₄), selenite (SeO₃) and boron. Selenium species react in the soil (reduction, release from shale), and all three sorb to soil.

Both groups move with water along the same paths as nitrate: surface runoff, lateral flow, tile flow and percolation in the soil profile, then through aquifers, channels, reservoirs and wetlands. Inputs come from initial conditions, rain and dry deposition, fertiliser, irrigation, urban runoff and, for salts, road salt.

docs.title: Transport in soil water
docs.text:
Salt ions and constituents are transported in each layer with the nitrate leaching equations, including anion exclusion. For each ion or constituent \(m\) in a layer:

\[ C_m = \frac{M_m}{w}\left[1 - \exp\!\left(\frac{-w}{(1 - \theta_e)\,SAT}\right)\right] \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(C_m\) concentration in water leaving the layer kg/ha per mm \(M_m\) mass in the layer kg/ha \(w\) percolation plus lateral flow, plus surface runoff for the top layer and tile flow for the drained layer mm \(\theta_e\) fraction of porosity from which anions are excluded fraction anion_excl in soils.sol \(SAT\) water content at saturation mm

Percolation, tile flow and lateral flow below the top layer remove mass at concentration \(C_m\). Surface runoff and lateral flow from the top layer remove mass at \(\beta_N C_m\), where \(\beta_N\) is the nitrate percolation coefficient n_perc in parameters.bsn (adjusted per HRU by calibration). Percolation moves mass to the next layer and out of the bottom of the profile to the aquifer. When gwflow is active with solute transport, groundwater discharging into the soil profile also adds mass.

docs.title: Salt chemistry
docs.text:
In each soil layer and in each aquifer, the dissolved ions are brought into equilibrium with five minerals and with the exchange sites of the soil:

  • Precipitation and dissolution of calcite (CaCO₃), magnesite (MgCO₃), gypsum (CaSO₄), epsomite (MgSO₄) and halite (NaCl). A mineral dissolves when the ion activity product is below its solubility product and precipitates when above it.
  • Activity coefficients from the ionic strength \(I\) of the solution: the extended Debye-Hückel equation for \(I \le 0.1\) mol/L and the Davies equation above. For \(I \ge 5\) mol/L the Davies equation is evaluated at \(I = 0.5\).
  • Cation exchange among Ca, Mg, Na and K.

The calculation iterates until concentrations converge. The solubility products are fixed in the code:

Mineral Solubility product CaCO₃ 3.0702 × 10⁻⁹ MgCO₃ 4.7937 × 10⁻⁶ CaSO₄ 7.888 × 10⁻⁵ MgSO₄ 7.244 × 10⁻³ NaCl 37.3

docs.title: Salinity stress on plants
docs.text:
When the stress option in salt_plants is on and salts are simulated, each rooted soil layer gets a reduction factor from the FAO crop salt tolerance relation:

\[ f_{salt} = \begin{cases} 1 & EC_e \le a \\ \dfrac{100 - b\,(EC_e - a)}{100} & EC_e > a \end{cases}, \qquad 0 \le f_{salt} \le 1 \] \[ EC_e = \frac{TDS}{k_{EC}} \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(EC_e\) electrical conductivity of the soil water dS/m \(TDS\) sum of the salt ion concentrations in the soil water, scaled by water content mg/L \(k_{EC}\) TDS to EC conversion factor (mg/L)/(dS/m) salt_plants \(a\) salinity threshold of the plant dS/m salt_plants, per plant \(b\) yield loss per dS/m above the threshold %/(dS/m) salt_plants, per plant

For gypsiferous soils (soil type 1 in salt_plants) the threshold is raised by 2 dS/m. A plant with \(a = 0\) has no salt stress. The smallest factor over the rooted layers is the plant's salt stress.

Salt stress reduces daily biomass growth. With the "after other stresses" option (salt_effect = 1), growth is multiplied by the salt stress after taking the smallest of the water, temperature, nitrogen, phosphorus and aeration stresses. With option 2, salt stress is included in that minimum.

docs.title: Salt uptake by plants
docs.text: If the file salt_uptake is present, each ion is removed from the soil in the amounts it specifies (kg/ha per day), distributed over the layers in proportion to root mass. The first plant of the HRU's plant community is used. Without the file, plants take up no salt.

docs.title: Selenium reactions
docs.text:
Selenate, selenite and nitrate in each soil layer are solved together each day (fourth-order Runge-Kutta, one-day step). The processes are:

  • reduction of selenate to selenite and of selenite to elemental selenium, both first order and slowed by nitrate through the inhibition term \(I/(I + C_{NO3})\);
  • oxidation of selenium-bearing shale by oxygen and by nitrate, which releases selenate and consumes nitrate, in proportion to the shale fraction of the soil.

Rate constants, the inhibition constant, oxygen content and shale fractions are given per soil group in cs_reactions. Boron does not react.

docs.title: Sorption of constituents
docs.text:
Selenate, selenite and boron are split between soil water and the soil matrix with a linear partition coefficient:

\[ M_{sol} = \frac{M_{tot}}{1 + \dfrac{K_d\,\rho_b\,V_{soil}}{V_w}}, \qquad M_{sorb} = M_{tot} - M_{sol} \] Symbol Meaning Units Input \(M_{tot}\), \(M_{sol}\), \(M_{sorb}\) total, dissolved and sorbed mass in the layer kg \(K_d\) partition coefficient for each constituent L/kg cs_reactions \(\rho_b\) bulk density Mg/m³ \(V_{soil}\), \(V_w\) volumes of soil and of soil water in the layer m³

Aquifers use the same reaction and sorption equations with the aquifer parameters in cs_reactions.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Source File Initial soil and aquifer content salt_hru.ini, salt_aqu.ini, cs_hru.ini, cs_aqu.ini; channels: salt_channel.ini, cs_channel.ini Rain and dry deposition salt_atmo.cli Fertiliser salt_fertilizer.frt, fertilizer.frt_cs Irrigation water salt_irrigation, cs_irrigation Urban runoff salt_urban, cs_urban Road salt (monthly, daily or annual amounts added to the top layer) salt_road Plant tolerance and stress options salt_plants Plant uptake salt_uptake, cs_uptake Reaction and sorption parameters cs_reactions Point sources recall files (see Recall and point sources)

docs.title: Aquifers, channels and water bodies
docs.text: In the 1D aquifer, recharge adds salt and constituent mass; the salt chemistry, constituent reactions and sorption are applied; and baseflow and seepage remove mass at the concentration of the aquifer water (mass divided by groundwater volume). Channels, reservoirs and wetlands mix incoming mass with the stored water and release it with outflow. With gwflow, salts and constituents are transported between grid cells.

docs.title: Pathogens and heavy metals
docs.text:
constituents.cs can also list pathogens and heavy metals.

Pathogens (bacteria and other microorganisms) are followed on foliage and in the top soil layer. Each day their number changes by first-order die-off minus growth, corrected for temperature:

\[N_d = N_{d-1}\,\exp\!\left(-(k_{die} - k_{grow})\,\theta^{\,T - 20}\right)\]

with the rates of pathogens.pth for foliage or soil, \(\theta\) = t_adj and \(T\) the mean air temperature. Rain of at least 2.54 mm washes a fraction of the pathogens on foliage to the soil; pathogens then leave the top layer with percolation, surface runoff and sediment. In channels they die off over the travel time at do_stream, corrected to the water temperature. The pathogen routines of 62.0.1 do not form a complete model: the HRU routines use one pathogens.pth row for all pathogens, the runoff step removes all pathogens left in the top layer every day, and the channel die-off does not act on the routed water. pathogens.pth lists these points.

Heavy metals are not transformed. They enter the network only from export coefficient and delivery ratio objects and move with the water as conservative loads (see metals and Recall and point sources).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The soil profile is the main water store of an HRU. Water that infiltrates is stored in the soil layers, taken up by plants, evaporated from the soil surface, or moved down and sideways as described in Hydrology.

docs.title: Soil layers
docs.text:
Each HRU uses one soil from soils.sol. The soil can have any number of layers, each defined by the depth to its bottom (dp) and its physical properties.

If the first layer of the soil is deeper than 19.5 mm, SWAT+ adds a 10 mm surface layer with the properties of the first layer, so most HRUs have one more layer than the soil in soils.sol. The thin surface layer is used for soil evaporation, surface nutrient processes and erosion. When a file named soil_lyr_depths.sol is present in the project folder, SWAT+ instead rebuilds the layers of every soil at the depths listed in it, with a 10 mm surface layer on top. HRUs with an active septic system get extra layer boundaries at the top and bottom of the septic biozone.

Missing or out-of-range layer properties are replaced when the soil is read:

Property Replacement Bulk density bd 1.3 Mg/m³ when zero; at most 2.0 Mg/m³ Available water capacity awc 0.005 mm/mm when zero; at most 0.8 mm/mm Saturated conductivity soil_k When zero: 50, 20, 5 or 2 mm/hr for hydrologic group (hyd_grp) A, B, C or D, 10 mm/hr otherwise Rock fragments rock at most 98% Soil albedo alb at least 0.1 Calcium carbonate caco3 and ph 2.8% and 6.5 when zero Anion exclusion anion_excl 0.5 when zero; at most 0.99

docs.title: Water retention
docs.text:
SWAT+ stores soil water as the depth of water above the wilting point. The volumetric water contents of each layer are

\[\theta_{wp} = 0.40\,\frac{m_c\,\rho_b}{100}, \qquad \theta_{fc} = \theta_{wp} + AWC, \qquad \phi = 1 - \frac{\rho_b}{2.65}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(\theta_{wp}\) Water content at wilting point (−1.5 MPa) mm/mm \(\theta_{fc}\) Water content at field capacity (−0.033 MPa) mm/mm \(\phi\) Porosity mm/mm \(m_c\) Clay content, clay in soils.sol % \(\rho_b\) Moist bulk density, bd in soils.sol Mg/m³ \(AWC\) Available water capacity, awc in soils.sol mm/mm

If field capacity reaches the porosity, it is set to \(\phi - 0.05\) and the wilting point is moved down with it. The water a layer can store above wilting point is then

\[FC_{ly} = (\theta_{fc} - \theta_{wp})\,depth_{ly}, \qquad SAT_{ly} = (\phi - \theta_{wp})\,depth_{ly}\]

where \(depth_{ly}\) is the layer thickness in mm. \(FC_{ly}\) is the water that plants can use, and the difference \(SAT_{ly} - FC_{ly}\) is the drainable water that can percolate or flow laterally.

docs.title: Initial soil water
docs.text:
Each layer starts the run with the same fraction of its field capacity water. The fraction is sw_init in parameters.bsn. When sw_init is zero, SWAT+ estimates it from the average annual precipitation of the HRU's weather generator station:

\[f_{init} = \frac{P_{an}}{P_{an} + \exp(9.043 - 0.002135\,P_{an})}\]

with \(P_{an}\) in mm. Dry climates start near zero and wet climates near field capacity. The water content then adjusts during the warm-up years skipped in print.prt.

docs.title: Actual evapotranspiration
docs.text: Evapotranspiration covers every process that turns liquid or solid water at or near the land surface into water vapour: evaporation from the canopy, transpiration, sublimation and evaporation from the soil and from ponded water. SWAT+ starts from the HRU's potential evapotranspiration (PET, see Climate and weather) and removes water in this order.

docs.title: Canopy evaporation
docs.text: Water stored on the canopy (see Hydrology) evaporates first. If PET is smaller than the canopy store, the canopy loses PET and there is no transpiration or soil evaporation that day. Otherwise the canopy is emptied and the remaining demand is \(E'_0 = PET - E_{can}\).

docs.title: Transpiration and soil evaporation demand
docs.text:
The maximum transpiration on the day depends on the leaf area of the plant community:

\[E_t = \frac{E'_0\,LAI}{3} \quad\text{for } LAI \le 3, \qquad E_t = E'_0 \quad\text{for } LAI > 3\]

The soil evaporation demand is reduced by shading from plants and residue:

\[E_s = E'_0\,cov_{sol}, \qquad cov_{sol} = \exp(-5.0\times10^{-5}\,CV)\]

where \(CV\) is the above-ground biomass plus surface residue (kg/ha). When the snowpack contains 0.5 mm of water or more, \(cov_{sol}\) is 0.5. If \(E_t + E_s\) is larger than the demand, \(E_s\) is reduced so that the two together do not exceed it. The transpiration demand is met by plant water uptake (see Plant growth and land use management).

The same leaf area rule sets the transpiration demand for all three PET methods. SWAT+ 62.0.1 does not use the crop transpiration computed by the Penman-Monteith method.

docs.title: Sublimation and ponded water
docs.text:
On days with a mean air temperature above 0 °C, the soil evaporation demand is taken first from the snowpack as sublimation. On HRUs with ponded water (wetlands and paddies), the evaporation demand is

\[E_s = \mathrm{evap}\left(1 - \frac{LAI}{4}\right)E'_0 \quad\text{for } LAI \le 4, \qquad E_s = 0 \text{ otherwise}\]

where evap is the evaporation coefficient in hydrology.wet. It is taken from the ponded water, and the soil itself does not evaporate while ponded water remains.

docs.title: Soil evaporation by layer
docs.text:
The remaining demand is distributed with depth. The demand down to depth \(z\) is

\[E_{soil,z} = E''_s\,\frac{z}{z + \exp(2.374 - 0.00713\,z)}\]

where \(E''_s\) is the remaining demand and \(z\) is in mm. Half of the demand comes from the top 10 mm and 95% from the top 100 mm. The demand on a layer with its top at \(z_u\) and bottom at \(z_l\) is

\[E_{soil,ly} = E_{soil,z_l} - E_{soil,z_u}\,(1 - \mathrm{esco})\] Symbol Meaning Input \(\mathrm{esco}\) Soil evaporation compensation factor esco in hydrology.hyd, 0 to 1

With esco = 0 each layer meets only its share of the demand. As esco increases, deeper layers can make up for demand that the layers above could not meet, so more water can be evaporated from lower in the profile. This direction is the opposite of SWAT 2009, where lowering esco allowed more compensation.

When a layer is drier than field capacity its demand is reduced:

\[E'_{soil,ly} = E_{soil,ly}\,\exp\left(\frac{2.5\,(SW_{ly} - FC_{ly})}{FC_{ly}}\right)\]

and a layer never gives up more than 80% of its plant-available water on one day. Only layers whose top is shallower than 500 mm evaporate. As water evaporates from the second layer, a small amount of nitrate moves up with it into the surface layer.

docs.title: Soil temperature
docs.text: Soil temperature affects water movement and the rate of residue decomposition and nutrient transformations. SWAT+ computes the temperature at the centre of each layer every day from the soil surface temperature, the annual average air temperature and a damping depth.

docs.title: Damping depth
docs.text:
The maximum damping depth depends on the average bulk density of the profile, \(\rho_b\):

\[dd_{max} = 1000 + \frac{2500\,\rho_b}{\rho_b + 686\,\exp(-5.63\,\rho_b)}\]

The damping depth on a day is scaled by the soil water content:

\[dd = dd_{max}\,\exp\left[\ln\left(\frac{500}{dd_{max}}\right)\left(\frac{1 - wc}{1 + wc}\right)^2\right], \qquad wc = \frac{SW}{(0.356 - 0.144\,\rho_b)\,z_{tot}}\]

where \(SW\) is the profile water content (mm) and \(z_{tot}\) the profile depth (mm).

docs.title: Surface temperature
docs.text:
The temperature of a bare soil surface is

\[T_{bare} = \bar{T} + \frac{T_{max} - T_{min}}{2}\cdot\frac{H_{day}(1 - \alpha) - 14}{20}\]

where \(H_{day}\) is the solar radiation and \(\alpha\) the albedo of the day. Biomass, residue and snow insulate the surface. The cover weighting factor is

\[bcv = \max\left(\frac{CV}{CV + \exp(7.563 - 1.297\times10^{-4}\,CV)},\; \frac{SNO}{SNO + \exp(6.055 - 0.3002\,SNO)}\right)\]

with \(CV\) the above-ground biomass and residue (kg/ha) and \(SNO\) the snow water content (mm); the snow term is 1 above 120 mm. The surface temperature is

\[T_{srf} = \frac{1}{2}\left[T_{bare} + bcv\,T_{ly2} + (1 - bcv)\,T_{bare}\right]\]

where \(T_{ly2}\) is the previous day's temperature of the second soil layer.

docs.title: Layer temperature
docs.text:
\[T_{ly} = \ell\,T_{ly,prev} + (1 - \ell)\left[df\,(\bar{T}_{AA} - T_{srf}) + T_{srf}\right]\] \[df = \frac{zd}{zd + \exp(-0.8669 - 2.0775\,zd)}, \qquad zd = \frac{z_{mid}}{dd}\] Symbol Meaning Units \(\ell\) Lag coefficient, 0.8 - \(T_{ly,prev}\) Layer temperature on the previous day °C \(\bar{T}_{AA}\) Average annual air temperature of the weather generator station °C \(z_{mid}\) Depth to the centre of the layer mm

Layers start the run at the average December maximum temperature of the weather generator station. In septic HRUs, layers at and below the biozone are kept from falling far below 10 °C.

docs.title: Output reference
docs.text:
SWAT+ writes text files with results for each object type (HRU, landscape unit, channel, aquifer, reservoir and so on) and for the basin as a whole, by day, month, year and as an average over the simulation. Which files are written is set in print.prt: each row names a group of outputs and has a y or n for the daily, monthly, yearly and average annual files. A few files are written in every run.

The files go to the output folder named in file.cio, or to the run folder when none is named. Every run also writes files_out.out, a list of the output files it opened, which is the quickest way to see what a given print.prt produced.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page Content Naming convention How files are named and laid out, print timing, and the print.prt row behind every file. Water balance hru_wb, hru-lte_wb, lsunit_wb and basin_wb: precipitation, evapotranspiration, runoff, percolation, soil water and snow. Channel, sediment, nutrient channel_sd, channel_sdmorph, sd_chanbud, the sediment budget files ch_sedbud, chanbud_order and sedbud, their basin sums, and the legacy channel files. Hydrographs hydout, hydin, deposition and ru: water and loads passed between objects, and the hydcon.out connection list. Recall recall and basin_psc: loads released by point sources, inlets and diversions. Nutrient balance and losses hru_nb, hru_ls, lsunit_nb, lsunit_ls, basin_nb, basin_ls and hru-lte_ls: nitrogen and phosphorus balances and the sediment and nutrient losses from the landscape. Aquifer, reservoir, plant aquifer, reservoir, wetland, crop yields and the plant and weather (_pw) files. Carbon Soil, residue and plant carbon files. gwflow Outputs of the gridded groundwater module. Checker and diagnostics Files written in every run: checker.out, diagnostics.out, files_out.out and others. Post-processing The Python scripts in the test folder of the SWAT+ source.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This page covers four groups of output files:

  • aquifer storage and fluxes (aquifer_*.txt, basin_aqu_*.txt)
  • reservoir storage and fluxes (reservoir_*.txt, basin_res_*.txt)
  • crop yields (crop_yld_*.txt, basin_crop_yld_*.txt)
  • plant growth, stress and weather (hru_pw_*.txt, hru-lte_pw_*.txt, lsunit_pw_*.txt, basin_pw_*.txt)

Each file is switched on in print.prt. The suffix gives the print interval: _day, _mon, _yr or _aa (average annual). When csvout is y, a .csv copy with the same columns is written beside each .txt file. The first seven columns of every file except the crop yield files are jday, mon, day, yr, unit, gis_id and name; see Naming convention.

docs.title: Files and switches
docs.text:
File print.prt row Scope aquifer_day.txt, aquifer_mon.txt, aquifer_yr.txt, aquifer_aa.txt aquifer one row per aquifer per interval basin_aqu_day.txt, basin_aqu_mon.txt, basin_aqu_yr.txt, basin_aqu_aa.txt basin_aqu one row per interval for the whole basin

The aquifer files report the one-dimensional aquifers defined in aquifer.aqu and are opened only when the model has such aquifers. When the gwflow module replaces the aquifers, use the gwflow outputs instead.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
Line 1 is the project name and version, line 2 the column header and line 3 the units. After the seven leading columns come 17 value columns:

# Column Units Description 1 flo mm return flow leaving the aquifer 2 dep_wt m depth from the ground surface to the water table 3 stor mm water stored in the aquifer 4 rchrg mm recharge entering the aquifer from other objects 5 seep mm deep seepage from the bottom of the aquifer 6 revap mm water removed by plant uptake and evaporation (revap) 7 no3_st kg N/ha nitrate-N stored in the aquifer 8 minp kg P mineral P sent out with the return flow (see the notes) 9 orgn (header) % organic carbon content of the aquifer (see the notes) 10 orgp (header) kg N/ha organic N in the aquifer (see the notes) 11 no3_rchg kg N/ha nitrate-N entering with recharge; rchrgn in earlier documentation 12 no3_loss kg N/ha nitrate-N lost in the aquifer (decay); nloss in earlier documentation 13 no3_lat kg N/ha nitrate-N leaving with the return flow; no3gw in earlier documentation 14 no3_seep kg N/ha nitrate-N leaving with deep seepage; seepno3 in earlier documentation 15 flo_cha mm part of flo routed to channels 16 flo_res mm part of flo routed to reservoirs 17 flo_ls mm part of flo routed to other aquifers

Notes on individual columns:

  • Columns 9 and 10 are mislabelled. The header says orgn (kg/ha_N) and orgp (kg/ha_P), but column 9 is the organic carbon content from the carbon column of aquifer.aqu, constant through the run, and column 10 is organic N, which 62.0.1 never updates, so it stays zero.
  • minp is the mineral P concentration from the sol_p column of aquifer.aqu multiplied by the day's recharge volume. The value is a mass in kg for the whole aquifer; the units line gives kg/ha_P. It is computed from the recharge volume and leaves the aquifer with the return flow.
  • flo_cha, flo_res and flo_ls split flo by the outflow fractions in the aquifer's connection file. Only outflows of type tot are counted, so the three columns add up to flo only when every outflow is of that type.

docs.title: Aggregation
docs.text:
Fluxes are summed over the interval. Three state columns are averaged instead: the monthly file divides stor, dep_wt and no3_st by the number of days in the month, and the yearly file divides the sum of the monthly averages by 12. The average annual file divides the yearly values by the number of printed years. Column 9 is never summed: every interval reports the starting value.

The basin file is the area-weighted average of all aquifers, each weighted by its share of the basin area.

docs.title: Example header
docs.text:
basin_aqu_yr.txt from the Ames_sub1 reference dataset run with 62.0.1:

   jday   mon   day    yr   unit  gis_id  name                       flo          dep_wt            stor          rchrg           seep          revap         no3_st           minp           orgn           orgp       no3_rchg       no3_loss        no3_lat       no3_seep        flo_cha        flo_res         flo_ls
                                                                       mm              m              mm             mm             mm             mm        kg/ha_N        kg/ha_P        kg/ha_N        kg/ha_P        kg/ha_N        kg/ha_N        kg/ha_N        kg/ha_N             mm             mm             mm

docs.title: Files and switches
docs.text:
File print.prt row Scope reservoir_day.txt, reservoir_mon.txt, reservoir_yr.txt, reservoir_aa.txt reservoir one row per reservoir per interval basin_res_day.txt, basin_res_mon.txt, basin_res_yr.txt, basin_res_aa.txt basin_res all reservoirs added together

The reservoir files are opened only when the model has reservoirs.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
After the seven leading columns come four blocks: 4 water body columns, then 18 storage, 18 inflow and 18 outflow columns.

Block Columns Units Water body area, precip, evap, seep ha, m³, m³, m³ Storage at the end of the interval flo_stor, sed_stor, orgn_stor, sedp_stor, no3_stor, solp_stor, chla_stor, nh3_stor, no2_stor, cbod_stor, dox_stor, san_stor, sil_stor, cla_stor, sag_stor, lag_stor, grv_stor, null see below Inflow during the interval the same 18 names ending in _in see below Outflow during the interval the same 18 names ending in _out see below

Units of the 18 constituent columns, which repeat in the storage, inflow and outflow blocks:

Constituent Units Description flo m³ water volume sed t sediment orgn kg N organic N sedp kg P organic (sediment-attached) P no3 kg N nitrate-N solp kg P soluble mineral P chla kg chlorophyll-a nh3 kg N ammonium-N no2 kg N nitrite-N cbod kg carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand dox kg dissolved oxygen san, sil, cla, sag, lag, grv t sand, silt, clay, small aggregates, large aggregates and gravel null °C water temperature (the header gives null and no unit)

The inflow columns are flo_in, sed_in, orgn_in, sedp_in, no3_in, solp_in, chla_in, nh3_in, no2_in, cbod_in, dox_in, san_in, sil_in, cla_in, sag_in, lag_in, grv_in and null. The outflow columns are flo_out, sed_out, orgn_out, sedp_out, no3_out, solp_out, chla_out, nh3_out, no2_out, cbod_out, dox_out, san_out, sil_out, cla_out, sag_out, lag_out, grv_out and null (the last column of each block is headed null).

Inflow and outflow are volumes and masses for the interval, in m³, t and kg. The storage block is the reservoir content when the line is written, so in the monthly, yearly and average annual files it is the storage on the last day of the interval.

docs.title: Aggregation
docs.text:
Inflow, outflow, precipitation, evaporation and seepage are summed over the interval, and the average annual file divides the totals by the number of printed years. The surface area is averaged over the days of the month, and the yearly value is the average of the monthly values.

reservoir_mon.csv has one extra line after the units line, RES reservoir_mon.csv, which the other reservoir files do not have.

docs.title: Files and switches
docs.text:
The crop_yld column of print.prt controls all crop yield files: y gives yearly files, a average annual files, b both, and n none.

File Written when crop_yld is Content crop_yld_aa.txt a or b one row per HRU and plant at the end of the run crop_yld_yr.txt y or b header lines only (see below) basin_crop_yld_yr.txt y or b one row per plant per year for the whole basin basin_crop_yld_aa.txt y or b one row per plant at the end of the run

With crop_yld = a, only crop_yld_aa.txt is produced; the basin files need y or b. In 62.0.1 no data rows are written to crop_yld_yr.txt (or its .csv). For yearly yields use basin_crop_yld_yr.txt, or yield.out (switched on by mgtout) for every harvest.

docs.title: HRU columns
docs.text:
crop_yld_aa.txt has a title line, a line --YIELD (kg/ha)--, the column header, and one row per plant in each HRU:

# Column Units Description 1 jday - day of year of the last simulated day 2 mon - month 3 day - day of month 4 yr - year 5 unit - HRU number 6 PLANTNM - plant name from plants.plt 7 MASS kg/ha dry mass of the harvested yield 8 C kg/ha carbon in the yield 9 N kg/ha nitrogen in the yield 10 P kg/ha phosphorus in the yield

The values are the total yield over the whole run divided by the number of harvests of that plant, that is, the average yield per harvest. A plant that was never harvested reports zero. The .csv header lists a single yield column, while each data row contains the four values MASS, C, N and P.

docs.title: Basin columns
docs.text:
# Column Units Description 1 year - calendar year (the last year in the _aa file) 2 plant_no - plant number in the basin plant list 3 plant_name - plant name 4 harv_area(ha) ha area harvested; an HRU harvested twice in a year counts twice 5 yld(t) t total dry yield 6 yld(t/ha) t/ha yld(t) divided by harv_area(ha)

The yearly file skips the years before nyskip. In the average annual file, area and yield are divided by the number of printed years, and yld(t/ha) is total yield divided by total harvested area.

docs.text:

docs.title: Files and switches
docs.text:
File print.prt row Scope hru_pw_day.txt to hru_pw_aa.txt hru_pw one row per HRU hru-lte_pw_day.txt to hru-lte_pw_aa.txt hru-lte_pw one row per HRU-lte lsunit_pw_day.txt to lsunit_pw_aa.txt lsunit_pw one row per landscape unit basin_pw_day.txt to basin_pw_aa.txt basin_pw whole basin

All use the columns below. The HRU files add plant_cov and mgt_ops at the end of each row: the plant community and the management schedule of the HRU's land use.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
# Column Units Description 1 lai m²/m² leaf area index 2 bioms kg/ha total plant biomass 3 yield kg/ha harvested yield (dry mass) 4 residue kg/ha surface residue 5 sol_tmp °C temperature of soil layer 2 6 strsw days water (drought) stress days 7 strsa days aeration (excess water) stress days 8 strstmp days temperature stress days 9 strsn days nitrogen stress days 10 strsp days phosphorus stress days 11 strss days salinity stress days 12 nplt kg N/ha nitrogen in the plant biomass 13 percn kg N/ha nitrate-N leached below the soil profile 14 pplnt kg P/ha phosphorus in the plant biomass 15 tmx °C maximum air temperature 16 tmn °C minimum air temperature 17 tmpav °C mean air temperature 18 solarad MJ/m² solar radiation 19 wndspd m/s wind speed 20 rhum fraction relative humidity 21 phubas0 °C accumulated base-zero heat units 22 lai_max m²/m² maximum leaf area index (always 0 in 62.0.1) 23 bm_max kg/ha maximum total biomass during the interval 24 bm_grow kg/ha biomass growth 25 c_gro kg C/ha plant carbon growth

The units line writes kgha for columns 2 to 4 and 12 to 14 and ---- for the stress columns.

docs.title: Aggregation
docs.text:
Columns Monthly Yearly Average annual yield, stress days, percn sum sum yearly sum averaged over the printed years nplt, pplnt plant N and P at the end of the month at the end of the year at the end of the run bm_max maximum in the month maximum in the year maximum in the run all other columns daily average daily average daily average

nplt and pplnt are the N and P contents of the standing plants. They do not report uptake during the interval. After a harvest or kill they drop to zero, so yearly and average annual values are often zero for annual crops.

docs.text:

  • aquifer.aqu and reservoir.res: the objects reported here.

Sources
